AN SWIM, A LLEG RO. When the rooks wiihin thoern - 'Gin to tmild their windy realm, While the botrhs still etch the sky-iiiie sharp and dark;

When a faint green filrny mist, Pale eu palest amethyst, Weaves a fine web o'er the beech's rugged bark; Then I know. ah, then I know, When the melting of the snow Every mountain brook is tilling, And a vague new life is thrilling Underneath the budding hedges, And the yellow river sedges; That the Spring is coming, coming back again, That the Spring is coming, coming to her English home again. When across the April rain , As it whips the shivering plain, There are tearful gleams of sunshine bright and sweet; When a wind comes from the south. With warm kisses on its Month, And the east wind and the west wind seem to meet; Then I know, ah. then I know, •-• When I hear the west wind blew„ .1 4nd the routh wind in'it3 coming 'Makes a rythmical low humming, _ i That the Spring is corning, coming back again, That the Spring is coming, coming to her Northern home again.
When the cuckoo, lucky rover. Makes his magic passage over Viewless patnwavi from the citron groves of Spain, And his song goes calling, calling, Where the forest brooks are falling,

And the valleys love the echo to retain; Then I know, ah, then I know, ' When the bird to birds a foe Mourns his own unfriencled lot - To the winds that heed him not, ; That the Spring is coming, coming hack again, That the Spring is coming, coming to her English home aaain • • Then at last, one April dawn, r High above the glimmering lawn. While the first faint fires are scattering the dark; Lo, I hear a buoyant note On the dewy: dusk afloat, And I catch the first fine preludes of the lark; Then I know, ah, then I know, . When I hear that glad song flow, That the sweet of all the year In a little will be here, And the Spring is coming, coming back again, And the Spring is coming, toming to her Northern home again, - To the weary hearts that wait her in her English home
aaain. —Good Words.
ROBERT RICHARDSON.

I want somebody I can play with." ,There is certainly a very fine distinction here. A New York urchin unconsciously perpetrated a great' joke at the expense of his teacher. The lady was announcing to her pupils the holiday of February 22, and asking them some questions concerning its observance, among others, why the birthday of Washington should be celebrated more than that of anyone else. "Why," she added, "more than mine? You may tell me," she said to a little fellow eager to explain. "Becau-e," he exclaimed with great vivacity, "because he never told a lie." KTSSING DAY.—It was customary for the Indiana, long I before they became Christians, to bave a great feast at the beginning of the New Year. In the :old times the principal article of food at these horrid feasts was dogs, the eating of which was accompanied by many revolting ceremonies. The missionaries, instead of abolishing the feast, turned it into a religious festival. I carried out the msthods of my worthy predecessors at Norway House, and so we had a feast every New Year's Day. The Cress call this day a Onche-me-eou Kesigow," which literally means "the kissing day." as on this day the men claim the right to kiss every woman they meet: and, strange to say, every woman expects to be kissed. It used to amuse me very much to see thirty or forty Indians, dressed up in their finest apparel, come quietly I marching into the Mission House and gravelynciss Mrs. Young on her cheek. When I used to rally her over this strange phase of unexpected missionary experience she would laughingly retort, "Oh, you need not laugh at me. See that crowd of women out there in the yard, expecting you to go out and kiss thorn r It was stir- prising how much work that day kept me shut up in my study; or if that expedient would not avail, I used to select, a dear old sweet-faced, white-haired grandma, the mother of the chief, and say, "Now I am 'going to kiss grandma; and as I kiss her you must all consider yourselves kissed.—Among the Cree and Salteaux Indfans Fge..ton. R. Young. A Movasei's Filli.isros.—" You know that we are not allowed to consult our own feelings. We are servants of the State," said the Queen or Italy to a visitor. A strik- ing illustration of this subj,ction of Royal wnnen in the State was given when Orsini attempted to iesassinate the Emperor and Empress of France by exploding bombs eneath their carriage. The explosion, which l'ook place just as the Env eror's carriage drew up at the Opera Donse, wounded several soldiers of the escort and killed one of the horses. The Emperor was not harmed, and the Empress escaped with a slight cut in one of her -c.beeks by a piece of br,ken glass. She retained her -dimness, and, having entered the theatre, smiled her -thanks from thet Royal box to the audience, who had greeted their majesties on their entrance with the wildest -enthusiasm. 'Yet a horrible anxiety was torturing the mother's heart, for she feared that the life of heitchild.,at the Tuileries, might be threatened by the conapirators. She forced herself, nevertheless, to sit with a forced smile on her lips, until an attendant had returned from the palace with the news that the Prince was safe, and that, no attempt had been made to kill him. Tie mother would have flown to him, but the Ern/ tow had to • remain at the opera till midnight. The attemp failed, because the conspirators so over-loaded the bombs, that in exploding they were pulverised into powder. The ' Emperor's baton being held up to the light, was seen to be pierced by a thousand tiny holes, as if it had been perforated by a charge of ensall shot. The tragic is fol- lowed by the comic. Aftet the bombs had been exploded, an inspector of police hastily pulled open the carriage to see if the Emperor and Empress had been injured. The Emperor, thinking him an assassin, dealt him a blow that sent him rolling in the gutter. "I am satisfied that the Emperor is uninjured !" said the inspector, picking himself up. div.head: YON LA.D OV EA.RW ABE'S.
div.p: YON LA.D OV EA.RW ABE'S.
HY GEORGS HULL.
At this point there was a pause; and one or two pipes were lit silently. Presently Chirpin' Charlie broke the spell. " Owd Fanny Haydock's deead, dun- yo know.?" he said.
, Nowe,".replied Roger," when dud boo de e ?"
.„ " Yesterday at noon." " Tha doesn'd say !" exclaimed Rovin Fondle. "Poor owd Fanny ! hoo wer a lonely owd sowl, iv ever there waur one."

~„.. " Aye," said Roger, "an' still boo wer one o' them as everybody liked, hoo wer so good-hearted an' kindly." 800 waur sooa!" said Charlie; "aw wer terble ill- off to hear tell on her deein' ; but for o' thad aw laughed when t' news wer browt to me." And Charlie gave a chuckle greatly at variance with the nature of his news. " Nay, sure !" exclaimed Rondle, " wodever could ta find to laugh at in a bit o' bad news like that ? ' "ti wer o through you young'st lad ov eawr Abt?s."

Wod, Billy?" enquired Roger. "The varra same cowt. He's a quare stick, is thad lad. lie's one day gaurnless an another day sharp. Yo hit him off, Roger when yo said he Ater one hofe a foo an' th' other }lore a filosifer (philosopher). As soon as ever he heeard as owd Fanny Haydock wer e.eead yesterday, he rushed off tort eawr heawse to tell th' wife, for he knew hoo'd .awlus ta'en a gred interest i' Fanny ; an' t' poor owd lass went sudthqi, yo known. " Aw war just, startin' o' mi dinner when Billy coom 'soylin' in, puffin' an' blowin' woss nor a steeam engine. 'Eh. Aunt Betty !' he said, as soon as he could ged his breath, yo've to come deawn tot' fowd fost thing; owd finny haddock's deead, an' yo've to help to lay id eawt !

" Goo' lad Billy !" exclaimed Roger, " it's just like him. He's a quare lad. Dud he nod laugh, his-set' ?" "Nod he laugh ! He ne'er knew wod he'd said, aw believe. Booath t' wife an' me stared at him as soon as he spooak, but he wer as sayrious as a judge. Th' wife kept a straight face, and soyled off wi' him ; but aw bract eawt laughin' an' Billy ne'er knew what o'er till to-day. . . . Eh, bless yo ! eawr Abe an' t' wife's tired rough an' ready they ne'er teych th' lad a bit o' manners. Aw'm a bit ov a rough-yed misel', but aw do teych my childer a bit o' summat. Aw domed alleaw urn to' theaw ' me, heaw't be. . . It's bod a week or two sin' Billy seet o' th' chaps agate o' laughin' wheer eawr Abe warks, wi' his uncouth talk. Abraham warks at th' brewery just at th' teawn end, yo known, an' tha.d day as aw'm speykin' on, Billy's mother towd him run across to th' brewery, an' tell his feyther come to his dinner straightway, for id wer a bit after th' time. Off he soyled, full speed, as usual, an' when he landed in- side o' th' brewery, he sheawted " Fayther, tha's to come to thi dinner; its twelve o'clock. Thi porritch is gooin' cowd, mi mam says !' " " A w'd ha' fot him a rattle o' th' ear-hole," said Spinner Dick, after he had finished laughing, " iv he'd ha' theaw'd' me." " Never fear," replied Charlie, "eawr Abe an' t' wife ne'er bothers. Aw've towd um o'er it mony a time, but they'll tae no nooatice. They letten him hear o abeawt everythin' welly, brass an' o. One day eawr Abe's wife had gettin a new 'dolman—they wer terble fashionable just then—an' hoo wer trvin id on afoot one or two ov her nebbers. Hoe wodn'il tell um wod it cost, an' hoe wer happen wise, for id wer th' badger's wife (grocer's wife) an' t' clogger's wife as wer wi' her, an' hoe owed urn booath brass. Just as mi lady had getten th' dolman nicely fit on, in comes Billy, as merry as a lark, an' as wick as a snig. After he'd capered reawnd th' hoyle a time or two, an' bumped up ageeon th' table leg as a sign that he wer rkdy for a feed, he sails up to join i' th inspection o' th' new dolman. •• Eh ! he said, " are yo lookin' at mi mam's new dolman? Is'nd id a bonny un, eh? By gam !it's grander than owt i' this fowd. Id cost three peawnd ; ducrnd it, main ?" His mam fair skriked, an' fot him sich a cleawt across t' ineawth that boo knocked one ov his loce teeth eawt ; an' thad seet him agate o' yellin' like a cauve. Th' neb- bers piked off varra sheepish, i' t' spite ov eawr Abe's wife's tale abeawt th' disceawnt as hoo'd getten off th' dolman. Hoo'd hotter ha' howden her din, tor they' believed th' same as Billy that th' dolman lied cost three peawnd ; and there 'lrmue a storm i' th' fowd for two o' thre' days at after. 1 "Aw tell yo wod, chaps," said 3ill o' mi Granny's, " these youngsters lets a deel o' things eawt as are nod meant to see dayleet, dornd they ?" " Yigh," responded Cock Robin, "they do thad ! But they ged into trouble sometimes. Tha's ne'er towd us tiled other crack o'er yore Abe's lad, Charlie ; an' it s as good as t' rest." " Aw dornd recollect id," said Charlie. "Wed ! "exclaimed Robin, "dud ta nod hear o'er him welly geddin smothered th' other day ?" "Dud aw the dickens! Aw've nod bin deawn to eawr Abe's lat'ly. Heaw waur id 2" "0, keep thi yed cool," said Robin, with a grin," it's nowt sayrious, mon." "Well, lets hey hi," said Charlie. " Aye, eawt wi't," said Roger. " Varni weel," resp3nded Robin, "yo see, chaps, id just happened o' this rooad :—There's a new chapel bein' built deawn th' valley yon—a breek un." " Brick wi' stooan facins' " remarked Captain Lol, who belonged to a family of builders, " aw know th' shop ; they're just agate e' th' steeple at th' present time." "Rest, Captain ; they are. It wer just o'er that same steeple—or at leeast under id—that young William geet into trouble. Id seems Dicky Robi'son's agate o' brick- settin' theer, an' he's partly wort reyched th' top o' th' teawr, or steeple, or wodever tha coes id. Dick's latourer's a young lrishman—Dannis summat or other— aw corn-1 tell his other name gradely ; an' a 'witty lad Dennis is, too. Th' other day, Dick and Dennis !wer workia' away like two good uns—Dick settin' t' breek, an' Dennis carryin' th' hod up th' long ladders 'at reyched up th' side 0' t' steeple. "They'd hit on a varra good plan, as they thowt, a day or two afoot. Seein' 'at id wer a gred way fro' th' top to th' bottom, Dick and Dennis had agreed to send messages to one another wi' whistlin'. When Dick wanted a hodfull o' mortar he wer to give a good, sharp whistle, once ; an' when he wanted a hodfull o' break he wer to whistle twice. Yo see, there wer bod just reawm for one chap to stan' at th' top wi' a hodfull o' breek' an' another o' mortar, aside on him. This plan o' theirs hed bin workin' varra weel for a day or two up to this day as aw'm teas' yo o'er. But, as Bobby Burns says : The mat laid 'Themes o' mica and men

, Gang aft a-gley. Sometime i' th' foornoon Dennis hears t' whistle gooa, 'just once. "Roight!" said he to his-eel', "that manes mortar, oi guess." An' he seet to work to till th' hod; an' varra soon he wer climbin' up th' long ladders tort his mate. Dennis wer a varra nimble lad, but id wer no yessy (easy) job climbin' o' t' way up theer, for they'd gotten a good height wi' th' steeple. Heawever, he rayched th' top after a while, an' looked reawnd to see wheer he mut plank his mortar deawn, but there wer no reawm, for Dick hed plenty; "Here, here, said Dick, " wheer are ta bringin' th' mortar, Dennis? There's a lot here, si tha." "Sure," said Dennis, "an' ye whistled for it, Dicky, mi boy, didn't yez ?" "Dud aw the dule !" said Dick, " aw've ne'er whistled sin' tha fotched me thad last lot o' breek." Dennis looked at Dick, an' Dick looked at Dennis quite bewildered. Dennis seemed a bit suspicious that Dick wer chaffin' or summat, but Dick swore he waurn'd an' after two-o'-thre' minnats Dennis toddled deavtn ageean, dalled puzzled, an carryin' tie mortar back wi' him. _ .

Well, a quarter ov an heawr or sooa passed quately, an' then Dennis heeard th' whistle ageean, an' this time Id wer a double un. "Now," said he, "there he goes agin ! Oi'm sartin that's Dick, annyhow. An' he wants brick this toime."
Dennis filled his hod, an' once moor, but when he la]

breek as id could hutch. "Wed the dickens are ta after neaw ?" Dick axed, when he see'd him; "are ta bewitched, Dennis, or wed ?" "Bewitched, is it ye say? Now look here, Dick, av you're goan' to play larks on me, oi'm marchin' from this shop; but befoor oi go, oi'll just give yez a dose that'll make ye whistle to another tune.' "Come, come, Dennis," said Dick, quately enough, "domed ged thi rag eawt, ml lad. Aw con assure tha Id waurnd me as whistled oather this time or th' last. Does t' think aw'm sich a foo' as to whistle for stuff as ' aw've no reawm for ?" An' booath on 'em loked o reawnd to see iv ther wer owt abeawt, but nowt could they see; an' Dennis lied to go deawn ageon, an' carry th' breek back. But AS he wer gooin' deawn, he happened to catch sect ov a face peepin' eawt ov a window hoyle th' lower part o' th' steeple. For a second, he wer thad mad he thowt o' cloddin' t' breek at id ; but he soon thowt o' summat better nor thad. He toddled to th' bottom, an' sect to work as iv he'd ne'er seen owt. In. bit, bigum, off gooas th' mortar whistle ag,eeon Off Dennis skips; fills his hod wi' some gradely thin mortar; an' sets off up th' ladder steps. But he dudn'd go far. Th' same face wer peepin' eawt o' t' window, loekin' up, meawth wide oppen, grinnin' at Dennis. He couldn'd see whooa th' face belonged to; an he bed gave a sly look, for he dudn'd want id to know as he'd sin id. 0 at sudden, Dennis slips th' hod o'er, an deawn coom th' mmtar slap onto t' face below an' into id meawth. "There," sheawted Dennis,as" Mesthur Larker" skriked ' an' wriggled, "that's a mowthfut for yea, ml darlin.' Ye'll whistle ayin whin ye want mortar, will yers ?" • •

" Well," remarked Chirpin' Charlie, as soon as he had succeeded in straightening his features, " it's laughable enough, is thad last touch, but aw con hardly see wod its getten to do wi' eawr Abe's WY." " Well, tha art a warpheyd !" said Robin. "Parliamentary language, iv yo pleease," interposed Roger. " Well, aye; reel enough," said Robin, "but o t' same—" " Whey couldn't ta see," interrupted Bill o' mi Granny's," at after Robin lied gi'n tha sich brooad hints o'er yore Abe's lad geddin welly smothered, an' sich like, thad id wer hint as wer under th' steeple, an' geet th' meawthful o' mortar ?" "0, aye" exclaimed Charlie 1" aw see neaw. Aw mut ha' known id wer him beawt ony hints ; for there's nod a bigger fluttermuck i' this waurld than yon lad ov eawr Abe's !"—From The Preston Guardian.

div.head: " CAPITAL " CHAT.
div.p: " CAPITAL " CHAT.

A great deal of interest attaches to the approach- ing conference on the Housing of the Poor, which has been summoned to meet at the National Liberal Club. This is a new departure of considerable importance.

In addition to the winter garden, which has cost about £4,000, Madame Patti has built a priv ate theatre at the side of Craig-y-nos Castle. It was designed by a Swansea architect, has cost just three times as much as the winter garden, and will be in- augurated by Mr. Irving in October.

It has been practically decided by the Front Opposition Bench that the Land Bill shall be vigorously opposed. No formal step will, however, be taken till after EaAer. In the Lobby it is gener- ally believed that the Bill will largely be used, like the Ashbourne Act, to buy out the big Ulster land- lords, and that it will have little or no effect in Nationalist Ireland.

The Queen likes semolina puddings. She has one every day for her lunch. Her Majesty has an ex- tremely plain diet herself, whatever goes on in the royal kitchen in the way of providing for gourmands. Wine is still interdicted for her, and weak whisky and water is the only alcoholic beverage allowed. She has a special kind of French bread made for her. It has a soft crust, and saves the teeth.

The Queen Dowager of Portugal, an Italian Princess, married at the age of fifteen, was very extravagant in her ideas. It is reported that on one occasion she brought home from Paris one thousand pairs of shoes. On another occasion she ordered sixty-nine dresses from Worth, and on the way home they were lost at sea. Not discommoded in the least, she duplicated the order.

A human curiosity is on view at Nice, in the person of M. Kobelkoff, known as the "artiste tronc." M. Sebelkoff, although born without arms or legs, has managed to so far triumph over the difficulties which nature has placed in his way, that he can not only feed himself without assistance, but can write and paint. He is thirty-eight, married, And has seven children, none of whom show any kind of deformity.

An old Irish prophecy declares that wl:en an O'Doherty rules in Derry and an O'Donnell in Rap- hoe, Ireland will be free. Old Irish prohecies have before now been verified by events, and it is cer- tainly curious that Dr. O'Doherty has just been con- secrated Bishop of the diocese of Derry, in St. Eugene's Cathedral, Londonderry, and that the preacher on the occassion was Dr. O'Donnell, the Bishop of Raphoe.

Over thirty thousand volunteers from London and the home counties will be engaged in the Easter manoeuvres. The total falls considerably short of former Easter gatherings the reduction being due mainly to the fact that the commanding officers of many regiments think that the proposed reviews at Aldershot, Portsmouth, and other military and naval stations later in the season will be not only more acceptable, but that the benefit to be derived from them is greater.

--- Prince Bismarck has been somewhat ostentati- ously shaking the dust of Berlin off his feet, and giving its inhabitants to understand that they will see his face no more. Among other farewell visits, he paid one to Herr Eye, the landlord of a restau- rant in the Grunewald, near Berlin, a man who had formerly been for many years the Chancellor's servant. He asked for a cup of coffee, which he drank with all the more relish because, as he said, it was forbidden him by the doctor, lie then shook hands with Herr Eye, and departed amid the cheers of the assembled public.

Mr. Henry George lives in East Nineteenth-St.. New York, in an ordinary brown stone house. The locality is not by any means an aristocratic one. It is low-lying, and near the elevated railroad, which is not a very congenial' companion for literary workers. Mr. George is always "at home" on Sun- day evenings, and his house is a meeting place for the leading free traders and land reformers in New York. One of Mr. George's most ardent sup- porters is Mr. Thomas G. Shearman, who frequently advocates his views in the "Forum and other re- views. Mr. Shearman is a millionaire. A rich farmer recently bequeathed £2,000 to Mr. Gem*, to be devoted to the propagation of the principles I laid down in "Progress and Poverty."

This story,a strange melodrama in real life,has tra- velled from a foreign capital to London. A young Englishman became passionately devoted to a lady, who, however, did not return • his affection. He obtained leave of absence, and went on a long voy- age of travel and adventure in order to rid himself of his attachment. In vain ;he came back to the capital more in love than ever. He found the lady at a public ball, and proposed that she should elope with him. She declined, and he immediately left the room, and placed a revolver at his head. An officer who had followed saw the act, and knocked down the hand as it pressed the trigger. The shot was fired and entered the young man's side. He was carried back to the ball-room amid an indes- cribable scene of panic and confusion.

Everyone is united in praise of the new Educa- tion Code. its chief feature is, of course, the abolition of the payment by results. That was one of the recommendations of the Royal Commission, and on the whole the Code improves on those re- commendations. The change is made by practic- ally trebling the fixed grant (raising it from 4s. 6d. to 12s. 6d. and 145.), which cannot be withheld unless on the ground of real and general inefficiency. Beyond this 12s. 6d. to 14s. grant, there will be the following merit grants:- Is. to 7s. 6d. for education and discipline (the 6d. dependbnt on the report). is. for needlework (dependent on teaching). Is. for teaching singing by note, 6d. by ear. Is. and 2s. for class subjects. 4s. for specific subjects.

It is impossible to see at present to what lengths the statute which Mr. O'Kelly's lawyers have dug up, may not be carried. Look at the Olphert tenants. Thirteen hundred of them are at this moment homeless. Only six tenants are nbw in occupation on the whole estate, and those six are under eviction notices. For the time they are housed, like the Clongorey tenants, in temporary huts; but wherever these huts do not stand on

Mr. Gladstone is a voracious reader of current periodical literature and nearly always reads the advertisements. He subscribes for the American edition of certain American-English magazines, in order that he may obtain from the advertising new ideas as to American industries and enterprise.

Charles Dickens, the younger, wears spectacles, is getting bald, and works as hard as any other literary laborer in London; he has a considerable moustache, and in addition to editing "All the Year Round" contributes largely to other periodi- cals. He is on kindly terra& with all the literary celebrities of the day, and says the aim of his life is to bring back Gad's-hill into his fainilOf he can raise the money.

Says an Aix-les-Bains correspondent met the' Queen on'Thursday morning in her little donkey chaise going at a fairly brisk pace. On her arrival she -went in an open landau through the principal streets of the town, and was welcomed in a very cordial manner by the inhabitants,,whci,by the bye, are greatly elated at the fact that her Majesty is after all going to build a villa on the ground she purchased some years ago. The Queen has decided to try what massage will do towards the cure of her rheumatism.

On committing a burglary it is well not to leave your address behind you. ThroUgh the neglect of this precaution Thomas Dearmen has brought upon himself a sentence of five years' penal servitude. In the pursuit of one of his latest enterprises at Norwood he seems to have rearranged the contents of his pockets, no doubt to make room for some of his victim's plate. An envelope left behind was as good as a visitor's card to the owner of the house, who returned the call by proxy--, i.e., the polide. On this return call the visitors had ample entertain- ment in the inspection of many curiosities at Mr, ' Dearmen's residence, including housebreaking tools and the produce of several Norwood burglaries. Upon this narrative a jury at the Central Criminal Court were obliged to record a verdict of "Guilty " against the owner of the envelope. After that a cruel prison warder produced a damning record of previous convictiqga,.,and then the comrhon Sergeant sent him to mourehiS mistake in penal servitude for the period already named. • • Mr. Harry Furniss has made full and free confes- sion of his method of taking grotesque portraits of notable personages. •It -is very simple. He takes them" how and when he can,' and is careful, above all, never to let his "victims," as he calls them, know he is.' on their trail." Sometimes, " regard- less of their doom," like Gray's Eton boys, they are riding in the Park, sometimes just getting into a train, or they are chatting to a friend in the Lobby. or fast asleep in the House during some very dry debate. It is all the same to this chartered libertine of the pencil, the great object being to avoid the conventionality of a photograph. A photographer ; may often loose all the salient points which go to make a man's individuality; but Mr. Furniss aims to seize them all. The uninitiated ,will readily take the artist's word that this is not alfrays easy work even with the same men. Mr. John Morley's face, we are told, changes every hour almost,and one day he looks young enough to be his own grandson of the day before. Sir William Harcourt, on the other hand, is always good ; and so is Mr. Chaplin.

div.head: PRINCE BISMARCK.-PROPOSED MONU-
div.p: PRINCE BISMARCK.-PROPOSED MONU-
MENT.

Prince Bismarck returned- to Friedrichsruhe late on Saturday night, and was' heartily cheered by the large crowds who had awaited his arrival. Before leaving Berlip he laid a wreath on the coffin of the Emperor William 1., and took leave of all the Royal Princes. A proposal having been made that a national monu- ment should be erected to Prince Bismarck in Berlin, a number of influential men of all shades of political opinion met on Monday to take preliminary steps for issuing an appeal to the public for contributions to a fund to be raised for defraying the cost of the proposed monument. The Memorial Committee intends inviting the Emperor to give his patronage to the scheme. Herr Von Levetzon consents to act as Chairman of Committee. Prince Bismarck's birthday—he is 75—was celebrated on Tuesday throughout the Empire. The Emperor sent the ex-Chancellor a life-sized portrait of himself.

div.head: DARESBURY HIGHWAY BOARD. APPOINTMENT OF SURVEYOR.
div.p: DARESBURY HIGHWAY BOARD. APPOINTMENT OF SURVEYOR.

-......-- - A special meeting of the Daresbury Highway Board was held in the Sessions-room, Daresbury, on Monday afternoon. Mr. Joseph Uliffe (the vice- chairman) presided, and there was a large attend- ance of members. The business was the appointment of a surveyor in the place of Mr. Harold Peerman (resigned). The assistant clerk (Mr. H. G. Lmaker) read the names of the candidates (who had been reduced to six in number) and their testimonials. The applicants were—Mr. A, W. Chrystall (42), surveyor of roads, Cart- mel ; Mr. Alfred Caldwell (28), surveyor, Reddish Local Board ; Mr. R. M. Carter (30), surveyor, &c., Stretton ; Mr John Swinton (32), contractor, Middlewich ; Mr. John Whitlow (28), assistant overseer, &c., Preston Brook; and Mr. Thomas Kenyon (39), road superinten- dent, Altrincham. The salary is £l5O a year. Each candidate was sepatately called into the room, and asked a series of questions to test his knowledge of the duties of the. office. The Board then proceeded with the voting, which resulted in the election of Mr. Swinton. who obtained 18 votes, and who promised to enter upon his duties as early as possible.

div.head: WIGAN MURDER.
div.p: THE WIGAN MURDER.

William and Ann Dickinson were again before the Wigan county magistrates, on Tues_Ly, when the hear- ing was resumed of the charge againit them of having murdered Hannah Lydia Birchall, the illegitimate daugh- ter of the female prisoner, at Ince, on March sth. Mr. Ellis again prosecnted for lthe Treasury. The prisoners were representedlry Messrs. Lees and Wilson. Medical evidence was Open as to the cause of death, this being from fracture ofiithe skull. The child had been cruelly outraged. It was not possible that the injuries could have been caused by the body falling on anything down the pit. The injuries were inflicted before death, and were such as would cause excessive bleeding, which would last for some time, and was likely to bring about insensibility. There was blood on the male prisoner's clothing and on a counterpane covering the bed. Dr. Chronnell, of fliodley, was of opinion that the cause of death was the injwy to the head, and the hemorrhage. The injuries to the body were inflicted before death. The presence of a clot of blood on the right side of the heart showed that the child had not died suddenly. Evidence was then given by a number of witnesses called before the coroner. The case was again adjourned. William and Ann Dickinson, who are in custody accused of the murder of the child of toe female prisoner at Ince, were on Wednesday committed by the Wigan county magistrates for trial at Liverpool Assizes on the capital charge. •

CHAPTER VIII. TIE STRONG VACLIP.,;,;,ii " yes, gentlemen, I confess it, I do really. Ha, ha, ha! Yes, I do confess it; we have been a very, very long time getting the job done." "Horribly," said Mr. Klopstock, from his place at the table in the manager's room:. which bore an' excel- lent luncheon, the principals in the firm being PrWkirat„ including a couple of sleeping partners--gentlemew who thoroughly bore out their appellstion, for they looked plump, rosy, and well-to-do, fi...nd as if they were only there on sufferance. But for the matter of that, Mr- Humphrey, senior, and Mr. Humphrey, junior, as they were milted, brothers, and principal partners with Mr. Lighthtkly, who also belied his name, all seemed to be the're on sufferance, and to treat al Riopstock - with a 'great deal of deferential respect. He seemed, to be the bead of everything—even totaking the head of the table on this particular day, when, the strong vsult being finished, it was to be handed direr 10 the trim. "Horrible !" exclaimed Mr. Klowtock. " You've been a disgracefully long time, Mr. Middlecombe." "Hear, hear," said one of the sleeping partners, for lilopstock had looked at him severely; but the safe- maker looked round so sharply, and leaned forward so markedly beget a glimpse of the speaker who had said " Hear, hear," that the sleeping partner felt quite con- fused, and reached out his hand for the champagne. "With pleasure, sir," raid Mr. Middlecombe. meet- ing his eye, and be reached out also for the champagne. "shall we all join, gentlemen," continued Mr. Middle combs, "and drink security to the safe?" " Not a bad toast," said Mr. Humphrey, senior, when the wine bad been sipped. "Thank you, sir. Ha, ha, ha!", laughed' Mr. Middlecombe. "As I was saying about the vault, we have been a long time about it. Yes, Mr. Klopstock, sir, I own it: a.veryloag ; but you must please give .me credit.for.one thing. It was a contract, sir, eh? I have only been a 10. g while over the job so as r to do it well, sir, and I am proud to say, Mr.. Klop- stock, sir, that that safe is safe. Fire-proot.burglar- proof —2" "Waterproof," suggested the other sleeping partner; laughing. "Well, I could almost promise that, gentlemen, for it is so nearly air-tight that I wouldn't give much for the chance of the man who was locked in—no, that I wouldn't, young gentleman," he continued, as he met Martin Woolford s eye fixed on him, in a peauliarly interested way. "That vault, gentlemen, is, I am sure, all that you can desire, and your books could, not be safer in the Bank of England.' "Well, well," said Mr. Klopstock, drily, as every' one turned to him as if expecting him to make some reply, 'I hope it will turn out, as well as you promise, Middlecombe; but mind this, you've praised it SO highly, that I shall look out for flaws." "And welcome, sir. Ha, ha, ha! yes and welcome. Mr.Wooltord,too,l hope ycu'll look for them, and I give you leave' to point them out. Now, gentlemen, if you like, I alien be happy to show you my chef d'auvre, for Pm proud of it, gentlemen—l am really. On my word. He looked pleased too, as he laid three co four small keys before him upon the table, and then, as the party rose, be proceeded to open an iron door in one corner of the room—a door whose ponderous bolts shot back with a loud click upon the insertion of a. brightly polished key, right in the centre of an iron cross. As the door swung silently open, it showed a short flight of stone steps leading into a black-looking stone passage, just wide enough to allow two people to pass, and going along a short distance between what seemed to be two iron walls, in the centre of one of which was an iron door. Then, turning off at right angles, it continued for about a dozen steps, turned off again, and then again, bringing the visitors back to the foot of the short flight of steps. " There, you see, gentlemen," said Mr. Middle- combe, "I surround my vault with a passage, which passage is surrounded by a dense concrete wall, six feet thick, and of the hardest materiil. If anybody mined through that—" "But they might mine through the floor,*
said

Martin. "Six feet thick, young gentleman," said Mr. Middle- tombs, laughing. "Or the ceiling," said Martin. "Six feet thick too, young gentleman. Well suppose they did mine through that six feet of concrete, or got through that iron door, and down those Mops. What then ?" " They'd have cracked your nut, Mr. Middlecombe," said Mr. Humphrey, junior. "No, sir. Oh dear no," said the safe-maker. "Ha, ha, ha! Not at all. They would have got into this passage—One side of which is my strong vault, which holds another strong vault. See here, gentlemen." He applied another bright key to the centre of that iron door, after pointing out how impossible it would be for any one to use there a wedge or lever, or even gunpowder to blow the door off. There was another sharp metallic click and a dozen bolts shot back, when, instead of swinging open on hinges, the door glided softly as a handle was turned, along a grove into the wall, leaving the opening quite clear. " That does away with hinge', gentlemen—the weakest part of a safe door, to my thinking," said Mr. Mideilecombe ; and he now led the way to a massive grating, beyond which, in a narrow passage, a gas jet that had been burning with a dim blue light, now sprang up brightly, showing the interior of the vault. It was of no great dimensions, but just held eight people after its maker- had unfastened the door or grating of steel, which also glided back into a deep slit, leaving the passage perfectly free. On either side now were doors, each of which was in itself a safe, but the stronghold of all was at the end of the passage, and the door that sank down into the floer as it were was of enormous weight, and yet it glided down almost at v. touch, so exactly was it balanced by some internal mechanism. "There, gentlemen—there, Mr. Klopstoek, sir— there's a strong vault in which you might keep the crown jewels in safety. and I deliver over to you the keys." ' No, give 'em to Mr. Wool'ord there," said the old man. "I don't like the place. There are too many new fangles for me." "But you will like it, sir. I warrant von will." ex- claimed Mr. Middlecombe. "Now, Mr. Woolford, pee, here are the keys—three of them. all opening my patent juggle-tumbler looks. Then,.for the small sale, here is this key, which is a pass-key for all." Mark took the handsomely-made little keys, and as he did so, it might have been fanny, hut he seemed to catch his brother's eyes fixed upon the glistening little pieces of steel in a very peculiar way, and a shiver ran through his frame. It was quite a momentary affair, and be could not have explained his thoughts, as he took the keys in turn, and tried them in the locks, while the partners, Mr. Klopstock and Martin Woolford, who, upon the strength of his brother's position, and at Mark's request, had been asked in to the luncheon, tried the various doors, and the capacity of the different strong places, with the result that all were fain to, deelare that they might now laugh at the efforts of the cleverest gang of burglars in town." " Yes, gentlemen, I'd give them eight-and-forty hours at any time to make their first attack," said Mr. Middlecombe," and then laugh at them.. It isn't to be done, gentlemen—it len- to be done. It's the strangest vault in the City of London, and you can't find a stronger. "And yet," said Mark, quietly, "it has a very weak place." "Weak place, sir! Where, sir? Show it to me, sir, and I'll forfeit what you please. Where is it, sir? Ha, ha, be ! I should like to see." "In the door," said 3d ark, thoughtfully," for the man who holds these keys or an imitation has eaerything at his mercy." He repented having said it the next moment, for once more he seemed to encounter Martin's eyes, look- ing at him euriously, and Klopstoek said testily: "Well, I don't think tl.at'x a very nice remark." At this moment Martin walked straight into the farthest safe at the end of the passage, and seemed to be trying the size of the divisions, as if for the fitting in of the great ledgers and cash books of the firm. "Well, if you come to that, Mr. Woolford, sir„y,pu must have a way into your vault somewhere, so I doll% think your idea's quite square. That, of course, de- pends upon the man who keeps the keys. Now, in this ease—hold stip, young gentleman," he said to Martin, "we have a defor here that—the key one moment, sir," and be turned the handle at the side of the narrow passage, when there was a sharp clang, a heavy crashmg fall, and the massive door shot up like light-' ming, and closed the opening of the inner safe, leaving Martin Woolford shut closely in. "It's the spring of the balance given way, that''s all, gentlemen," said Mr. Middlecombe, turning rather white. "It is vexatious; but it does not interere with the stability of the safe, and it can be put right in a few hours." " Bitt my brother!" exclaimed Mark, excitedly. "How are we to get him out?" "I forgot him," said the safe-maker, ruefully. men MIMI t.. ',War • -ft. . . •

div.head: noinena of Nature.
div.p: noinena of Nature.

W,hatever the cause is, it must certainly be sought far away from the whirling body of wind itself. Its results are powerful ; its cause must also be powerful. Let us, therefore, consider a few facts. The appearance of a cyclone is invariably , preceded by dark spots on the face of the sun. These spots indicating a disturbed condition of the solar system, necessarily affect the atmosphere of our earth. Any unusual generatim of heat always creates; a vacuum. • Air must rush in to fill this vacuum. Hence the disturbance which results in the cyclone. This theory finds additional confirmation in the fact that cyclones always occur during the day and not at night. The dark spats upon the surface of the sun, whatever they may be, cause great commotion in the atmosphere of the world. 'Fhe cause is remote, but the effect is here: This rule finds its application in nearly every depart- ment of life. The telegraph operator is in Paris, yet the click of the instrument manipulated by his fingers is heard in London. An uneasiness and disgust with everything in life, commonly called home-sickness, is felt by many people, when the cause is to be found in the distant home hundreds of miles away. An uncer- tain pain may be felt in the head. It is repeated in other parts of the body. The appetite departs, and all energy is gone. Is the cause necessarily to be found in the head? The next day the feeling increases. There are added symptoms. They continue and become more aggravated. The slight pains in the head increase to agonies. The nausea becomes chronic. The heart grows irregular and the breathing uncertain. All these effects have a definite cause, and in nine cases out of ten it will be found to exist in a deranged condition of the kidneys and liver, far away from that portion of the body in which the effects appear. But one may say, "I have no pain whatever in my kidneys and liver!" Very true. Neither have we any evidence of a cyclone on the surface of the sun ; but it is certain that the cyclone is here. Sri it is with these great organs of the body: they are the real cause of the painful effects in other parts of the body,. although there is no pain experienced in the organs themselves. Exactly this condition of affairs was the experience of Mr. J. Lewis jones, o 16, Battersea- Rise, Clapham Common. For twenty years he was a martyr to aches and pains. 'He nearly impoVerished 'his health and made himself a poor man by taking and paying for various medicines, which did him no good. He finally decided that his kidneys were at fault, and commenced the use of Warner's " SAFE " Cure. The remedy helped him and he soon got relief. Writing under date of March 11th, he says, "When 1-tell you I have takentwenty bottles of this wonderful Medicine, it will convince you that my case was a serious one ; but I am happy to say' that, since taking the medicino, I have not enjoyed such good health for twenty years." This great remedy can be had of all chemists and medicine vendors, at 4s. 61 and 2.5. 91:1_ per bottle, according to size, or of H. H. Warner and Co., Limited, 86, Clerkenwell-road, London, E.C.

div.p: FIVE TIALES RESPITED..

The condemned man O'Brien was to have been hanged at 'Limerick on Monday morning for poisoning his father- in-law, but on Sunday morning another respite was granted till the Ist Of May. No fewer thatri five respites have taken place since the date originally fixed fOr O'Brien's execution—the 14th of January. This last respite is to enable the Court of Appeal to review the Queen's Bench decision upholding the .prisoner's convic- tion.

div.head: – IMPERIAL PARLIAMENT.
div.p: - IMPERIAL PARLIAMENT.
HOUSE OF LORDS.-SATIIRDAY,

Their lordships met on Saturday morning, at ten o'clock. Besides the Commissioners, the only peer present was Lord Stratheden and Campbell. ROYAL CommissioN.-L-The Royal Assent was given by Commission to the following Bills :—County Councils Associations Expenses, Crown Office, Army (Annual), Consolidated Fund (No. 1), and Lunacy Consolidation
Bill. The Commissioners were the Lord Chancellor, the Earl
of Limerick, and Earl Brownlow. Their lordships adjourned at twenty minutes past ten o'clock Until Thursday, the 17th April. HOUSE OF COMMONS. —SATURDAY.

The Speaker took the chair at ten minutes past ten o'clock. Two members were present at prayers, Lord A. Hill and Mr. Sydney Herbert, and a third (Lord Burghley) arrived a moment before the Black Rod was announced. ROYAL COMMISSION.—The Yeoman Usher of the Black Rod (Colonel Sir R. C. S. Clifford) appeared at the bar, and desired the attendance of the House in the House of Feers to hear the Commission read, giving the Royal Assent to several Bills. The Speaker, preceded by the Sergeant-at-Arms with the mace, and followed by the three members present, at once responded to the summons and went to the Upper Chamber. After a few minutes interval, the Speaker returned and reported the Royal Assent to the Bills agreed °ruby both Houses. The House adjourned at twenty minutes past ten.. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—MONDAY. The Speaker took the chair at five minutes past three o'clock. • QuEsTioNs &c.—Sir James Ferguson informed Mr. Howard Vincent that a new extradition treaty between her Majesty and the United States had been duly ratified, and would come into force on April 4th. Sir MICHAEL HICKS BEACH, replying to Mr. Dillwyn, said there were no funds at his disposal which could be used in assisting

_ pilots to obtain the necessary provisional order fOr securing to them the benefits of the Merchant Shipping (Pilotage) Act of 1889, which granted to the pilots a seat on every Pilotage Board, but if special circum- stances should arise which would justify a repre- sentation to the Treasury, to forego the fee, or a portion of it, he would direct, such representation to be made. Postage rates to the colonies, the sentence on a marine: officer, the. distress near Suakin, personal declarations at Consulates, and the Fastnet Lighthouse formed the subjects of further questions. Sir JAMES FEBOUSSON informed Mr-. W. Red- mond that the negotiations between the Australian colonies and-the Chinese Government on the subject of Chinese immigration had not Joeen concluded, but the subject was under consideration. - Sir W. Hart Dyke gave.uotice to introduce, on the 14th inst., a Bill to make operative certain articles in the Education Code. On the motion of Mr, W. H. Burnt, it was resolved that the House meet at two o'clock next day. Mr. E. V. Knox took the oath and his seat for West Cavan. Sureem—On the motion for going into Committee of Supply, Sir J. COLOMB moved a resolution setting forth the expediency of instituting a special inquiry into the organization of the Customs Department, particularly the position; the hours, and the overtime of the out-door officers, upon which subjects the Royal Commissioners on Civil Establishments were pliable to report, and therefore remitted them to the Treasury to deal with. Mr. BEADLAIIGH seconded the amendment, and Mr. GLADSTONE said it appeared to him that there appeared definite :and conclusive ground for ' moving it. He suggested, however, that it should be withdrawn if the Government gave an undertaking to institute an inquiry. The Chancellor of the Exchequer agreed, and Mr. R. Nsvms, in thanking him, said that in Liverpool there had been rather an abuse of the acting system—the system of appointing officers of one grade to act as officers of a superior grade without the addi- tional emoluments, while the attempt to ventilate griev- ances had resulted in the removal of some men to other ports.

--- -- THE POSTAL SERVICE.—Mr. RAISES said an arrange- ment had been made with the Post Office at the Cape with the view of establishing communication by post- cards. He would endeavour to make similar arrange- ments with regard to Natal and other South African States. With reference to the parcel post, he would be elad to make any modification in the scale of charges likely to 1-e Jeneficial to the public and not injurious to the revenue. The present parcel post arrangement with th, railway companies was for 2/ years from August, 1833. YEOMANRY CAVALRY.—Mr. STANHOPE said a scheme was being worked out which would fully recognize the usefulness of the yeomanry cavalry, and which he hoped • soon to lay before the House. THE EDUCATION CODE.—Sir W. HART DYKE Old Mr. Powell that the new Education Code would come into force on the let September. He hoped the necessary instructions to the inspectors would be sent out shortly. SUPPLY.—The House went into Committee of Supply on the Civil Service estimates, and passed a number ' of votes. MIAs ADVANCED.—A Bill having for its object tha extirpation of pleuro-pneumonia among cattle was react a second time; as was also Ole Criminal Law Procedure Amendment Act. ADJOURNMENT.—TheHouse adjourned at 6.35 until the 14th inst.

CHAPTER, IX. inv v 4 STEEL TOMB, Fr wr.B.Burrible position for those whortoodlistening to the beating of the man enclosed in the patent safe, and it is possible that their sufferings were wore acute than those of him who, half stunned by the accident, found himself so suddenly incarcerated. Mr. Middle- combe looked as white as ashes, for he had been boast- • fog of the place being air tight, and had felt so proud of his achievement, thinking it perfect, while now for' the first time it had revealed itself in quits a nevr character—namely, that of a dangerous trap. It was very terrible, and he felt ready to flee from the place, piercing his fingers in his ears to shut out the appeals made to him for help. But after a few moments he became more composed, and, holding up his hand to command silence, he said firmly: "We can do nothing by growing excited. I'll have the men here as quickly as possible, and get the place to pieces." He ran out of the vault, and started himself to fetch. his workpeople and the necessary tools, while Mark took out his penknife and tapped gently on the door. To his great delight, there was a reply to his signal —proof positive that some air must reach the prisoner,. and with s joyful glance at those- stesent, he ex- claimed

"We shall save him yet!" Mr. Klopstock pullsd out his snuff-box, and took a pinch as a peculiarly cruel thought entered his mind- -a horrible thought at such a time—and it was that as Martin was shut up there—buried as it were in a vault—it was a most fortunate thing for all concerned, and far from being evil, least of all perhaps, for the young man himself. Meanwhile the excitement in the vault continued to increase, and suggestions were made as to the pos- sibility of pouring liquid food in through the keyhole, forcing in fresh air ; and a dozen more impossible ideas were propoeed, in 07.'3 midst of which Samson HO, the great burly porter of the place, came in armed with a heavy hammer and the big iron chisel he used to wrench open chests and coxes of goods and samples "Let me come,. gentlemen," he said, " soon got
through." "My good fellow,' exclaimed old Kloptock, "

„ can make no impression with that.” - The man smiled derisively, stripped off his coat, rolled up his-sleeves, and delivered a tremendous blos upon the face of the safe. It made a great noise, and that seemed to afford him some satisfaction; for directly after he began with his great chisel trying to drive it in at a chink where the door closed, and hammering away with all his might, but apparently without the faintest notion of how or whereto direct his energy. He hammered here, he-hammered there, with the great drops of perspira- tion gathering upon his I,row, and at last he stopped short to examine the edge of his chisel, which was completely battered away. "I don't seem to make much way," be said, grimly. "It's 'bout the hardest bit o' stuff I ever touched." A. dead silence fell upon the group at these words, for they gave a fuller realisation of the strength of Mr. Middlecombe's work, and it was plain enough that kamsen Hall might have gone on hammering there for the term of his natural life without injuring the safe in the least. Then the idea woe suggested that a blecksmith should be sent for to bring a sledge-hammer.; but a glance round showed that if he 'did dome he would not have room to swing it, and with a chill feeling of despair gathering force, the party, silent now, stood waiting for the safe-maker's return. Mark Woolford did not leave the door after Hall had ceased his noisy useless hammering, but from time to time tapped the steel panel softly with the handle of his knife, and for awhile he obtained responses. At last, however, these grew less frequent, and then stopped altogether. He struck the door again and again, and then in an access ot despair, he seized the porter's hammer and beat with it fiercely, trying to rouse the prisoner, but in vain—there was no reply. There was not a man present who would not have offered Mark Woolf ord his sympathy. but at such a time it seemed like insulting him, and, oppressed by the horror of the situation, they stood perfectly silent iii the oppressive space, which was now growing so hot and vitiated by the number of people crowded down there, that the gaslight began to burn feebly. Mark was the first to observe this, and, seeing the reason, he bestirred himself, for he felt that it was Like robbing the imprisoned man of his last chance for life. A few words sufficed, and at the end of a minute the place was emptied, windows and doors were opriaol the manager's room, anri tue c':ange was manifest. i,‘ a very few minutes in the increased brilliancy of !lie light. Under these circumstances, Mark kept outside in the passage, merely going in from time to time to give a few taps upon the stel door, hot all was in vain, and at lag he seated bi [wolf upon the teeps, with bit head bosee:l clown upon his hands, and tried to think out hex be was to break the terrible news to •

For hope seemed dead within him as in iningin-t ion - be pictured the interior of the safe, and saw what hhci taken place there; the frantic horror that had cono upon his brother, and then the overpowering ~:Tects of the mephitic air, until he had sunk down, hie awful tomb. Ile felt that he must get air, and run and dash him "- self against the steel door, and it was only by fightl"g‘ hard to gain the mastery over his nerves, that he 00 able to restrain himself and sit here patiently waittot for the help that seemed so long in coming. ' And as he waited, the remembrance of their 011: boyish days came back; all Martin's baseness andwew follies were forgotten, and he could yea nothing hilt that i handsome lad, so idolised by his mother—the brig, sliver man who made him by comparison seem so dui' and poor. And this was to be the end of it all: a terrible delltb. here close at his hand, while be was helpless t" 6a".1,4 It was too horrible. It seemed more than he bear, and at last he was compelled to get up and round and round the passage enclosing this terrible' vault, listening the while to the low. murmuring-el: venation that came down to him from the room. At At last. There were sounds above which, told' of the return of the safe maker, end upon his hurryil down with his workmen M. -..rk .tood asule, and waite wt eight long weary hours more of suspre, lile thee steel floor was attacked, and the trut of the maker's words words plainly attested; for not till the wholes strength of the mechanism could be brought to Nor for the destruction of the Dart (known only .to the maker) were they able to attack the door, and-. 1. working in relays, succeed at last in getting it uncloset, th,3 door slid open once more, the men NIA ; and, stepping over the &bra liavle. hastens* where his brother lay in an easy position, with. 01'. arm beneath his bead, and as if sleeping. • tbe' "Better let nat, come, Mr. Woolford," doctor, who had been waiting with him for boil! ready to render asiistance. A Yptixti GnAltilarit iECIIIMg. .; At the Warrington County Petty Sasions. on Wednes- day, a lad named Patrick Cooney, nine years of age, was charged with having stolen sixpence on the 23rd ult. A little girl named Wton,,, feveg, years of age, was seat ,with sixpence to wal:eitnirchise at a shop in Wright:st, ' Sankey bridges, and placed" the coin on the counter. Young Cooney, who was in the shop at the time, snatched it up and ran away. He had been previously convicted 4• for felony, and the magistrates now ordered that he be ' sent to prison for ten days, and be afterwards kept in a refortnatory- until he reaches the age of 1.1; years. A LUNATIC STOPS A TRAIN. A man named Michael Saunders was on Saturday. committed to the Workhouse, by the Warrington usagis-' trates, as being of unsound mind. A Policeman said that Saunders had behaved in a very eccentric manner on the previous afternoon. He had been walking into Private houses, much to the surprise and alarm of the inmates, and he wentinto Dallain forge,where he stopped -work to a certain extent for a time. • After this he found his way to the Central Station where he got on the line and stopped a train. After this, the officer thought it advisable to take him to the Police Station for safety. While in the dock Saunders made an incoherent state- . r relent of some sort. "A SAUCE IN THE FACE." At the Police Court, on Thursday, Georgina Hunt, a married woman, was summoned for assaulting James Warburton on the 27th March. Complainant stated that heand the defendant's hitiband Wined at Platt's fustian. cutting shop and had had some words. Later in.the day the defendant came to his house and gave him a smack in the face. One of her sons challenged him to come out and fight, but a neighbour told him that all the family were waiting for 'him outside.—Mr. Longton. Who appeared for the defendant, submitted that the case was of a frivolous nature and the assault had been brought about by the complainant's conduct.—Defen- dant was ordered to be bound over to keep he peace for Six months. AN EXTRAORDINARY CASE OF CHILD "DESERTION." A man named Charles Whitehead, who is employed on • •

....... • the Ship Canal, -was brought up' on warrant It the Nice, Court, at Warrington, on Monday, it being alleged against him that he had left his child chargeable to the • Daventry Union. Prisoner said that whilst be was away at sea his wife --warried again. She ~wa tried for • bigamy at the Liverppq Winter Assizes, and sentenced. , to six months' imPiisonttiint. During prisoner'sabsence Ins 'wife sent, the child :awaycand ,althoughlie had

made.repeated applications for it, she would never tell , him where it was. ' He was perfectly willing to pay for itsifiaifitehatiee. If he were sent away now he would • , ' Probably lose bie. work. , The Mayor explained that the iWarrington magistrateis had no power to deal with the ,t , Case,:aloid Could eiily{keifiiind him to the custody of the - Daventry policei tit fell .• • • , • • • Mai= Mcumis,R.oll ASSAULT/NO POLICEMEN. A hawker, named .Thomas Burke, was committed by the Warrington'"niagistratee' o'SaturdaY •for three months hard latimr for.an assault on Sergeant Cheney and P.C. Hampson on the previous night. Lfight had ' been going pe in Turner-st., and Cheney, who was in his Private clothes, interfeied and had finally to take one of the combatants in charge. After he did,Burke,who was art onlooker, came up ' and struck Cheney a. swinging blow In the eve, knocking him to the ground. Hampson afterwards came r•el the scene and was kicked and struck by the prisoner. Burke pleaded guilty, but said he had committed the assault when drunk. The magistrates held that drunkenness was no excuse, and as the prisoner had before been sent, to goal ,for three months for an exactly similar offence, .they again committed him for the same period. A PROBLEM : WHERE DTD RE GET ALL PRE DRINK? Michael Varley, whb, judging from his tongue, was of Irish nationality, was before the Warrington magistrates cc Saturday morning, accused of having been helplessly . drunk in Mill-lane, the previous night. Varley talked to the Bench in a friendly and confidential way, apparently not 'wishing to hold anything back which would help the magistrates in coming to a verdict. He said that up to the time when his memory forsook bin he hadhad four or five pints, but after, that he did not know how many he had had. He was kPpt supplied with pints as long as he took them. He had had 4s. 6d. in his pocket when he started and there was Is. ed. left. He supposed he must have spent 3s. in drink, but he treated a few people 'Who " stuck up for him." The result was that he was found lying in a helpless state across a footpath. Alder; man Burgess thought there must have been a very large quantity of drink served to the man before he got into that condition. A fine of ss. and costs was imposedrdr seven days' imprisonment. A GENERAL Row. On Thursday, at the police court, Peter Carey, his wife Mary and his daughterMary,tvere summoned for assault- ing a labourer named James Doddard on Saturday night. Complainant stated that he was on his way home when the younger female defendant struck him on the head With a can several times, and while he was attempting te take the can from her her mother came out and broke a jug over his head. lie NEM rendered insensible by a severe wound on the head, and P.C. Hughes took him to the Infirmary, where his wound was dressed.—Mr. A. Rrowne,who appeared for the defendants,contended that the complainant was the aggressor and that the defen- dant was only assaulted after the great provocation he had given. There was a cross-summons against Dod-• dard by the younger female for assault. After hearing the evidence the Bench dismissed the case against Peter Carey, and remarking that the others seemed to be of a Pcgnacious disposition, fined each 10s. and costs. The croes-summons was dismissed.
A GIRT, KLEPTOMANIAC,-A SAD. CASE:

A girl of twenty, whose parents live at Bolton, and Who gave the name of Edith Walworth, was brought before the Warrington magistrates on Wednesday, on a Charge of wandering abroad in Irlam-street, without visible means of subsistence. Early the same morning Constable Jones (29), found her sitting on some steps'in Buttermarket-street, and took her to the police station for safe custedy. The Chief Constable (Mr. Hunt), said from what he could gather the girl had been sent to Prison for eight months for stealing something, 'and she. told him that it would be useless for her to go homes She seemed to be a self-willed girl, and made threats ae to what she would do to herself. She seemed to hay, got the idea that she was without a friend in the world- and she was without a doubt troubled with klepto raania. That seemed to be her only fault. When she aaW a thing she could not help taking it. It was resolved to remand the case until Saturday, in order • that further inquiries might be made. SATURDAY NIGHT DISTURBANCES: POLICEMEN ASSAULTED The circumstances of two disturbances that took place Oil Saturday night were investigated by ths Warrington Magistrates on Monday, at the Police Court. In the first cue a powerful-looking man named William West was Charged with having been drunk and disorderly in St. James'-at. on Saturday; and with having assaulted P.C. Bollingworth, and James Johnson and William Burrows, a.t the same thne and place. Prisoner was creating a disturbance at Bridge Foot, when P.C. Elollingworth tried to persuade him to go horn Prisoner would not listen and struck him in the face. The officer accord- ingly took him into custody. Prisoner then became - very violent, and struck and kicked anybody who went near him. It was with the utmost difficulty that he was removed to the station. His wife also struck the officer And threw eggs at him. Prisoner pleaded guilty, saying that he had had some drink, and it "took advan- tage of him:" He was committed to prison for a month with hard labour. In the second case James Collins, a Militiaman, was charged with having assaulted P.C. Davies in Winwick-st.' on Saturday night; and Winifred Jennings and Thomas Knockton were charged with hay- 1g been ‘lrunk and disorderly at the same time and ' Place. The constable was taking Jennings and Knock- ton to the bridewell,'when Collins attempted a rescue . and assaulted the officer. Prisoners were each sent to Brison7for 14 days,. with hard labour. ..„ WYCLIFFE Y. ST. MARY'S (Pmmx.rß). —This match was played on the ground of the former in brilliant weather, on Saturday afternoon. The visitors arrived with a strong team, but Wycliffe were but indifferently repre- sented, and only played 14 men. In the first half Johnson scored a meritorious try by charging down the full back's kick, the point remaining unimproved. In the second half Hampson, after some exciting play near the Penketh line, scored in a favourable position, and Brown placed a goal. Shortly afterwards Brown narrowly missed drop- ping a goal. The visitors played up towards the finish, • eventually scoring a try, and the place failing time was called/the final score being—Wycliffe, one goal, one try, two minors' St. Mary's one try, one minor. On behalf of Wycliffe, Lloyd, Ball, Noon, Johnson, and Hampson played well, the latter being by far the best forward on the field. St. Mary's were best represented by Helsby, Smallman, and Plinston WARRINGTON" A" v. Sr. HELENS RECREATION " A."— This fixture was played at Warrington on Saturday in boisterous but beautiful fine weather, a 'capital attend- ance assembling to witness the game. Warrington win- ning the toss, the visitors started against a stiffish breeze and with the sun in their faces. No return Was made, and for a time play hovered dangerously near the home line, and after a spell of passing between Little, Mathew, and Seddon, the latter sprinted along touch, and but for a capital tackle by Boscow would have scored. Jolley at length brought about relief by a punt past the quarter-flag, when Ashton was conspicuous with strenuous endeavours to break away. Later on Thorn- ley broke through the line-out, and the whole of the for- wards dribbled grandly over the line, Thornley claiming a try. From the drop out Isherwood made his mark,and the ball being plated for Webster, this player made a grand attempt to effect the downfall of the visitors'goal, a minor accruing. Following the drop out a miss by Lally allowed Fildes to get possession and he raced grandly down the touch line, and a rare chance was lost by throwing forward. Some loose exciting play ensued, but still the home team had none the best of matters, although assisted with a strong wind. A kick from amongst the ruck by one of the home forwards got the ball away, and from a pass by Rowe, Jolley got clean away, but'his final pass was faulty. Directly afterwards, from a long kick, the visitors touched down. Jolley Bext put in a clever bit of play, and from his kick Lally ran very smartly to the Saints' quarters. Very soon after this Holmes secured from a line-out, and after a good run threw across to Webster, whe tried a drop at goat, and Rowe dashing Wong secured a capital try, which Webster converted Holmes shortly after this got awav again and passed to Jolley, and Webster getting the ball almost scored after a strong run. Mather, however, obtained a clever try from a pass by Rowe the next Minute, but the place failed. The visiting team were now defenders for some time, but ultimately relieved slightly. The relief was of short duration, for a grand bit of work by Webster was the means of taking play to the line, and a minor was conceded. Then came a pretty piece of passing between Rowe. Mather, and Jolley, and arlother minor resulted, half-time arriving with Warrington 1-2-4 to nil. No reply was made to Isherwood's kick, and a dribble by Ashton, Berry, and Isherwood took play near the line. The visitors, headed by Rushton and Collins, dribbled right away down mid- field, but Rowe came round splendidly and stopped the rush. Berry, Bate, and Russell then got away, and the first-named dribbled grandly to the line, but the ball was sent dead. After this &strong run by Webtser, who ran half the length of the ground, was loudly applauded, and following this Rowe got finely away, but ended up by a poor pass. After some exchange kicking, Jolley got beautifully away, but some passing by the homesters was overdone, and the ground gained was lost. A minor was given to the visitors shortly afterwards. The game continued to be of an uninteresting nature for a length- ened period, but eventually Jolley again got away. Berry and Thornley next broke away, and Mather throwing across to Webster, the latter ran grandly to the line, when Mather dodged over and secured another try. The game proceeded in the same monotonous way, exception being made to Jolley, who on one or two occasions got away from amidst the ruck of his oppon- ents, a poor game ending with Warringfon 1-3-5 to 0-0-2. Teams :—Warrington: Boscow, back; Webster, Jolley, and Lally, three-quarters; Mather and Rowe, half backs;

WARRINGTON v. ST. HELENS RECREATION.

If Saturday's match be a criterion on which to gauge future meetings of the above dubs, then from a financial point of view success is assured. Fully 9,000 peopl&as- sembled on the ground of the Recreation Club to witness the return fixture with the Warrington Club, and of this number considerably over 1,000 had journeyed from Warrington to urge their team on in hopes of gaming a victory. The day was particularly fine, and when both teams entered the arena clad in their spotlessly clean costumes and surrounded by such a great crowd of spectators, quite a murmur of intense excitement was noticeable and a hearty cheer was accorded each team. Warrington were without the aid of their skipper, Fair Turner, and Massey winning the toss took advan- tage of the high wind which prevailed. A lofty kick sent the oval near to the Warrington line, and smart follow- ing up by Fildes and Pilkington seemed to baffle the visiting defence, and in less than a minute a minor was accorded the homesters. Frank Turner's drop out was only feebly responded to by Gerrard, and from a pack at the half way flag Bate ran round and improved Warring- ton's position with a neat run and kick. A free kick to the visitors sent the ball over the line and Gerrard saved. No relief was brought from the drop out, and despite the endeavours of Smith, Pilkington, and Seddon, the War- ringtonians still kept up their aggressive attitude. Faulty play-by the Warrington backs allowed the Recs to enter the visitors' quarters, and although Ellison had a rare chance afforded him the sound tackling of Massey was! of immense service to his side and disaster was averted. Seddon essayed a drop at goal, but the shot went wide and Warrington cleared. Lawless spoiled Gerrard in his endeavour to cross the line, and although a clear field was presented to the Warringtonian Pilkington managed to pull him up at the half-way flag. Nevins here made a bold bid, but the effort was staved off by Pilkington, who ran round the pack, and was not brought down until the half way flag was reached. A fine piece of play by Barnes, followed closely by an equally brilliant run by Antrobus, once more endangered the Recs' goal. The visiting forwards now seemed to work with renewed energy, and Povey picking up in the loose dodged tlirough and through until he was close to the line, and handing over his charge,to Barnes, that player crossed the line and to all appearances gained an unmistakable try. The point was, however, not allowed. Following this Evans compelled a minor with a long kick. A spell of irgive-and-take play now ensued, until the monotony was relieved by a beautiful piece of play by Bate, who dodged Pilkington and ran to half way, pas- sing to Lawless, who unfortunately failed te take the chance. A series of passes betiveen Antrobus, Barnes, and Lawless again saw the game near the home goal, aid whilst Warrington attacked in desperate fashion the St. Helens team, aided by Jackson, their custodian, defended their charge admirably. Just on the call of ' half-time a minor accrued to the visitors, the scrare then reading as follows: Warrington, three minces; St. Helens Recs., one minor. On change of ends it was thought that the St. Helens team with the aid of the wind; had &somewhat easy.taskLbefore them,_ but in this those who had dared to prophesy a runaway gaine were mistaken, for Warrington opened the second half in a determined manner. Frank Turner kicked off, and no reply being made to the restart, a, little groin d was gained with a useful run on the part of Bate. A kick by Gerrard was brilliantly responded to by. Evans, and no impression whatever could be made on the visitors' defer-Ice. A free kick by Frank Turner was got away by Jackson, and useful rushes of the St. Helens forwards, supplemented by a long kick by Seddon, were produc- tive of a minor. Two more followed in rapid succession, on one occasion Ellison just missing a goal from a free kick. However,' Warrington played up in surprising manner, and more than held their own. The forwards worked with renewed vigour. tackling strongly, awl never aliowingthe home backs to travel far. After Seddort had had a futile shot at goal, a grand display of passing between Bate, Antrobus, Barnes, Lawless, and Nevins raised the siege on the home line, and although the Recs. tried hard to clear, they foqnd in the Warring- toaians foemen worthy of their steel, and all their ener- gies proved abortive. Pilkington relieved a little, only to find Frank Turner, Bandies, and Povey each in turn showing up to distinct advantage. Pilkington made another effort to score, but Evans was particu- larly, safe, and danger was averted. Randles next came away with a smart dribble, and Lawless effected a capital run along touch, Jackson pulling him up. Then ensued the prettiest piece of play during the whole of the match. Bate secured from a pack, and passing to Nevins the last-named headed the oval to Barnes who threw to Massey, who, rounding his men in fine style, crossed the line, gaining to all appearances another unmistakable try. After...he had grounded somehow he lost possession, and the oval was kicked into touch in I goal. Some of the homesters appealed against the 1 legitimacy of the try, with the result that the referee I decided against the Warriagtonians, and to the sore disappointment of the visitors' supporters only a minor , was allowed. Such a decision was certainly not. war- ranted, as the point was so clearly gained. The drop out took place, and the Rees taking the oval down at a rapid pace Massey in staying their progress was injured and taken from the field of play. Soon after the whistle sounded, and the game had an unsatisfactory conclusion, the final score reading as Warrington 0-0-4, St Helens Recreation 0-0-5.

A surprise was effected in the semi-finals for the York- shire Cup. Huddersfield displayed such irresistible form that they on Saturday actually knocked out Hunslet by five goals and two tries to a try—a marvellous record in la match of such importance. The tie between Wakefield Trinity and Bradford was of a much more even descrip- tion, but the finish V 73.13 not generally anticipated. Brad- ford were supposed to have a better set of backs, but it was here they were out-classed, as the Trinitarians never made a mistake and kept their lines intact, whilst they ran up a goal and a try. The result of the final between Huddersfield and Wakefield would be difficult to fore- cast. The two ties of Saturday were witnessed by something like 40,000 spectators.

FOOTBALL—ASSOCIATION. People who study Association football are now wonder- ing how on earth Sheffield Wednesday managed to fight their way to the final for the Football Association Cup. They were no match whatever for the Blackburn Rovers, who created a new record by vanquishing the Yorkshire- men on Saturday by , the large number of six goals to one. In the previous rounds Sheffield Wednesday had upset three powerful League clubs in Accrington, Notts County, and Bolton Wanderers, not to mention the London Swifts, and by these performances had made many friends. Notwithstanding these successes, how- ever, good judees who had seen them during the season knew they could not cope with such a talented team as the Rovers, and this turned,.out correct. The Rovers have now the proud satisfaction of holding the cup for the fourth time in their histery, having previously triumpbed over the Queen's Park (twice) and West Brom- wich Albion, whilst the first time they appeared at the Oval they were beaten' by the Old Etonlans by a goal to nothing, this being their first check of the season. ,

div.p: MISCELLANEOUS.

Members of the Warrington Gymnasium were again pretty well to the fore on Saturday at the tournament at Liverpool promoted by the National Physical Recreation Society. Fair Turner was fortunate enough to be unop- posed in the physique competition and carried off the splendid silver shield valued at ten guineas. Warren and Podmore were well up in the high jump in which Lenton of the Liverpool gymnasium took the first prize. T. Locker was only beaten by one mark in the rope-climbing contest.
