div.p: STATES.
EILTItItICANE IN TIIE UNITED

BURIAL OF VICTIMS. NEW Yonx, MONDAY.—Reports continue to be received which show that the terrible storm scattered terribly fatal destruction throughout its course. At Clay, Ken- tucky, fifty persons were killed. In Union and Webster counties fifty.were killed and injured Twelve persons were killed and thirty injured at Kuttawa. The town of Golconda, Illinois, was nearly doraolished by the furious wind, and many of the inhabitants were killed. Yesterday was a day of sorrow, a great number of Thursday's victims being buried. The city could not furnish sufficient accommodation in the way of funeral cars or hearses, and so great was the demand that some of these carried as many as five bodies at one time to the burying grounds. The Mayor of Louisville has declined all subscriptions offered by other cities or States. NEW Yonx, MONDAY.—The floods in the Mississippi Valley still prevail. The town of Greenville, Missouri, is isolatea by the surrounding waters. Disha County, Arkansas, is submerged to a depth of fifteen feet. Three thousand men, women, and children have taken refuge on the housestops, and are famishing for want of food and shelter. The town of Skilowith, and Missouri is deeply flooded. The place is entirely deserted. Accounts continue,to be received showing the wide track taken by the tornado in Kentucky and Tennessee. At Dixon eight persons were killed and thirty injured by the fall of Nildings during the storm. Floods are doing great damage and causing much distress in Northern Louisiana and Mississippi. In Yazoo County, in the latter State, breaks varying from 600 to 1,500 feet in length have occurred in the levees, and a great tract of country is under water. Railway traffic is almost entire- ly stopped in the Mississippi Valley. The town of Greenville is entirely surrounded by water. A small place called Skipwith has been almost washed away, and at Laconia 2,000 people, provided with but little food, are cut off from communicating with the outer world.

div.head: MORFA DISASTER.
div.p: THE MORFA DISASTER.

The inquiry into the cause of the Morfa pit disaster, near Taibach, was resumed on Tuesday at Aberavon. Mr Cuthbertson, the coroner, stated that there were still 44 bodies unrecovered, in consequence of the outbreak of fire in the mine. The manager of the pit was examined, and said on the morning of the explosion the firetriers' books showed that the workings were free from gas. The doors of No. 3 heading were blown out- ward, and he therefore judged that the explosion originated in that heading. One of the firetriers gave evidence, and said en the Sunday night previous to the explosion he was through the Cribbwr vein, and found the workings free from gas. A shot was fired in No. St heading on the preybus Friday. Powder and a safety fuse were used, and the lamp lock was opened forithe purpose. Another shot was fired on the following day. On Monday, March 10, the day of the explosion, there were not any shots ready for firing. The Cribbwr vein was clean; there was not any coal-dust , lying about. He had seen blowers in No. 7 heading, but not one to fire. Other evidence was given, and the inquiry was adjourned until next day. The inquiry into the Morfa pit disaster was resumed on Wednesday_at Aberavon. Aubrey, the fireman, was recalled, and explained that in the shot firing the fuse was lighted at an open lamp. During the three months previous to the explosion he had found gas in the working places. He had no written authority for shot aring. William David, a repairer, said he went down the'pit in place of the night foreman on the Sunday night preceding the explosion. He found gas in Eley's stall, but did not attempt to clear it away, because miners were not at work there. He found gm in the same stall on Saturday, and also a danger mark. The Coroner produced the report-book, and ascertained that the witness could not read or write, and that the entry for Sunday night had been made by another miner. 'David admitted that he did not report the gas he found on Saturday night. In reply to further questions, he said the colliery rules were read to him by his son that he thought the explosion originated in Eley's stall, and that in his opinion the manager as to blame for not working the hand fan throughout Saturday and Sunday. The enquiry was again adjourned.

div.head: LABOUR AND CAPITAL. \ GREAT STRIKE IN THE LONDON BOOT AND SHOE
div.p: LABOUR AND CAPITAL. \ GREAT STRIKE IN THE LONDON BOOT AND SHOE

TRADE. On Monday morning a strike in the London boiiit and shoe trade commenced. Between four and five thousand men have been called out by the National Union of Operative Boot and Shoe Rivetters and Finishers, and in addition about six hundred Jewish workers are out. The dispute is on of the terms under which workshops shall be provided by masters, and arbitration resorted to for the settlement of disputes. The principle is con- ceded ; but the parties cannot agree on the details.
LONDON CHAMBER OF COMMERCE AND LABOUR

DISPUTES. The annual general meeting of the London Chamber of Commerce was held on Monday, Sir John Lubbock presiding. In the course of his presidential address, Sir John Lubbock said that the council of the chamber proposed that there should be appointed a Conciliation Committee, composed equally of employers and employed, for the settlement of labour disputes, the prevention and termination of strikes, and for any analagous or cognate purposes. Such a committee would, he though, enable points of difference to be settled by mutual consent, without any stoppage of trade. The proposed board would be one of conciliation rather than arbitration, and would, he thought, offer every inducement to parties to come to amicable arrangement before coming to the ulti- mate ratio of a strike. FAILURE IN THE IRON TRADE. On Monday, the shareholders of the Moss Bay Hema- tite Iron and Steel Company, Limited, of Workington, received circulars intimating that owing to the recent fall in prices, and to low-priced contracts, the company had been compelled to suspend payment. The directors believe, however, that the company is able to pay its debts in full, and propose reconstruction.

div.head: LIVERPOOL DOCKERS' STRIKE. WORK RESUMED.
div.p: THE LIVERPOOL DOCKERS' STRIKE. WORK RESUMED.

Work was resumed on Saturday by the Liverpool dock labourers on all the ships whose owners had conceded the rates demanded. There were some sharp collisions between unionists and non-unionionists, and in one in- stance au imported hand,, mad with terror, jumped into the river to escape from his assailants, and was rescued with considerable difficulty. Serious rioting occurred in Harrington Dock, a mob of 200 unionists swarming on board the steamer Merchant, and knocking the non- unionist labourers right and left. On Police-constable 651 remonstrating they threatened to throw him into the dock, and Inspector Hamilton, who came to his as- sistance, was assailed with stones. His assailant was identified as Robert Bolton, and was sentenced by thd stipendiary magistrate to two months' hard labour. Mr. Davitt, arrived in Liverpool from Ireland on Mon- day morning, and after conferring with the leaders of the strike movement, sought an interview with the Em- ployers' Labour Association. Subsequently Mr. Davitt stated at a mass meeting of dock labourers that he had proposed the concession of a dinner hour from twelve to one; two hours' pay if work is required during this hour; the men to be at liberty to work only nine hours per night if they object to work more; the union and non-union men to work harmoniously together. The Employers' Labour Association, Mr. Davitt proceeded, had accepted these terms, and he earnestly advised the men to go to work at once. He had obtained two reasonable concessions for them, and the other condi- tions, though they might not be palatable, were such as they could accept with honour. Mr. Wflugh after- wards addressed the men, saying that Mr. Davitr's advice to return to work was sound. On the question being put to the vote, only nine hands were held up for con- tinuing the struggle, and it is believed that their owners Fere under a misapprehension. Mr. Davitt made another earnest appeal to the men to keep all the conditions of their pledge, and was heartily cheered. On Tuesday a general resumption of work took place by the unionists, who seemed only too glad to find em- ployment. There was very little fricton throughout the day in the carrying out of the new arrangements. Mr. Davitt's advice to the men, and their promises to him, were respected with great fidelity. The harmonious working arrangement was carried out to the letter, and the head-constable, in consequence, was able to withdraw a considerable number of his reserve force from the docks. There being no longer a raison) d'etre for the retention of the military, the greater portion was quietly withdrawn on Tuesday, after Captain Nott-Rower had had consulta- tion with the Mayor. The situation is gradually be- coming normal, and Mr. Davitt's prophesy that the non- unionists would disappear is being everywhere fulfilled, for numerous batches of them took their departure on Tuesday on their own accord. Everywhere along the line of docks union men were at work early on Wednesday morning taking the places of great numbers of imported men, vvh3 had left the city during the night. Great numbers of the imported labourers began to demand their wages at the North docks on Wednesday forenoon, with a view to departing for their homes. Preparations were made to despatch them in batches during the afternoon and evening.

THE HOUSE OF COMMONS' STEEPLE- CHASE. The point-to-point steeple-chase by members of the House of Commons took place near Rugby on Saturday, there being thirteen competitors. The twelve-stone race was won by Mr. Elliott Lees' Damon, and the fourteen- stone race by Mr. Long's Crusader.

div.head: TRIPLE MURDER BY A MOTHER.
div.p: TRIPLE MURDER BY A MOTHER.

At Lewes Assizes, on Saturday, Mary Ann Taylor was found guilty of the murder of three of her children at Polegate, Sussex, by cutting their throats. The jury found she was insane at the time of the deed, and she was ordered to be detained during her Majesty's pleasure.

div.head: CHILD MURDER IN LONDON.
div.p: CHILD MURDER IN LONDON.

At an inquest at Canning Town, London, on Monday, a verdict of wilful murder was returned against Joseph Woods, for causing the death of his female child aged three weeks by striking it on the head with a poker. It was stated that the baby and another child who was ill had caused the prisoner sleepless nights.

div.head: 40s. BREACH OF PROMISE.
div.p: A 40s. BREACH OF PROMISE.

Mr. Justice Dav, sitting without a jury, at Leeds Assizes, awarded 405., without costs, to the plaintiff in an action for breach of promise. The plaintiff was a domestic servant, eighteen years of age, and stated to be a sufferer from epileptic fits. The defendant, twenty- three years of age, was getting 15s. a week, as a farm labourer.

div.head: QUEEN AT AILLES BAIN S.
div.p: THE QUEEN AT AILLES BAIN S.

MONDAY. —Queen Victoria continues to take walks in the morning and evening. Yesterday evening the Duke of Rutland, at present Minister in attendance upon the Queen, visited her Majesty, and was included in the Royal dinner party. This morning Prince Henry of Battenberg went for a ride, accompan- ied by Major Bigge and Lieut.-Colonal O'Neill.

div.head: Ni'REXHIM AND MANCHESTER.
div.p: Ni'REXHIM AND MANCHESTER.

The new route from Wrexham to Chester and Man- chester, and the intermediate villages and towns, by way of Harwarden and Hawarden Bridge, was opened on Monday, the first train conveying passengers over the new line leaving Wrexham at seven a.m. There are five stations on the new line, the first being Buckley Junction, where the new line diverges from the Wrex- ham and Connales Quay system. The other stations are Hawarden, Saughall, !Bacon, and Liverpool-road, Ches- ter. The Junction with the Cheshire Lines system is at Northgate Station, Chester. There will be five trains each way daily between Wrexham and Manchester.

div.head: IRISH LAND BILL.
div.p: THE IRISH LAND BILL.

The Purchase of Land and Congested Districts (Ire- land) Bill was issued to the public on Monday. Clause 1 provides for the sale of the holding for an amount t.,be fixed by reference to the L \rid Department created under the bill. Clause 3 provides for the securing of the advance by a purchase annuity charged on the holding in favour- of the Land Department for a term of forty.nino years,. and calculated at a rate of 4 per cent. per annum on the advance. Clause 5 provides that the guaranteed land stock shall be a capital stock, consisting of annuities yielding dividends at the rate of £2 15s. per cent. per annum on the nominal amount of the capital, which shall be payable by equal ha f yearly dividends on the first days of June and December in every year out of the Land Purchase Act. The Act is to come into force on the Ist November, 1890. unless the Lord Lieutentant may see fit to postpone the operation of part 3 till January Ist, 1891..

of our continental neighbours. Pretty much ths same may be said with regard to the decisions as to restriction on the labour of children— they do not go in recommendation beyond what is, broadly speaking, enforced under the Factory Acts in England. Touching Sunday labour, the Conference affirmed "that the day of rest for workmen under age should be Sunday, subject to the exceptions and the delay in execution which each country may consider necessary." This con- clusion, it will be noticed, is vague in terms, and it Would appear that it was purposely vague, as the French delegates, for instance, were careful not to commit themselves on what may be called the Sunday question.
_ . Lord SALISBURY suggested not long since that our continental competitors had an advantage over us in England in the use they made of Sunday labour; but this view of the subject may

fairly be questioned. Apart • from any con- sideration of religious observance, a day of rest one day in seven is valuable to man, looking at him merely as a working machine. The day of rest becomes a day of recreation, a day for the filling up of those wells of energy which have been drawn on too freely during the previous Rix days. Take, for instance, the case of the English navvy; he does not always employ his day of rest in the most restful fashion; but we venture to say that if he were kept at work every day, Sunday included', it would be found that, at the end of the year, less work had been done than is now accom- plished under our system of Sunday rest. As to the navvy himself, it is a matter of course to say that it would make a great difference to him ; his leisure would be gone; and his life would become shorter without being merrier. No ; the advan- tage, let Lord SALISBURY say what he will, is on the side of the nation that holds to its day Of rest one day in seven; and the sooner continental countries recognise this the aconer will they put themselves in a better position for competing with us. Of course, in so far as labour is ill-paid and badly organised on the Con- tinent, or not organised at all, there is scope on the part of employers for that cheap production Which is so terrible at times in its competitive Pressure. International Labour Conferences will tend to rectify this evil by diffusing knowledge and leading to uniformity of action. The discs- on on the results of the present conference which is taking place in every capital of Europe must have the effect of widening the information of artizans of all classes; and thus lead them to see that they must organise and act within their or- ganisation if they would reap some of the fruits of Industry which are already enjoyed in this country. Our faith is strong in a future in which the toiler thall be the first taker,while the capitalist shall have his share but no more than his share. It is a right reeve, little as has come of it, to hold this Into r- Oationai Conference ; it will be followed, in due tune, by International Conferences of workers ; and then when the workers everywhere perceive that they have interests in common, and that they are all-powerful, we shall have arrived at the dawn Of a lyrighter day.

Michael Varley pleaded that he had but " had a feW pints when he was brought before the War- rington magistrates on Saturday, for being drunk and disorderly. " A few pints"--not to quench his thirst, surely. Perhaps he was collecting "pints," with a VIQW to having a bath.

According to current reports, the Emperor of Germany is rather sore at Prince Bismarck's refusal to accept the offered dukedom. Matters have not been mended by a joke which Prince Bismarck cracked on his birthday. He said, referring to recent events—" The Emperor has made his best general a chancellor, and his best chancellor a general."

--- Sunday last, the Sunday before Easter, was Palm Sunday, a day which is always observed Ittoongst Roman Catholics as commemorative of Christ's entry into Jerusalem, when the multitude ttrewed palm leaves in his path. As the palm 'loos not grow in this country, a substitute is found in the early flowering' willow. It is not what hig popularly believed to be—a palm; but what luatters ? It serves.

There is not much likelihood of anything coming very soon of the agitation for reducing the hours of labour; but the factory operatives of Bolton 111:1 other parts of Lancashire are securing the next beSt thing—that is, an extension of the time for holidays. Two days extra holidays in the year have just been conceded by the employers. Wages Itre not paid during holidays ; and yet it is a clear gain to soul and body. All work and no play ends In Poor work all the day.

~., A London correspondent says :—" The sagacious Earl of Derby, foreseeing the not distant day when smoke of Prescot will make Knowsley unin- abitable, has bought a number of small properties Kent, and is Tit o w one of the most considerable landlords in that charming county. Lancashire for rent and Kent for residence is his motto. He 1,8 spending the Easter recess at one of his Kentish 11011Ses—liolwo0d, once the residence of Mr. Pitt."

When ti farmer _ (1, rank champagne with the 's I : _ qu. leire he said it was very nice, but they "didn't Seem to get no forrader." It is not so with the 3''unr, folk of the present day—they are as a rule ti ~ forrad" enough. In Liverpool the other day the lhop boys had a demonstration against long hours; -‘• 0,,, V now we Mar of a boy and a girl sending in esig'ils for the Watkin Tower. Well, well ; things raight be worse, although it is a little out of the eonnuon to hear of " designing" boys and girls.

Sunday, the Bth June, is the date of the Silver %Jubilee of Cardinal Manning's episcopal conseere- ktion • and already a movement is on foot to pre- nt his Eminence with a personal testimonial. All ~,ftsses, religions or non-religious, are proud of Cardinal who has laboured herocially to better ihe condition of the masses; and we anticipate a arge subscription list, which will be world-wide in character.
For modes of faith let graceless zealots fight; Ills can't be wrong whose life is in the right.

Spring, in the words of the poet Heber, not only I unlocks the flowers to paint the laughing soil;" it unlocks the gates of the gardens at Walton Lea, 5,11(1 reveals to admiring thousands one of the finest 1111"3 of camellias in the country. Alderman Oros- ;l.9ld runs some risk to his stock in thus throwing ,fus grounds and greenhouses open to the multitude; put it is characteristic of him to share with others ".liat which so much delights him; and it is to be n()Ped he will never have occasion to say that the Public abuse the privilege.

, With the inhabitants of Warrington it has u'een a case, of late, of water on the brain; but at Salford for some .time the difficulty has been one of gas in the upper chamber. Gas has a tendency t<3. explode; there was an explosion, on Wednesday, nen the gas frauds were under discussion by the 'Town Council, for one member said to another "I should like to smash your face, you ugly uttle devil." There was a scene, of course, and the eting adjourned. They haven't got to that at w arrington ; water is cooler. Ma,
nchester is interested, as all towns are inte- ted, in these gas frauds. The Gas Committee !aye decided to investigate the allegation against /* former gag. ofacial of the Manchester Corporation,

and to refuse to do business in any way with per- sons or firms who have been or may hereafter be found guilty of bribing in connection with the supply of coal, &c., to the Salford Corporation. This is a very sensible conclusion. Couldn't War- rington follow suit? Why not make these plun- derers of the public realize that it doesn't pay to be dishonest?

The Isle of Man is in the enjoyment of Home Rule, but it is just now in the throes of a redistri- tion of seats struggle. It does not seem to be generally known, and yet it is the fact, that the Warrington Improvement Bill provides for a redistribution of the electors of the various wards, consequent upon the extension of the borough. It is very desirable that there should be a reform in this respect; and yet it is a very delicate task. It is something, however, that, in order to comply with certain legal forms, the redistribution cannot be done in a hurry.

Mr. J. Slater Lewis set a good example as a County Councillor in giving an address to his con- stituents at Kingsley, on Saturday. He dealt with a large number of topics in an out-and-out fashion, and his address evidently gave great satisfaction. He is doing good work in exposing evils, and pointing to remedies; but now and again injures his argument by such unguarded expressions as speaking of landlords and lawyers as "vermin." We admit that he has had a great deal to annoy him, but it does not mend matters to give his opponents a handle' against him.

Emin Pasha has accepted service with the German Government, and is going back into the interior of Africa with "several German officers and 200 Soudanese soldiers." What a comment is this upon Stanley's " rescue" from the interior of Africa of Emin and his people! It would be laugh- able if it were not tragical in its suggestiveness ; for it cost hundreds of lives and terrible sufferings —that " rescue " of Emin Pasha! Ye poor Za,nzibaris ! and is it for this that life became a torture, and that so many of your brothers perished in the dark continent of fever and famine ?

The financial year for the nation closed on Monday, and it is now known that the Chancellor of the Exchequer has received £3,150,000 more than be reckoned on when framing the budget. What will he do with it? That is the question. The surplus was pramised by Lord Salisbury; on behalf of "assisted education " ; but the Prime Minister is understood to have backed out of that. Free Education was too Radical. So the question now is—what is to be done with the surplus? How would it be to reduce the duty on the cup which cheers," &c? That would suit most people to a "T," wouldn't it?

The question is being discussed in Liverpool whether, and under what restrictions, fishing should be permitted in the Vyrnwy Lake. Some years ago a similar question arose as to fishing is Walton Reservoir. Sir Gilbert Greenall, who has this matter in his hands, made a promise that the public should be allowed to fish as soon as the water was well stocked again. How about the stock? Is it growing? And what about the promise? Is it to be redeemed? and if so, when? As soon as steps are being taken for another election cam- paign? People would "like to know, you know," if the angling for votes and the angling for fish have any relation to each other.

APPOINTMENT OF OVERSEERS FOR RUNCORN DISTRICT. At Runcorn Petty Sessions,on Monday, the Magistrates appointed the following overseers :—Actori Grange, , Joseph Halliday and Robert Wade; Aston-by-Sutton, George Percival and Wm. Wilkinson ; Clifton, Wm. Baker and Joseph Stokes: Halton, Thomes Wright and Hugh Rowe ; Norton, Thomas Percival and Clement Baguley ; Stockham, Richard Nixon and James Clarke; Runcorn, E. unison and Samuel Taylor ; Sutton, Wm. Lowe and John Edwin Bate; Weston, E. Aaron; senr., and Thomas Ford.

CAMDEN MUTUAL IMPROVEMENT SOCIETY, RUNCORN. The last meeting of the session was held last night week, when there was a large attendance of members. Mr. S. C. Beckett occupied the chair. A lec- ture on "Socialism" was delivered by Mr. A. Harrison, the president, who made a vigorous attack on the pro- paganda of the social democrats, and explained the objects of socialists in Germany, France, and London. To carry out their programme, he said, would mean con- fiscation and robbery. The lecturer dealt with the question of capital aiid labour, and destitute condition of the masses. The lecture was most instructive and interesting, and a lively discussion followed. Messrs. A. Wardle, J. Moulton, J. Dutton, J. W. Woodland, J. Palin, W. Millington, and D. Bisbrown took part. • SPRING PAM:llo.'7ff, Spring Fashions.—J. & W. Durrosr, and 18. Sankey-st., Warrington.-Advt. WOHENS TEMPERANCE MEETING AT RUNCORN. Under the aupices of the Runcorn Circuit Wesleyan Temperance Society, a temperance meeting for women was held in Camden Sunday School on Tuesday after- noon. About 40 persons were present. Mrs. R. Spring. a lady representative of the U.R.A., Liverpool, delivered an eloquent address in which she described her labours amongst women. In the evening a public meeting was held at the same place, and there was a good attendance. The Rev. 11. Burson presided and he was supported by the Rev. C. Norman (llidsbury), Messrs. S. C. Beckett, T. Cooke and D. Bisbrown. Addresses on temperance topics were given by Mrs. Spring and Mr. F. J. Norman. • SPRING FASHIONS, Spring Faahions.—J. & W. DUTTON, 16 and IS, Sankey-at., Warrington.—Advt. GREENWAY-ROAD BOARD SCHOOLS, RUNCORN. An entertainment, illustrated by means ef the oxy-hy- drogen light, was given to the children attending these schools,last Wednesday evening. The views thrown on the screen consisted of the following series of slides :—" The Franklin search Expedition," "Billy's rose," by George R. Sims ; and "Jane Conquest,' a poem, by Dr. Croft ; together with a large variety of miscellaneous comic pic- tures. Songs and recitations wefe given by the chil- dren. - "Billy's rose" was very ably recited by Master W. Williams, and the recitation "Jane Conquest was well rendered by Miss Agnes Davies. The solo entitled "Bells" *as sung by Miss M. J. Williams. In addition to the large number of scholars who attended, there were also present a number of parents and friends, including Mr. Pritchard (chairman of the Board), and Mr. Moss (clerk). The teachers gave descriptions of the various , views, and the singing of the National Anthem con- cluded an enjoyable entertainment. SPRING FASHIONS, Spring Fashions.—d. &W. DUTTON, 16 and 18, tioaakey-et., Wartinglon.---Adat.

FOOTHILL MATCH AT RUN CORN. The return match between Runcorn and Owens Col- lege was played at Runcorn, on Wednesday evening. Tile visitors were assisted by several prominent players from Warrington club, but nevertheless, retired defeated by four goals, five tries, foie minors, to two minors. CONFIRMATION AT RUNCORN PARISH CHURCH. The Bishop of Chester, Dr. Jayne, on Tuesday held a confirmation service at Runcorn Parish Church. About 150 candidat, s were presented from the various churches in he parish and from Halton, and the whole of the local clergy took part in the proceedings. Time vicar of Runcorn (the Rev. A. M. Wood) read the exhortation, and the Bishop delivered the usual address to the confirm ees.

----------- LACEY-ST. BIBLE CLASS, WIDNES. In aid of the fund for renovating Victoria-road Wesleyan Chapel, a concert, organised by the above class, was given in Lacey-st. School, on Tuesday evening. There was a moderate attendance, and Mr. B. Brown presided. The vocalists were, Miss Fanny Bouffieur, soprano; Miss Millie Simon, contralto; Mr. Carl Benjons, tenor ; Mr. T. S. Smith, bass ; and Mr. W. J. Lofthouse, humourist. Miss Tinning was the accompanist, and performed a couple of solos. An admirable programme was gone through in good style. BASINETTES, new designs—Garland. Ironmonger, War- rington.—Advt. BRUNSWICK MUTUAL IMPROVEMENT SOCIETY, RUNCORN. 'Me closing meeting of the session was held on Wednes- day, when a good company sat down to an excellent tea arranged by MissSimister and Miss Crosbv,the hon. secs. Subsequently a concert was given, in which Miss Nellie Handley, Mr. It. Norris, and Mr. F. Scott took part. Mr. Bixton and Mr. Walter Millington gave readings. A most enjoyable evening was spent. At the finish of the proceedings a" Rambling Club" was formed in connec- tion with the class,and a Cemmittee,consisting of Messrs. B. Crosby, J. Povah, and Vs. Millington, was appointed , to arrange for three rambles in the country during the summer months. Botany and geology will principally attract the attention of the members. ButoakrioN.—lntending emigrauts to New York, Boston Philadelphia, San Francisco, Canada, China, Japan, Ans- i trails, or New.Z,aland, 6houla take tickets (lowest rates) at ! the " Examiner " Odice, by Cunard, Gunn!, American, and other lines.— John walker, agent, " Examiner ' Office, Bewsey-St.. Warrington.—Advt. ASSAULT ON A POLICEMAN AT WIDNES. At Widnes Police Court,ou Tuesday, before Mr. H. W. Deacon and Mr. ti Pilkiugton, Christopher Daley a powerful fellow, was charged with being drunk and dis- orderly and also with assaulting I'. C. Evans. About a quarter to two on Tuesday morning, the prisoner's sister ran out of the house in a terrified state and told P. C. Evans her brother was going to murder her. This an e pri- soner followed, d when the constable told him he would be reported, he struck him on the mouth with his fist. He then fetched a large table knife from the house, and attempted to stab the officer, but being foiled he returned into tlw house and Evans follow.. d him. There the prisoner seized 4 hatchet but. Evans wrenched it from his grasp arid took him into custody.--For being drunk, the prisoner was fined Sc. and costs and for the assault he was fined 40s. and costs.

GOOD FRIDAY AT RUNCORN AND WIDNES. The Christian festival was celebrated in the usual fashion in these towns. Religious services were held in cennection with the churches and the Catholic chapels, and on the whole the congregations were good. At sev- eral Nonconformist places tea parties and entertainments were held in the evening. At Widnes the railway com- panies afforded facilities for pleasure seekers by cheap bo.,kings, but the trains were run as on Sunday. Run- corn railway station was closed entirely, and the towns- people who wished to travel to any pleasure re3ort had to walk across the bridge to Widnes, an inconvenience which caused widespread grumbling. The various trains were well filled. Passengers for Liverpool and Southport were the most numerous. The weather was very favourable for outdoor enjoyment, and the pro- prietors of livery stables had a brisk business. GOSPEL MISSION BAND OF HOPE, RUNCORN. On Monday evening last, the children who had taken part in the recitals during the past winter, were regaled with a good tea at five o'clock, after which the last meeting of the Eeason was held. The temperance and sacred songs, dialogues, and recitals were rendered wonderfully well by the members of the band, and gave great satisfaction to the audience, as evidenced by their hearty responses. The chair was to have been occupied by the Rev. C. Finch, but being bereaved of his little girl last week, he was unavoidably prevented. Seven sisters of the band sung a beautiful hymn from Sankey's collection, with great effect, in memory of the departed 1 one. At the conclusion of the meeting a vote of thanks was unanimously accorded to the president of the band, ' Mr. S. Tickle, for devotion to the children, and for preparing them for the successful manner in which they displayed their ability at the public meetings, gratify- ing alike to parents, teachers, and friends. In response, he said his experience with the Band of Hope was the happiest in his life, and he hoped that after this their firstyear, they would develop both in numbers, interest, and usefulness, year by year, aild that all the members would grow up to be holy and useful men and women in the great cause of temperance and Christianity. Each of the children received an orange as they lett the meeting, and went home joyful and happy. SPRING FASHIONS. Spfing W. Durrox, 16 and 18, Sankey-at., Warrington.—Advt.

WIDNES LOCAL BOARD ELECTION. This annual election of five members of Widnes Local Board was decided on Wednesday, when the counting of the votes took place in the Board room at the Town Hall. Mr. Joshua Midwood was the returning officer and he was assisted by Mr. C. H. Lewin (legal adviser), Mr. J. T. Allen (clerk), and Mr. Goff (assistant overseer), and an efficient staff of counters. Each candidate had also a representative present. The contest was between five candidatesof the Owners' and Occupiers' Association and four candidates nominated by the rival organisation—the Ratepayers' Association. The fOrmer body nominated Messrs. F. H. Gossage, J.P., E. Carey, S. Sadler, T. Handley (retiring members), arid S. Owens. While their opponents were Messrs. J. Beech, G. I. Neil, W. J. Har- greaves, and James Tilley. The nominees of the Rate- payers' Association held meetings in various parts of the town, and conducted a strict canvass, while the other candidates adopted a policy of passive indifference, doing little active work beyond issuing an address. The result was declared as follows at 5 p.m. H. Gossage, 2,633; G. I. Neil, 2,104; E. Carey, 1,931; W. J. Har- greaves, 1,836; S. Sadler, 1,834; J. Tilley, 1,829; J. Beech, 1,819; S. Owens, 1,769 ;T. Handley, 1,712. The first five were declared elected. As the differente be- tween Mr. Sadler and Mr. Tilley is so slight there is a strong rumour abroad, that a scrutiny will be demanded. The poll was a very heavy one. 4,953 voting papers were sent out and 845 were returned undelivered, owing to change of residence. Of the papers collected 414 were blank and 317 were spoiled. After the declaration of the poll, Major Wareing (who represented Mr. Gossage) moved a vote of thanks to Mr. Midwood, for the con- scientious, painstaking and courteous manner in which I he had catried out the duties of returning officer.—Mr. 'Neil seconded the proposition, which was carried unani- mously. Mr. Midwood, in responding, moved a vote a thanks to the Clerk (Mr. Allen) and his assistants for the efficient manner in which they had carried out their part of the business, and the motion was seconded by Mr. Beech.—Mr. Allen suitably. acknowledged the com- pliment.
THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, APRIL 5, 1890

div.head: BRIDGET KILDARE AGAIN!
div.p: BRIDGET KILDARE AGAIN!

At the St.—liefens Town Hall, on Monday, Bridget Kildare again appeared before the magistrates on a i charge of misbehaviour. She was up" for the 181st time, and was committed to gaol for one month. • BICYCLER and TRICYCLES.--J. S. Garland. Warrington ; Branch, Earlestown. Advt. ADVANCE IN IRONWORKERS' WAGES. On Tuesday there came into operation throughout the whole of the Midlands the advance recently awarded under the sliding scale of 9d. per ton to paddlers and 7i per cent. to mill men. This raises the amount per ton of iron puddled to 9s. 9d. Eighteen months ago it was only 6s. 9d., so that ironworkers' wages have increased in that period by 44 per cent. The new rate is the highest that has been paid in Staffordshire for 12 years. SPRING FASIIIONS, Spring ntshonS.--..T. & W. DUTTON, 16 and 18, Sankey-at., Warrington.—Acirt.
TEM 'LANCASHIRE COUNTY COUNCIL-SELECTION OF
A MEDICAL OFFICER.

The comraittee of the Lancashire County Council appointe'l to select a medical officer for the county held a meeting on Monday, at Preston, at which it was decided to appoint Dr. Serjeant., medical officer to the Bolton Corporation, to the ofßce. The salary is .£BOO per annum, exclusive of travelling expenses. There was a large number of applicants, of , whom six were selected to appear before the ,committee. Dr. Serjeant is presi.,ent of the North-Western Association of Medical Officers. REUISTEIt GRA.TES.—J. S. Garland, 51, Bridge-street, War rington.—Advt. • SUBSIDENCES IN THE SALT DISTRICT OF CHESHIRE.

On Tuesday night,-aTte-r—tTe-Meeting of the North- wich Local Board, a conference was held between the members of the board; the suffering property- owners, and Mr. Brunner, the member for the division, to consider what steps should be taken in view of the refusal of the Salt anion, Limited, to entertain the application to compensate the property owners in, the division for losses from subsidences. M. John Clough, chairman of the Local Board, pre- sided. Mr. Brunner said he was intlined to think that if they again approached Mr. Ritchie for a Royal Commission, they would. be more favourably received than on the last occasion. As their member he would advise them not only to approach Mr. Ritchie, but to send a deputation to the House of Commons, and he would undertake on their behalf, what was a somewhat ,unusual step—namely, to move that their petition be read by the clerk at the table before the house. (Applause.)—A discussion ensued, and in the result Mr. Brunner's suggestions were adopted. SPRING FASHIONS, Spring Fashions.—J. &W. Dimos, 'l6 and 18, Saukey-st.. Warrington.—Adrt,

THE VYRNIVY AQUEDUCT UNDER THE MERSEY. At the meeting of the Liverpool Water Committee on Monday, under the chairmanship of Dr. Marsh, a report was presented by Mr. Deacon on the three crossings of the Vyrnwv aqueduct,—viz., at the Mersey, the Weaver, and the Manchester Ship Canal. With reference to the first place, it was stated that preparations are still being continued to carry the tunnel under the river. Operations in connection with laying the pipes in the bed of the Weaver are being pushed forward as rapidly as possible; and proceedings are being commenced to bring the aqueduct.across the Manchester Ship Canal.

div.head: DRAINAGE OF IRLAM AND DADIRHEAD. . . .
div.p: DRAINAGE OF IRLAM AND DADIRHEAD. . . .

--- On Wednesday, at the fortnightly meeting of the Barton Rural Sanitary Authority. a letter was read from Mr, George Ashley calling attention to the need of a main drainage system for these ham- lets. At present the sewage of these districts was turned into the watercourses which ran into the river Irwell, and as the river had been diverted in several places the flow of the water was stopped. The mouth of many of the drains would be too low to admit of the water being turned into the Ship Canal, so that there was every reason why a main drainage scheme should be prepared at once.—The Clerk was instructed to reply that the Authority had the matter under consideration. A BODY FOUND IN THE WIDNES AND ST. HBLBNS

div.head: CANAL.
div.p: CANAL.

The body of a middle-aged man, name unknown, was observed floating in the Widnes and St. Helens Canal, near Fiddler's Ferry, Penketh, on Wednesday morning. It was recovered from the water by seve- ral men who were discharging a fiat near the sta- tion. The clothes indicate that the deceased was probably a chemical labourer, and it is surmised that he fell into the canal while on his way to Widnes. An empty bottle which was found in one of the pockets strengthens the supposition. The body was removed to the Black Horse, Sankey Bridges, to await an inquest. An inquest was held on Thurs- day evening, at the Black Horse Inn, before Mr. W. T. Husband. Evidence was given to the effect that the deceased was a Ship Canal navvy, and not a chemical labourer, as was supposed, and that his name was Henry Fisher. He was forty years of age, and had lived with William Perry. a foreman on the Ship Canal, at No. 8, Birchdele View, Stock- ton Heath. Perry stated that lie had. known de- ceased for about fourteen years, and had lived with him at various places. He had lately been out of I sorts, and a little over a fortnight ago he left home to go to the doctor's to fetoti some medicine, and was not heard of or seen again until his body was found in t lie water. A small sum of money and one or two articles were found in the pockets of his clothes.. There was no e+idetice as to how he got into tiit water,and the jury returned an open ver- die; to the effect that he was found drowned.

'RUNCORN SCHOOL BOARD. The monthly meeting was held at the Town Hall on Tuesday evening. Mr. James Pritchard pre- sided. and there were present the Rev. Dr. Gastahli, Dr. MacDougall, Mr. S. Taylor, Mr. J. I. Howitt, Mr. G. Moss (clerk).

div.head: SCII" OOL MANAGNMENT.
div.p: SCII" OOL MANAGNMENT.

The School' Management Conitnittee4recom mended that the following scale of salaries be adopted for assistant masters (uncertificated) at Green way-road School : £5O, first year, rising by an annual increase of £2 10s. to a maximum of £65 per annum, each advance being sub- ject to a favourable report from the Committee. The sal- ary of Mr. R. H. Jarvis, assistant master, to be advanced to £55 per annurn.--On the proposition of the Chair- man, the minutes were passed with the exception of that referring to the scale of salaries, whioh was referred back for further consideration.

_ SCHOOL ATTENDANCE. The School Attendance Committee had held several meet- ings during the past month, when 110 parents were before the Committee for not sending their children regularly to school, and proceedings were ordered to be taken before the magistrates against 37 persons. The attend- ance at the school during the past month had been 83 per cent. of the number on the rolls—a considerable improve- ment on last month's, when the per-centage was 78 per cent ;83 per cent. was above the yearly aveiage. Accounts amounting,to £122 18s. 3d. were passed for payment.—The receipts for the month amounted to £129, including £lOO from the overseers.—The minutes were passed.
DRAWING TO RE T AUGHT.

The Clerk handed each member a copy of the New Education Codo.—Mr. Howitt said he was told at the last meeting that the Board could not teach the children drawing in their schools. The Education Department was not of that opinion for they had made drawing compulsory and he was very pleased to see it. The Board were compelled to do what some members said it was impossible to ao. PARENTS AND POLICE PROSECUTIONS. . . . .

Mr. Howitt said at present the School Attendance Com- mittee decided to send before the magistrates parents who did not cause their children; to regularly attend school. He thought it would be wise that such eases be first brought before the Board, grid that in the mean- time the attendance officvs warn those parents of the consequence of continued disregard of the Education Act. He believed that in the majority of the cases sent before the magistrates, the parents really deserved to be brought there because the primary object of the Board was to have the children educated, .Certain members got the blame for being severe in this matter, although he was of opinion that the Board were not severe, but if the cases were brought before the Board the members would all take their share of blame if there was any blatne.—Dr. McDougall: That is the course ; the Com- tnittee simply recommend the cases to the Board.—Mr. Taylor Said a miinber of the cases, read out that night were brought before the magistrates on the previous day, so that it had been the habit of the Attendance Committee to send these eases beiore the magistrates without taking the opinion of the Board. Heagreed with Mr. Howitt that every case ought to be considered by the Board. In his opinion there were some cases which were very hard indeed upon the parents, ..nd he did not know whether each case in all its bearings WaB taken into consideration, but he did think every case should be brought before the whole Board. There were. only two members of the School Attendance Committee, and it was not fair to them to take the responsibility.—Dr. McDougall. said they overlooked the Important fact that a delay of three weeks would often elapse before these cases could be dealt with. The recommendations of the committee were accepted by the Board and the. Board therefore assumed the whole responsibility. If they had the parents and children brought before the Board, the work of the Board would practically become inoperii,tive., They 'would he merely recapitulating proceedings which were infinitely better taken in Committee.—Mr. Howitt said he was of the opinion that the Board ought to give the final decision. He moved that in all future cases recommended to be brought before the magistrates. the. parents and children appear before the Board before the summonses are issued.—Mr. Taylor seconded the motion and remarked. that during the past month a very large batch had been summoned before the magistrates and to his` mind it looked alniost more than slavery dragging people down to the police court. It was all very well to say these children must go to school; there were always circumstances connected with each case that ought to he thoroughly investigated bythe whole Board. Parents, he said, got disheartened When sent before the magistrates, because they felt that they were made criminals—Dr. Gastaldi said if there , was any substantial good to be derived from this new I 'mode of acting he would vote, for it, but he doubted ' 1 whether it would be effectual, because the majority of the parents who were sent before the magistrates set the , law at defiance. It paid them better to pay the fine of ss. than to send their children to school. Many of those brought before the. Court spent all they darned is the publiehouse, and when Monday morning came they ha to pawn something to raise the money they needed for the school fees or other purposes. If they could prove that the new mode would produce a better at- tendance without sendingthe parents before the inagis- trates.:=-Mr Howitt : Because I think it will, that is the reason I move it.—Dr. MacDougall described the method proposed as circumlocution and contended that the Committee exercised their power with discretion ~,nd without any cruelty or oppression.—The Chairman did not think the work could be done more efficiently by the Board than it was by the Committee and he pointed out the waste of time that would occur if the Attend- ance Committee were abolished.—After further discus- sion Mr. Howitt's motion was defeated by three votes to two. The Chairman, Dr. Gastaldi, and Dr. MacDougall voted against the motion. • --

MALICIOUS PROSECUTION OF A WIDNES JOINER.—HEAV t DAMAGES. At the Liverpool Assizes, on Saturday, the case of Edwards v. Wynne and Lewin came on for bearing. —Mr. Kennedy, Q.C.. Mr. M'Connell, and Mr. nigh appeared for the plaintiff; Mr. Bingham, Q.C., and Mr. A. G. Steel were for the defendant Wynne, and Mr. T. Swift represented the defendant Lewin. The action was brought by the plaintiff. Thomas Edwards, against the defendant Peter Wynne, for mali- cious prosecution, and against Charles Edwin Lewin, .deputy magistrates' clerk, Widnes, for malicious prose- cution and slander. Mr. Kennedy, in opening the plain- , tiff's case, said that Edwards had gone through the , pain, degradation, and annoyance of being put on his trial on a charge of theft, a charge which was entirely without foundation. The plgintiff was a person who had worked his way from a small beginning to a position of respectability, and at one time he was of compara- tively good means. Re was a man about 52 years of age, and worked his way many years ago from his ap- prenticeship as a Joiner to be manager of the firm in which he was employed ; but subsequently he sustained considerable losses through being prostrated by illness. In July, 1889, he was not a man of any nieans, and was working as a joiner. Ile was brought info contact with the defendant Wynne, -who was engaged in house

. • .. building and land speculation. and who held the lease of certain land at Widnes, upon which he had erected six cottages, and upon winch he was about te erect six other cottages. Wynne sug- gested to Edwards that he should become a partner in the transaction, indeed the lessee of the land, that he should build the houses, and that they should make what profit they could by the sale of them. As a matter of fact that agreement was not carried out, and another one was drawn up, by which Edwards, for the sum of £620, was to set the work to build the houses, Wynne undertaking to pay the plaintiff that amount by instal- ments during the course of the erectien of the houses, and to supplliall the necessary bricks and timber. The , price of the bricks and timber were to be deemed as pay- ment to Edwards on the dates when supplied and deliv- ered. Wynne had apparently neither the cash nor the credit to supply the £620, or the timber and bricks. In December it came to the knowledge of Edwards that Wynne was going to oust him out of the possession of the houses. Edwards then determined, wisely or un- wisely, that the materials should not be in a position to be seized, and he made arrangements for the storage of the timber. But it did not occur to him that he could be accused of doing anything wrong or dishonest. An inspectorof police named Ross was present while the timber was being loaded, and when the carts arrived at the place where the material was to be stored—at Elizabeth-st., in Liverpool—Ross and Wynne appeared on the scene' and Edwards was given in charge, on the 9th December,for stealing this timber. He was taken to the detective-office in Dale-st., and detained there until !evening, when be was taken over to Widnes. On the I 10th he was brought before the magistratesand remanded Ito the 12th, when he 'again came before the Bench. Wynne gave evidence, and put forward the statement that this was his timber, and Edwards was committed for trial. On the 16th he was put upon his trial before the magistrates at the County Sessions, and was there I defended by Mr. M'Connell and Mr. Pugh. The charge ' against Edwards was dismissed, and he weitt from the court a free man. The charge he submitted, ought never to have been made, and was prompted by personal vengeance. As to Mr. Lewin, he was in the office of Mr. Spencley, the clerk to the magistrates at Widnes, and appeared to have taken a rather keen in crest in the proceedings for the prosecution. The action against him was for having gone before the Grand Jury and made a speech in which he said that Edwards came at six o'clock in the morning and took away the timber which belonged to Wynne. Evidence was afterwards called in support of the plain- tiff's case. His Lordship said it was doubtful whether evidence could be given as to what took place before the Grand Jury who permitted him to make a statement. What took place before the Grand Jury was privileged, and he never before heard an attempt made to prove what took place before a Grand jury. Mr. M'Connell, in the absence of his leader, said after his Lordship's expression of opinion he did not think the case ought to be pressed against Mr. Lewin.—His Lord- ship : Then Mr. Lewin may retire from the case' unless Mr. Swift sees fit to object. (Laupter.)—Mr. Swift: That will be judgment for Mr. Lewin, with costs.—His Lordship: Yes.—Mr. Ilighain. addressing the jury on behalf of Wynne, said that Edwards had not the money to pay wages or anything at all, and Wynne had, from week to week, to lend him money for wages as lie went along. Nor could he get the man to find the labour or to go on with the job. There were continuous letters from Wynne to FAwards,informing him that if he did not go on with the job it would have to be taken out of his hands. Wynne alone bought that timber, and was alone responsible for the priceof it,and what the jury had to de- cide was whether Wynne had reasonable cause for think- ing that Edwards was trying to steal away timber which I belonged to him. That was the whole story. The plaintiff brought his action for damages for malicious prosecii- tion against Mr. Wynne; he brou„eht an action for slander against Mr. Lewin. and wanted damages from him, but he was not going to get any; and the next action to be tried, if it was to be tried, was another action for damages which was brought against Mr. Wynne's solicitor, Mr. Poole, for slander. The man wanted to make a fortune out of this thing, he himself being the cause of it all Loy the disgraceful manner in which he came behind the back of Mr. Wynne and tried to get away that timber. His Lordship, in summing up the case, said in order to recover damages the plaintiff must first satisfy the jury that there was no reasonable and probable cause fer putting him on his trial, and he must then satisfy the jury, that the defendant could not have acted honestly and fairly and in good faith in putting the criminal law, in operation against him. He had heard the • evidence, and in the discharge of his duty he held that the defend- ant had no reasonable and probable cause for putting the criminal law into motion. It was clear there was a dispute between the two men which could have been settled by civil law. 'The only question left for the jury to decide was the serious one as to whether the defend- ant—though he might have been wrong in his aetioil— was acting maliciously and from any improper motive. The jury found a verdict for the plaintiff, and assessed damages at £l5O.

RUNCORN BOARD OF COMM ISiIONERS. The monthly meeting was held at the Town Hall, on Thtusclay. Mr. J. W. Light burn presided, and there were present Messrs. H. White, J. Meadow- croft. J. Pritchard, E. Imison, S. Taylor W. Rankin- son, H. J. Grice, S. Lake (law clerk), E. Marshall (secretary), Dr. McDougall (medical officer), and M. Barker (surveyor).

HEALTH OF THE TOWN. The Medical Officer reported that the number of deaths registered during the past month was 38. Of these deaths 13 were due to bronchitis, 5 plithisis, 4 con- vulsions, 4 natural decay, 3 mesenteric disease, 2 pre- mature birth, 2 heart disease, and one each to inflamma- tion of the windpipe, softening of the brain, apoplexy, muscular disease; and scarlatina. These deaths showed an average death rate of a fraction over 25 per 1,000 of the ei•timated population.—The Surveyor said there were 38 deaths in the corresponding period of last year.

WORK IN COMMITTEE. The Highway and Building Committee recommended that several plans be approved. The tender of Messrs. Unsworth for supplying the Market Superintendent was accepted on the recommendation of the General Pur- poses Committee. The Finance Committee reported that the receipts for the past month amounted to : General fund, £699 3s. 74.; District Fund. £l3 14s. 103.4 Library Fund, £53 16s. sd. Accounts were recom- mended for payment amounting to £lBB 13s. Bd. on general fund and £lO5 13s. sd. on loan account. With respect to the assessment and levying of the general dis. trict rate for the year ending 25th of March, 1891, it was recommended that the owner, instead of the occupier, be rated, under tile provision of Section 211 of the Public Health Act, 1675, where the rateable value of any pre- mises !labia to assessment does not exceed the sum oT ten pounds, and, that he be assessed on a reduced esti- mate of three-fourths of the net annual value of such 'property.—The Health Committee recommended that notices be served on several persons to abate nuisances arising from overcrOwding. The various minutes were passed.

div.head: LEGAL BEST/4E39..0F THE BOARD.
div.p: THE LEGAL BEST/4E39..0F THE BOARD.

Mr. Mea-ciowcroft moved " That a statement be pre- pared by the Secretary showing the number of legs.; cases referred to the Parliamentary and Legal Committee since its existence by the various Corn mit!ties of the Board ; and the cases dealt with hi/ various Committees 'apart from tl7e Parliknientary and Legal Committee ; and also such cases 119 could not be so dealt with by the respective committees owing to the delay which would arise if referred to the Parliamentary and Legal Com- mittee.—Mr. Meadowcreft said be aid not intend to resuscitate the resolutions brought forward at the last meeting. fie 'pointen out that in the ,Legal Committee the Board had ready machinery which could be put in operation when there wits any important Matter which the other committee did not feel they could well take up with their other duties. Before the Committee was formed there was a law case which cost the Com" pany which he represented, in rates about £3OO, and naturally one felt a little anxious that every Safeg,uard should be taken to prevent a repetition of that sort being done in future. However, the Board had taken the responsibility of the disestablishment of . the committee, and he could not readily ask the majority to reverse heir decision.—Mr. Imison seconded the motion, in order that Mr. Meadowcroft might receive. the information desired.—Mr. Pritchard. said the legal ommitiee was a very useful committee, and it was un- wise to abolish it. He -suggested that the Board should be supplied with the amount of legal expenses incurred during the MK years since the appointment of the Com- mittee, and daring the six years previous to its existence, and then he thought it would be demonstrated the use and service arid saving that the committee had been to • the ratepayers.—After further discussion the motion .was carried with this addition. -

- SHIP CANAL AGREEMENT. - The Chairman said an agreement had bem received from-the Ship Canal Company. and the question was should they get coullsers opinion upon it. Mr. Lake said it was a draft agreement carrying out the arrange- ments with the Ship Canal Company with regard to the nightsoil easement and the closing of different roads &c., which was dealt with at the last meeting.. The only point on which advice was required was with regard to the wharf arid tipping place between. -Mersey-st. and Ferry Slip. 'Fhis was an important item indeed, and as it was not quite clear, he thought it would be welt, for the small expense, to get counsel to settle the draft on behalf of the Commissioiiers.—Mr. Judson proposed and Mr. Hankinson seconded a resolution empowering Mr. Lake to crinsult counsel, and the resolution was carried unanimously. This was the whole of the business.

Richard Nicklingson was committed for trial at Ashby- de-la-Zouche on Monday, charged with murdering his broth er-i n-law. Damage to the amount of £2,500 was caused on Tues- day morning by fire in the flour mill occupied by Mr. J. W. Phillips, Vauxhall-road, in Liverpool. Dr. Peters is once again reported to be safe. The in- telligence has been furnished by Lieutenant Kehler, who at the end of December left Pangani, with a detachment of Major Wissmann's force, for Kilimanjaro. An anonymous donor has contributed £4OO to the Llanerch Colliery Fund, and £3OO to the Mona Colliery [ Fund.

div.head: FOOTBALL
div.p: FOOTBALL

-- WIDNES v. STOCKPORT " A " TEAMS.—This match was played at Widnes on Saturday. On two occasions Parkinson picked up and ran through his opponents in grand style, and was awarded a try, but the point was not improved upon. The play of the visitors was much ' superior to that of Widnes, and Heathcote succeeded in scoring a splendid try. At half time the score was one I try each. In the second half ‘Vidnes played up consider- ably better against the wind, and had the play in the I visitors quarter for the greater portion of that time. 1 Stockport eventually relieved their lines, and Mason from a line out, obtained possession and ran in good style scoring the second try for Stockport, which Downs failed to convert. Flockenhull next scored for Stockport. Final score: Stockport one goal, two tries, and three minors, to Widnes one t y and three minors. RUNCORN RECREATION T. BIRKENHEAD WANDERERS.— These teams met on Saturday at St. Anne's Field, be- ' fore 2,000 spectators. Sutherland kicked off at four I o'clock for the Wanderers, and no return being made, ; scrimmaging took place in Runcorn's 25; Runcorn picked up, bringing play in the Wanderers' 25, where several scrimmages were formed. Subsequently Morgan, May, and Garner broke away, carrying hostilities into the visitors' territory. From a line out Nelson ran and passed to Morgan, the latter player crossing, the line Bowyer failing at the place. Runcorn dropped out, scrimmages and line-outs being the order, when Kelly made his mark, but the kick was charged down, after which Hurst picked up, passed to Herbert, the latter to Norsworthy, who scored, Kelly failing at the place. Half-time score—Wanderers two tries, Runcorn nil. Restarting the Wanderers at once pressed, and from a line-out Hurst passed to Herbert, the same player land- ing a beautiful goal. Soon after C. Kelly gained another unimproved try. Continuing to press, a dead ball robbed the homesters of another try, a minor resulting. Another dead ball followed. Sutherland, Herbert, and May f.'ere next conspicuous, during which Kelky made a grand attempt at a drop, a try immediately afterwards being gained by Norsworthy, but again the place kick was a failure. The Recreation was by this time thoroughly disorganised, and after (3. Sutherland had run grandly into the Recs. 25, Norsworthy planted the ball behind the posts, Kelly kicking a goal, Hurst following with a fifth try, which was not converted. Result—Wanderers, 2 goals,6 tries, 7 minors; Recreation, nil. WIDNES T. STOCKPORT.—The return fixture between these two clubs was played at Stockport, on Saturday, the visitors being short of Hartles, full back, and Laws. The home tea in kicked off, and placed the visitors on the defensive. The play Was of an even nature, but the visitors had considerable difficulty in maintaining their position against the passing of their opponents. The forwards, however regained their lost position, and from a throw in on the line Farrell got over, and scored a try. Morris made a good attempt at goal from a difficult position. From the drop out the visitors again invaded the home quarter and a mira.r was conceded to them. The home team then pressed again, Cockrill having secured in his own quarter got away, and after a good run was not collared until he had reached the visitors' 25 flag. At half time the score was Widnes one try and one minor to Stock- port nil. On changing ends Farrell again almost got over. The wind being slightly with Stockport now the ball was rapidly taken into the home quarters,'where Morris failed to return, but Clarke came to the rescue. Dr. Smith then crossed the line for the home team, but Massey's attempt at goal proved fruitless. The pressure was continued by the home team, and a return from Morris was caught by Murray opposite the goal, which he sent over the bar, amidst enthusiastic cheers. From this point up to within a few minutes of the call of "no time, the visitors were constantly called upon to defend themselves against the pressure of their opponents. The game ended as follows :—Stockport one goal, one try, and one minor, to one try and one minor. The following represented the Widnes team :—Morris, back; Clarke, Brennan, and Peters, three-quarter back; McGurl, and Farrell, half backs; Gandy, Stubbs, Smith, Holt, Car- roll. Farmer, Gordon, Whelan, and Pearson, forwards. BROUGHTON RANDERS v. RUNCORN.—On the ground of the latter. Both clubs put their full strength on the field, and a grand game was witnessed. The home side having won the toss, Moxon started for the Rangers with the sun in their eyes. Davies returned with a grand kick, but the Rangers' forwards, getting the ball in the loose, dribbled to the other end of the field,where Brazen- dale got hold and relieved with a lofty punt. From this point Runcorn began to be aggressive, and from a kick by Wardley, Abrahams got possession and gained a try for the home team near the corner flag. Brazendale , failed at a place kick. On dropping out Runcorn became dangerous. From a scrimmage John Davies got over the Rangers' line near touch, and Crompton kicked a splen- did goal. The Rangers' forwards, by combined play, took the ball to the Runcorn 25, and Fligginbottom get- ting possession looked like scoring, but he was pushed into touch-in goal. Subsequently Runcorn scored two minors. Hugh Hughes afterwards crossed the line for Runcorn, but Brazendale failed at the place kick. Riley then gained an easy try for the home side, which Crompton had no difficulty in converting into a premier point. Despite the strenuous efforts of the ' Rangers they could not keep the home side from pressing and Riley WAS again prominent by-gaining a try against the ' Rangers. Brazendale's kick proved abortive. Still Run- corn had the best of the game, and from a pack near the quarter flag Davies got hold, and, eluding the Rangers' backs, put another try to Runcorn's credit. Crompton landed another goal. At half-time Runcorn were leading by three goals, three tries' and one minor, to Broughton ' Rangers one minor. The first to show prominently was Abrams, who put in a grand run, which was neutralized by good dribbling on the part of the Rangers' forwards, the result being that Runcorn conceded a minor. From a drop out the visitors still pressed, but they gained only minors. Dolan now got possession and ran into the Rangers' 25, and from a pack near the Rangers' line Crompton scored, but the point was not improved upon. 'The drop Out SAW the Rangers forcing their opponents back, and Skidmore picking up smartly gained a try against Runcorn, but Moxoefailed to improve the point. After re-starting Runcorn were forced back, and Long- worth gained a try for the Rangers in a favourable posi- tion. Maxon placed a beautiful goal. Towards the end of the game Broughton Rangers had considerably the best of matters, but their efforts came too late. and Runcorn proved easy winners by three goals, Pair tries, and three minors, to Broughton Rangers one goal, one try and five minors.
RUNCORN PETTY SESSIONS. MONDLY.—Before Mr. John Brundrit and Major Hazlehurst.

.... Tag QUEEN'S HEAD.—The license of this public-house, in Waterloo-rd., was transferred from Thos. McCommor to Thomas Whitfield. MUNE AND DISORDERLY.—For this offence a fine of ss. and costs was imposed upon George Jordan, John Moores, Robert Riddler, John Kilcross, and Thomas Corbett ; Ann Parkes was fined 10s. and costs; and Humphrey Ellis was fined 24. 6d. and costs.—Emma Howard, machinist, of Warrington, was sent to gaol for 14 days for disorderly conduct. Ax UNLICENSED Doe.—George Roberts, ot Greenway- road, was fined Ss. and costs for keeping a dog without a license. - BEOGlN6.—Chartes Dolby was sentenced to seven days' hard labour for begging in Lord-st. Smoot. Bosun CASES.—A number of parents were summoned for not sending their children regularly to school,and the usual -fine of 53. was imposed inch case.

div.p: WIDNES_ PETTY SESSIONS.

THU/MOAT. —Before Mr. Muspratt and Mr. Ga.skell. DRIINKENNESS.—MichaeI Connolly, Moss- st. ; And Chas. S. Sullivan Haley-mod were each fined ss. and costs for this offence. • AN UNIALIZZLED DOCl.—Jotm Roberts, Wright-st.ovas fined 2s. 6d. and costs for allowing his dog to be at large unmuzzled. Soloot. BOARD CesEs.—A number of persons were each fined ss. for neglecting to send their children regularly to school. CHIMNEY ON FIRE .—Thomas Sha.nagan, Oxford-st., was tined Is. and costs for allowing the chimney of his dwelling to be on Ere. CONTRIBUTION ORM R.—The magistrates ordered Edwards Dean, Moor-lane, to contribute is. per week towards the support of his son, who is an inmate of a truant school. A LIVELY 110179EHOLD.—Timothy Ellison of Ditton was summoned for assaulting Joseph Woodward on the 29th ult. On the date named Ellison was getting his dinner when his mother struck him on the um with the poker. Ile rose with the intention to take the poker from her, when the defendant, who lodged there, threw him down, attempted to choke him and "nearly kicked him to death." He managed to get outside, and the defendant then struck him on the head with a brick. Complaiiiant said Ellison, wanted to get the house in his own name.--The defence was that the complainant had thrown some medicine and water on his mother, and P.C. Porter heard Woodward threaten Ellison re- peatedly. The constable said Woodward gave the defendant great provocation.—Mr. Muspratt said com- plainant had brought this upon himself and dismissed the case. SHOCKING ASSAULT.—Thomas Ellis, 22, Oxford-street, was summoned for having assaulted Pasrick Cain a weak-minded young man of nineteen. On Thursday Cain was playing peggy, when the defendant threw a brick at him. The missle struck him on the eve, causing a serious wound. A fine of 10s. and costs 10s., was imposed.

Sarah Thomas was remanded at Haverfordwest on Monday, charged with attempting to poison her master. It was intimated that a second chargewould be preferred against her. SENTENCES ON A GANG OF SWINDLERS. The eight men charged with conspiracy to defraud were sentenced on Wednesday at the Old Bailey. Mr. Fulton said the gang had carried out systematic frauds for over twenty years. They had their legal represen- tative and their spiritual adviser, who was alluded to as most dangerous. He (Gurling) was sentenced to twenty, Farrell Grant to fifteen and Scorey and Wakeham to five r years' penal servitude. Brown (recommended to mercy) got six months, and Lewis four months, with hard labaur.
THINGS HEARD AND SEEN. Br AN OCCASIONAL CORRESPONDENT.

The researches of Mr. W. Handley into the charities of Cheshire and into the laws relating to Charities are likely to bear good fruit. The accounts of the Runcorn Charities are to be submitted to the ratepayers, for the first time, at an adjourned meeting of the Vestry during the present month; and from statements made at the Township meeting at Halton, the accounts of the valuable charities in that neighbourhood will also be produced at the Parish Church Vestry; at Sutton, two charities, supposed to be lost have been discovered; and at Daresbury inquiries are being made with regard to field, left for charitable puoses, which has been sold to the Ship Canal Company. A rather extraordinary revelation was made at the Runcorn township meeting. Mr. Handley showed that Bethesda Lecture Hall was the parish vestry room for the township, by an order of the Local Government Board issued about nine years ago; and inquiries made by the vicar and officials of the Parish Church have led them to the conclusion that the Hall is the legal place for the vestry meet- ing which has been usually held in the National Schools. It is understood that the Parish Church vestry will be held there some evening during next week. Perhaps this will be unpalatable news for some of our staunch Churchmen. . . .

—„ The result of Widnes Local Board election is only what could have been expected from the manner in which the opposing forces were working. Energy and determination were displayed on behalf of the candidates of the Ratepayer& Association; on the other hand. apathpand neglect prevailed, with the consequent result of defeat. Had it not been for the plural votes of the manufacturers, there is not the slightest doubt that the Ratepayers' Association would have returned their four candidates instead of only two. One outcome of the contest is to be an agitation for the incorporation of the township, when plural voting will be abolished. Mr. Hargreaves deserved to succeed, if only for the perseverance he has displayed in moving the ratepayers. This was the fifth occasion on which he had been a candidate for local honours, and verily he bath his reward. ' It was expected that Mr. Tilley, as a Catholic, would have occupied a position high on the list, and. the hopes of his party appeared likely to be ful- filled at one period of the counting. At three o'clock Mr. Tilley's return seemed 'assured, and he left the Boardroom confident in the result, lie informed a number of persons who were waiting outside for the result that he had been elected, an after responding to the cheer which arose, by raising his hat, he went home. His feelings when he learned that Mr. Sadler had thrown him out by the narrow majority of five votes would be the reverse of pleasant. Canon Dodd, of Stretton, has declared war on the sparrows, and has set a price on their innocent heads. The Vicar of Runcorn heeds not the spar- rows, but cherishes evil thoughts of the inoffensive fowl. In the grounds of St. Michaels Church, Run- corn, are planted some Lombardy poplars, the gift of Mr. J. N. Lelle, which are likely to prove a great ornament. Vicar Wood, commenting on these trees in the current month's parish magazine, thus con- cludes "We wish some one would catch and cook the fowls which constantly tear up the grass." Who can decide whether Canon or Vicar hears off the palm ? Would the Vicar grant absolution if some venturous person brought himself within the meshes of the law by carrying out his wish.
PENKETIL THE WESLEYAN SUNDAY SCHOOL,

The annual meeting in connection with Penketh Wesleyan Sunday School was held last evening, Mr. R.Gartiett presiding. The Secretary (Mr. B. Hobson), read his report which ihowed that the total 'number of scholars, teachers, and officers was 266. The average attendance in the morning was 118, and in the afternoon 157. The Librarian (Mr. Greenhouse) stated that there were 220 books in the library, and that these were used by 145 readers, the number of readers showing an increase lof 25 upon last year. An address was given by Mr. IC. E. Parker, and the prizes for good attendance, &c., were afterwards distributed.

div.head: PENKETH FRIENDS' SCHOOL.
div.p: PENKETH FRIENDS' SCHOOL.

The annual re-union of scholars took place yesterday at the Penketh Friends School, and proved very enjcy- able, the splendid weather being very favourable to out- door games and exercises. In the morning there was a football match, between the present and past scholars, which resulted in the present scholars proving victorious by six points to n.ne. Afterwards about 120 persons of whom 62 were old scholars, sat down to dinner together. Dinner over, the old scholars were photographed in a group by one of the masters. The annual meeting of the old scholars was held in the afternoon, the chair being occupied by Mr. Hodgson. of Manchester. Amongst those also ore4ent were Alderman Holmes, Mr. C. J. Holmes, Mr. W. Darbyshire, Mr. Sykes, Mr. and Mrs. W. Fletcher. and Mr. and Mrs. Priestman (Latchford). Mr. Follows gave a statement regarding the rise and progress of the school. The meeting unanimously requested Mr. Christropher Bradshaw (Manchester) to act as president for the ensuing year, and to prepare an address for the old scholars meeting of 1891. Mr. Samuel Whalley Davies was elected treasurer' and Mr. Follows secretary. During the meeting several speeches were made and Mr. J. T. Gumersall, the president of the school, referred to the necessity of keeping an eye on the old scholars, not in the way cf espionage, but with a view to helping thorn on in life, at a time, when they, perhaps, most needed help, just after they had gone from the school into the world. In the grounds the scholars enjoyed themselves at various games during the afternoon, and visitors had the pleasure of inspecting an exhibition of interesting articles, got together by the members of the Field Club, in connection with the school. Some of the specimens were of great interest, especially in the sense that they were representative of the neighbourhood, and the exhibition was a decided attraction. Among the exhillts were a flint and steel, once used at the house where the late John Bright lived when he was at Penketh. Tea was served at fiveo'clock, and in the evening there was a concluding entertainment, at which Mr. C. Jackson Holmes presided, and songs, recitations, itc., were given. It may be added that some casts formerly belwi,ging to the late Warrington Wood, have been this week presented to the scheri by a relative.
FRODSHAM. OVERSEERS FOR FRODSHAM AND HELSBY DISTRICT.

At Eddisbury Petty Sessions, on Monday, the magis- trates appointed the following overseers, amongst others: —Acton, J. B. Hough and J. Weave; Alyanley. Jas. Greenvray and S. H. Noden ; Dunham-oth-Hill, Jas. Povey and R. Littler; Frodsham Lordship, R. Bate and Jas. Percival; Manley, S. Newport and D. Evans; Newton-by-Frodsharn, Thos. Pickering and EL Frith. On the township of Helsby being reached, Mr. Fletcher, solicitor, said he had an application, which was that the ma2istrates'do not take the two first names on the list; but take one of them, Mr. Joseph Jeffs,and another, that of M. Taylor, whose name also appeared on the list. The reason why he did this vra4 because Messrs. Jeffs and Mains had occupied the position for some years, and the leading ratepayers thought it was just as well there should he a change, so that they might have some know- ledge of the way in which the affairs of the township were being managed.—He called Mr. Taylor, who said he represented a ratability of his own property of £6O or £7O gross, and also the Hetsby Telegraphic Manufactur- ing Company, which was between £5OO and £6OO gross. —Mr. Fletcher said they did not suggest any- thing wrong.—Mr. Guest, the second largest rate- payer, said he applied that Mr. Taylor's name be put along with that of Mr. Jeffs.—The request was acceded to.—Mr. Fletcher said he had another application to make with reference to the same township. The town- ship meeting was convened and held on the evening of March 27th. Two gentlemen were put in nomination for vvaywardens, and the Chairman declared the show of hands to be in favour of Mr. Blythe against Mr. Guest, and% poll was demanded. The Chairman, however, refused to take the poll, and he understood that he still persisted in his refusal. Under the circumstances, he thought the Bench would be of opinion that no way- warden had been appointed, and it would be for them to say so. He would suggest that unless a poll was taken the magistrates should refuse to make the appointment, so that, as by law required, a poll would be taken.—The Chairman said the poll must he taken, if not they woult have to make the appointment at their next meeting.

A blacksmith named George Osbaldistone, employed at Leigh, has received information that owing to the death of a great uncle he and his two sisters have fallen heirs to a sum of £12,000 and some valuable property in London. -------

THE ALLEGED MISCARRIAGE OF JUSTICE. The hearing of an extraordinary charge of poaching and assault was concluded at 'Derbyshire Assizes, on Wednesday, before Mr. Justice Hawkins. Alfred Tunni- cliffe, John Dytche, Henry Dytche, and Fred Barton were charged with the offence, which it was alleged was committed at Bentley Carr, near Ashbourne, last December. The singular part of the case was that four men are undergoing five years penal servitude far the crime, and that the prosecution now, which was under- taken by the Treasury, was the result of the present prisoners openly boasting that the convicts were inno- cent, and that they themselves were guilty. The defence was that the alleged confessions were nothing more than mere brag, and had no serious significance. The pri- soners were acquitted.
