div.head: 'WAILRINEVION TOWN .• COUNCIL.
div.p: 'WAILRINEVION TOWN .• COUNCIL.

A meeting of this Council, was held at the Town Hall, on Tuesday evening. The Committee recommended that £2 be granted P.C. Rowbottom for meritorious conduct in rescuing a man named William Dakin from drowning in the canal near Black Bear bridge 'on the '24th Feb. Also, that the tender of Mr. Wm. • Fletcher for the whitewashing and cleaning of the bride- , r ' well, at £7 45., be accepted ; and that the teem crier be supplied with a pair of trousers and vest. The minutes ,were confirmed on the motion of the MAYOR, seconded by Councillor MARSH. STREET IMPROVEMENT COMMITTEE. The Committee recorded that the plans of the following buildings, &c., be appreved :—" Give and Take" line in Church Place; for the church wardens of the Parish Church ; 9 house 9 in proposed street off Orford-lane, for Mr. Thomas McCue; additions to house, 67, Sankey-st., for Charles Nhite, Esq.; stock room behind premises in Bridge-st., for Mr. Kirby ; and that permission be given to Henry Milling and Company, Limited, to erect a lamp o over their premises, at 48, Sankey-st.,,to be fixed 12 feet ; -from pavements,„ and-3 feet 6 inches to centre of lamp from front wall. The Committee's estimate of expendi- ture amounted, to £2,440. . Alderman Waco moved,. and Councillor HEATON 1 ▪ seconded, the adoption of these minutes. Councillor FLEMING said a building was being put up in Butterniarket-st., on the site of an old dilapidattd cottage. The cottage had projected in the street, and he found the new building was being put down in the same position. The building projected nearly a yard on to ¶1 ap. the parapet, and he thought this was the most disgraces ful thing that had been done since he came into Warring. ' ton. He felt sorry about it, and there was not a man, woman, or child living in the town who did not see that • a mistake had been made. He should like to know how the mistake had been made. Alderman BURGESS said he had seen bills upon the • walls that day cautioning people' against 'encroaching upon the yard spaces behind their dwellings, and giving them fair notice of their liability to heavy penalties if the thing was persisted in. He hoped this would have its effect,and that they should have a sensible diminution of these encroachments. (Hear, hear.)' - Councillor MONKS, referring to the subject mentioned by Councillor Fleming, said it was evidently a blunder - • and he should like to know how it could have been made. Alderman WRIGHT, in replying, said there evidently • had been a blunder. He was not present at the Com- • mittee meeting which passed the plans, but owing toi , there not bong a definite bloek plan it had been taken I for granted that the street line would be quite satisfac- tory. The borough surveyor and the Committee had evidently overlooked the fact. It was one of those great u mistakes that ought never to have occurred. The minutes were then confirmed. SANITARY COMMITTEE. . • The total estimate of expenditure for the next twelve months of the Sanitary Committee was £9,992 3s. 11d. The minutes contained the following resolutions :—That in the opinion of this Committee it is aesirable that a " Medical Officer of Health be appointed for the adminis- trative County of Lancaster; that the area on the north ' side of Bewsey-road, declared by the Board of Agriculture to be an infected area, be now declared free from swine .fever. Alderman Burtosss, in moving the adoption of the minutes. said there was only about £2O difference be- tween the Committee's estimates this year and last. He believed also that they should have something to their credit that did not appear, and as the year went on he hoped they should find that they were somewhat within the limits of their estimates. They had estimated pretty freely, and had provided for some improvement at the hospital. (Hear, hear.) Councillor VOISEY seconded;the adoption of the minutes, which was agreed to. div.p: THE GAS COMMITTEE.

The Gas Committee reported the average illuminating power of the gas for tho past four weeks was equal to 18.38 eandlcs at both works. Aldermah HOLMES proposed, and Alderman WRIGHT seconded the confirmation of the minutes of this Com- mittee.

Councillor VOMIT said he would like.to have from the Chairman of the Committee a statement of the probable result of the year that terminated on the 25th March, as to the amount of profit the Committee were likely to have made up to that time.

Alderman ftOL3IES replied that there would be no hesi- tation whatever in presenting such a statement. One had been presented every year since the Corporation took over the Gas Works ; the annual statement would be presented to the Council as soon as the auditors had gone through the accounts. Councillor VOISEY said his question was : Could the Chairman of the Committee give him an estimate, or an approximate account, of what the profits had been? Alderman Hots said such a statement might be given, but he could not give it at the moment. It was very desirable that gentlemen should give him private notice of their intention to ask him such questions, and he would then be prepared with an answer which would be more satisfactory to the Council at large. The minutes were then adopted.

div.head: NEW BILL.-THE PRELIMINARY COSTS.
div.p: THE NEW BILL.-THE PRELIMINARY COSTS.

The minutes of the General Purposes Committee were unusually bulky, as they contained several resolutions, &c., which were submitted to the last Council meeting but not passed on that occasion owing to the Council prematurely dissolving. Amongst the resolutions of the Committee were several bearing upon • the purchase of the Water Works and other matters contained in the Parliamentary Bill, and the substance of 'which have already been given in our columns. Amongst theresolu- tions submitted to the Council were the following : (1). That the sum of £5OO, on account of Parliamentary costs-already incurred, be allowed, and a cheque for same forwardad to the Town Clerk's London agents. (2). The Town Clerk having reported that the County Coun- cil of Lancashire had, under the powers of the Local Government Act, 1888, delegated to the Corporation the powers and duties under that Act, relating to the licen- sing of houses and places for the public performance of stage plays (which powers and duties have been hitherto exercised by the borbugh justices), and in respect nf the execution as the local authority of th 3 Explosives Act, 1875, it was resolved, that the Council be recommended to direct the Watch Committee to consider all applications for licences and to take all necessrry 'Steps for the due execution of tbe powers and duties aforesaid.—(3). That the Ex-Mayer and the Borough Treasurer be appointed to attend the meeting of the Council of the Association of Municipal Corporations, on the 27th instant, when several import- ant matters affecting Corporations will be considered. (4.) That a petition be presented against the "London and North-Western Railway Bill, 1890," for the purpose of obtaining clauses for the protection of the interests of the Corporation affected by such Mill. (5.) That a peti- tion be presented against the "Manchester Ship Canal (Various Powers) Bill, 1890," with the object of obtaining provisions for the protection of the Corporation, similar to those obtained in the Principal Act of 1885. The Committee's estimate of yearly expenditure amounted to £2,186 17s. 4d. The MAYOR proposed, and Councillor GREENALL seconded, the confirmation of the minutes of this Corn-

mittee. Councillor FLOOD : IS it the intention of the General Purposes Committee to have a valuation of the stock'ind plant of the Water Works'now that they have succeeded in carrying the poll? The MAYOR said that a resolution, which appeared in the minutes, told the Counhil exactly what they must do :—" That the Town Clerk be instructed to submit to the Water Works Company the 'proposal of the Sub. Committee for the purchase of their undertaking, such proposal to be subject to the approval of the Council and the ratepayers, and also subject to an examination of the Company's pr&perty and accounts." Alderman HARRISON said he did not know whether, perhaps, some gentlemen were not entertaining too florid an idea of how far an examination into the Water Works

accounts and the nature of the property would be per- mitted to go. It should be borne in m'nd that the Water Works Company were not willing s U but that the Council were going to them, and had thereforeto depend upon the Water Works Company as to how far their in- vestigations might go. He was sure, however, that the , Company would throw no obstacle in the way of their taking the property, that they would behave both handsomely and straightforwardly, and would give the Council every reasonable facility for seeing what they were about to purchase.
Councillor ij.LACEHI7RST : Surely We half of the bargain to make. . .
shall have one-
Councillor Fioon asked whether it was the intention of the Committee to call in the services of an expert to value the stock and plant. Alderman HARRISON : It is intended to do so.

Councillor FLOOD said that in asking the question he was merely carrying out a view which was largely ex- pressed outside the Council. It was the general feeling that either the Council were paying too much, buying a pig in a poke, or running blindly at their bargain. ' Alderman HARRISON drew Councillor Flood's attention to a letter which he (Alderman Harrison) published a short time ago relative to the interview which he and other members of the Council had with the Water Works Company. At that interview, he said they could not, of course, bind themselves to do anything until scientific opinion had been obtained as to the nature and quality and probable supply of the water. Mr. Charlton Parr, in reply, said he did not see how the Council could dis- pense with that, and there would be no objection to it. Therefore, it was distinctly understood by the General Purposes Committee that every precaution would be taken. The public need have no anxiety about them buying a pig in a poke. (Hear hear.) Alderman HOLMES said that a second resolution on the minutes was to the effect that a cheque for £5OO, on account of Parliamentary costs already incurred, be sent to the Town Clerk's London agents. He would like to know whether that was a legal expenditure—whether the Council had power, under present circumstances, to remit the sum.

Councillor MONKS: I would like to supplement that enquiry by asking whether all the legal notices and forms repuired by Act of Parliament had been gone through, in reference to the expenditure of that money, before the poll of the ratepayers was taken. The TOWN CLERK said that the Borough Funds Act re- quired a further meetieg of the Council for the confirmation of the resolutions passed on the 19th December. The whole of the formal steps had been taken.

Alderman HARRISON remarked that a copy of the Bill was first printed in Warrington. Subsequently another copy was printed in London at an enormously increased expenditure. Before the Council committed themselves to the payment of that account he would like to know whether there was any item in that £5OO which would bind them, supposing they paid it, to the payment of the charge for printing. The Town CLERK said he felt placed somewhat in a dilemma. Really, no part of those expenses could be paid until after the second confirmatory meeting of the Council. The agents, however, required recouping for expenses they had incurred already. The sum of £5OO was intended to cover the cost of printing and House fees.

Alderman HARRISON .1 I should object to it, then, decidedly. Councillor FLEXING: It seems an enormous sum. The TOWN CLERK: But there are counsel's fees and House fees as well. Alderman HARRISON said that the Bill which was printed in Warrington was printed at a cost of about 2.40. Somebody got a duplicate of it printed. It might have been thought that the printers who did the first wculd do the second also, and that the expense would certainly not be greater; but somebody had the duplicate printed in London, at an expenditure of more than £2OO.
Councillor FLEmisa : Who is this" somebody "? Alderman llssiirsow I don't know. I want to know.
Councillor BLAMEHITIIST Am Ito take it that we pay this £4O as well as the £200?

Alderman HARRISON replied in the affirmative. The TOWN CLERK said he would advise the Council to pass the resolution or reduce it by the amount of the printing account, £2OO. If the Bill was to be proceeded with, the agents must be recouped payments out of pocket for counsel's fees, Ste. Alderman BURGESS : Am I to understand that, sup- posing you send the balance of £3OO, no part of that sum will go in payment of the printing account? The TOWN CLERK: That is what I would suggest. Alderman BURGESS said he thought that after the vote which had been given in the borough, and the emphatic opinion which had been given as to the desirability of obtaining the Bill, it would not, be becoming on the part of the Council to say that they opposed the opinion of the large majority of ratepayerswho had recorded their votes in favour of going on with the Bill, _

Councillor-MoNxs : This £5OO does not become legal until after the next statutory meeting P The TowN CLERK: It dries not. But it is usual to re- mit expenses out of pocket. Councillor MONKS: IS such a resolution legal. The TOWN CLERK: It is only reasonable that they should be recouped their expenses. Councillor VOISEY said he thought the Council were taking up a very undignified position in the matter. He would certainly not care to be a party to the captious spirit which seemed to have seized some members of the Council. The London agents knew nothing of the Council's local difficulties. The Town Clerk had, he dared say, selected very suitable people to conduct the Bill through Parliament, and they could not do their , work without payment. (Hear, hear.) The MAYOR: I think it would be much better if this matter were settled in Committee. Nobody knows any- thing about this £2OO.

Councillor BOLTON was of opinion that as the debt had been incurred it should be paid. ' The MAYOR said that Alderman Harrison had told the Council that a cer am n Bill had been printed in Wamng- ton at a cost of some £4O, and then, for some reason or other, the same Bill had been reproduced in London at a cost of £2OO. Councillor Simw-GREEtt, in seconding the proposition, pointed out that the claim upon the overseers was equiva- lent to over 2d. in the £ less than it was last year, and helped them materially in their reduction of ed. in the £.

_ Councillor VOISBY said it was a remarkable fact that, notwithstanding that both instalments and interest in respect of Longford depot and the widening of Bridge-st. had been included, the aggregate estimate for the ensu- ing year was less than it had been either for 1889 or 1888. That was gratifying, but it occasioned the ques- tion—How had it come about? He wished to ask the Chairman of the Committee what sums had been paid over to the Borough Treasurer in respect of profits on the gas, to be made available for reducing the rates. He wanted to know, also, what had become of the £2,500 which was shown as reserve last year; was it included in the bank balance? • Councillor VOISBY : We get that in the year now com- mencing? Alderman HOLMES : We got one half of it during the year Which has just expired. As to the £2.500, that is intact ; part is invested and part in the bank. It is not taken into this estimate. Councillor VOISEY : What is there in the shape of actual cash that helps the rate—what has beea mid that we are getting the benefit of in these estimates ? TUE NEW RATES. On the proposition of Alderman HOLMES, seconded by Councillor SRAW GREEN, the following resolutions were passed :—" That tie Council hereby estimate that the amount of £8,130 3s. 4d. will, in addition to the borough fund, be required and sufficient for the purposes to which the borough lurid is applicable, under the Muni- cipal Corporations Act. 1882, or otherwise by law, for the year to end 25th March, 1891."—" That the Council do hereby order a borough rate to be made in pursuance I of the Municipal Corporations Act, 1882, in order to raise the said amount."—" That the estimate for an im- provement rate as recommended by the Finance Com- mittee be confirmed, and that the Finance Committee do make an improvement rate accordingly at 2s. 6d. in tbe £, to be collected by two half-yearly instalments, and be authorized to affix the common seal of the borough thereto."—" That the estimate for a sewers rate as re- commended by the Finance Committee be confirmed, and that the Finance Committee do make a sewers rate ac- cordingly at 4d. in the £, to be collected by two half- yearly instalments, and be authorised to affix the com- mon seal of the borough thereto." div.head: ATHERTON MURDER.
div.p: THE ATHERTON MURDER.
DATE OF EXECUTION:

The High Sheriff of Lancashire has fixed the morning of Tuesday, the 15th of April, as the date on which William Chadwick, convicted at the last Liverpool Assizes of the murder of a pawnbroker's assistant at Atherton, will be executed. -The execution will take place at Kirkdale Gaol at eight o'clock, and it is expected that Berry will be the executioner.

div.head: WELSH SUNDAY CLOSING.
div.p: WELSH SUNDAY CLOSING.

The report of the Royal Commissioners on Welsh Sun- day Closing has been issued. The Commissioners say that in those districts which were already temperate and progressive in sobriety, the Sunday Closing Act has operated as a powerful aid to the cause Of temperance by removing a temptation from a weak minority. In dis- tricts, however, where it has been constantly evaded or defied by certain classes of the population the Commis- sioners cannot, in the face of evidence before them, say that it has been salutary in every respect. The Commis- sioners go on to say that they cannot endorse either the suggestion to repeal the Sunday Closing Act or to modify it by permitting the opening of public-houses for a short time in the middle and evening of Sunday. They dis- miss as equally impracticable the proposal to close public-houses absolutely and for all purposes for the whole of Sunday. 'rhey consider that the right to receive travellers on Sunday should be confined to houses of such rateable value as would afford some guarantee of the re- sponsibility of the landlord.

div.head: CrtEWE MI7RDER.
div.p: THE CrtEWE MI7RDER.
THE PETIrIONS FOR A REPRIEVE.

The petitions which have been sent out by Mr. C. U. Pedley in favour of a reprieve for the two prisoners, Richard and George Davies, have been numerously signed. A large number of petitions were distributed in Crewe and the district by John avies, the elder brother of the convicts, and Mr. Pedley has sent copies to all parts of England in response to applications from per- sons anxious to use their influence on behalf of the boys. Besides the petitions which have been drawn up by Mr. Pedley, a large number of distinct petitions have been framed and publicly exhibited for signature in various parts of the country. Among other persons who com- municated with Mr. Pedley, a telegram was received at midday, on Monday, from Mr. Griffiths, of Newport, Mon., who stated that since noon on Monday he had obtained the large number of 10,000 signatures. In all Mr. Pedley computes that there will be not less than 200,000 signatures to the various petitions presented.

THE PRISONERS VISITED BY THEIR FRIENDS.I The mother of the prisoners made •her first visit to them on Tuesday afternoon. She was accompanied to Knutsford Gaol by her eldest son, John, the laughter Emily, and the youbger boys. The party travelled by the train leaving Crewe at 10.40, having driven from the Hough in the trap which the murdered man was driving when he met with his doom. The trap was put up at the Royal Hotel, and the members of the family walked to the station without attracting any attention. The elder brother of the prisoners, John, had gone to Bunts- ford on the previous Thursday, but was refused an inter- view with the prisoners, as he had not obtained an order from the Governor of the gaol. He had been told that he could have an interview with the prisoners at any time, but had not been informed of the regulations which necessitated his having an order from the Governor of the gaol. The result of this attempted interview, how- ever, was that the boys, Richard and George, informed the Governor of the gaol whom they would like to come to see them, and orders for admission were accordingly given to the mother of the prisoners, Mrs. Davies ' • John Davies, the elder brother, and his wife; Miss Emily Davies ; Mr. Samuel Pimlett. an old schoolfellow of the boys ; the boy who gave evidence, Freddy, of the age of ten ; and a younger boy. These, with another friend, tra- velled by the train leaving Crewe at 10.40 for Knutsford, and on reaching their destination lost no time in present- ing themselves at the prison gates. They had an interview with the two prisoners together, at the same time, and the interview lasted nearly an hour and a half. As may be expected the interview was a most painful one, and during the whole time two warders were present. The convicts were much distressed during the whole of the interview, but managed to keep up their composure to a certain extent until the time came for parting. The mother, Mrs. Davies, was entirely overcome, and the meeting of the family was throughout of a most painful character. Although it lasted so long, little was said by any of the actors in the distressful scene, as all were too much overcome with emotion to speak. Not one word was said by any of those present as to the chances of a reprieve, and the interview was entirely of a family character, being characterized by erno ion which did not find words to express itself. The prisoners themselves kept up a sort of stolid outward calm, but at the end of the interview broke down completely, sobbing loudly and weeping copiously. The sad scene being ended, the visitors left the gaol, and returned to Crewe by the train arriving there at 6.53. The Crewe Station Was then comparatively quiet, and it being just about dusk, the sad party left the station with little notice.

div.head: • SHOCKING FOOTBALL FATALITY.
div.p: • SHOCKING FOOTBALL FATALITY.
A ST. HELENS PLAYER KILLED.

An accident of a shocking character occurred, on Saturday afternoon, to a young man named Edward Smith, who was playing for ,the St. Helens " A"' team against West Leigh, on the ground of the latter. Smith had not played with the team before, but journeyed as a substitute. for one of, the absen- tees. During the game, he joined in a scrimmage, and haying no bars on his shoes, he slipped and fell, several others falling upon him. He was heard to utter a faint cry, but everybody thought he was simply "winded," and expected a speedy recovery. His head had been crushed down upon his chest. and Dr. Jones, of Leigh, who was at once called, found that he had suffered a fracture of the spine, and paralysis speedily set in. He was removed on a stretcher to the Workhouse HOspital. in West Leigh, where, he lingered until Tuesday morning, when he expired. He was only nineteen years of age, and resided with his widowed 'mother in Waterloo-street, St. Helens, and was her only sup- port. The accident to Smith, and his death on Tuesday, occasioned a most painful feeling' in all football circles of St. Helens and district. Sympathy for the mother has been general, and it is likely to take a practical shape.

div.head: WARRINGTON RURAL SANITARY
div.p: WARRINGTON RURAL SANITARY

AUTHORITY. • • ' The monthly Meeting of the members of the War- rington Rural Sanitary Authority was held at the Workhouse On Thursday morning. The ,Rev. G. P. Roberts presided, and there were also present Messm. A. Jolley, A. Houghton, J. Houghton, J. Hutnphreys; It. Kilshall, S. Sutton (clerk). Dr. Sephton (medical officer), W. Owen (valuer), and F. Kerfoot (nuisance inspector.) THE LATerrionn DRAINAGE.—The Clerk said he 'had received several tehders for the construction of a new sewer at Latchford. They were—Mr. John Hougr,h,'£sl ; Mr. Bennie, Wellfield-st., £54 10s. •, and Mr. W. Williams, £57 13s. The tender of Mr. Hough was accepted.—The Clerk notified the Board of the receipt of a letter from the Local Governtnent Board, asking for the observations of the Authority on an enclosed fetter the Board had received from Mr. J. H. Gornatl, of Latchford. The Clerk was directed to send i reply, pointing out that. the Authority had taken steps to do away with the ditch complained of, and have a sewer constructed, previous to the date of Mr. Gornall's complaint. Unavoidable de- lay had, however' * bccurkvd in dealinv, with the matter, owing to the'cons truction of the ShipCanal,.and in con- sequence of recommendations made in certain quarters to separate the Latchford drainage district from that of the Authority. The death rate in the district compared favourably with the borough returns. The reply went on as follows:—" I am further to remind vour.honour- able Board of the very serious and repeated complaints to you by the Authority and by numerous inhabitants of the offensive condition of the Longford depot, and of the several other depots in the borough for the collection of excrement, and the Authority feel censtrained to say that for Mr. Gornall to strain over the comparatively in- significant discomfort he has experienced from the occa- sional want of cleansing of this ditch, partakes in the circumstances of the ludicrous."

VOTE OF THANKS.-Mr. W. Houghton said that as that was the last meeting of the Board for the year, he begged to propose a vote of thanks to the Chairman, for presid- ing over their deliberations.—Mr. J. Houghton seconded; the motion was agreed to, and • the Chairman briefly re- plied. This concluded the proceedings.

div.head: CHESHIRE LINES AMATEUR DRAMATIC'
div.p: CHESHIRE LINES AMATEUR DRAMATIC'
SOCIETY.

On the evenings of Monday and Tuesday the stage at the Public Hall was occupied by members of the Cheshire Lines ( Warrington works) Ama- teur Dramatic Society, who, with the assistance of a professional actress, gave performances of Shake- I speare's tragedy of " Macbeth.' The proceeds were in aid of the iunds of the Ragged Sunday School, in Bewsey-street, which is doing a good work among the poorest of the poor children of the town, and which, it may incidentally be mentioned, is worthy of substantial support at the hands of those who can afford it It is to be regretted that both on Monday and Tuesday evenings the " house " was scarcely so good as might have been expected, but it is only fair to say that those who did attend a.ppleci- ated the efforts of the company, and frequently applauded those who took the leading characters— Miss Adria Hill and Mr. W. M. Asher. The former is an actress already known to fame, and she sustained her reputation, filling the character of "Lady Macbeth" almost to perfection. She was evidently well practised in the part, and imparted to it such realistic power as to deeply impress the audience. Mr. William M. Asher is not unknown in Warrington, and further afield, aa a very successful amateur, and he also did justice to the expectations that had been formed of his -appearances in the role of" Macbeth." Of course, he and Miss Hill had the brunt of the work to do. They did it well ; Miss , Hill did her part especially well ; and on the termination of one scene they were in company recalled before the curtain. The other parts were more or less creditably filled, but a want of confidence was pretty generally ob- servable, and the impersonation of some of the characters was altogether of too " stiff " a nature to have a good effect. It was evident, however, that there is a good deal of talent in the company, but it is a question for con- sideration whether it would not have been displayed to much greater advantage if a less ambitious piece had been attempted. Other characters were assumed by Mr. Wm. Kilduff as " Macduff," by Mr. F. A. Tarbuck as "Banquo," by Mr. Eaton as "Duncan, King of Scot- land,' by Mr. T. C. Slater and Master Richard Jones as "Malcolm and Donalbain," respectively, and by Mr. J. R. Matthews as " Rosso' " and Mr. W. G. Hackett as •! Lenox." Miss Riley and Miss Clara Hedgcock had un- considerable parts as gentlewomen,and the following were down in the caste for minor parts :—Messrs. T. C. Mil- lington, J. Everett, H. Wildman. W. Unsworth, T.Lowe, J. Monks, John Oakes, A. Perry, F. B. Page, F. Moly- neaux, E. Hackett, C. Newall, Miss Mary H. Robinson, and Masters E. Whitham, Midgett, and J. Richard. Orchestral music was supplied by Mr. T. J. Down's cele- brated band ; Mr, James Carr, of Liverpool, had pro- vided the costumes, which were brilliant and well- chosen; and the wigs had been supplied by Mr. Toni Taylor, of Lime-st., Liverpool.

'RUNCORN TONIC SOL-FA CHOIR CONCERT. Sir,—ln your report of above you say the concert was a success financially. As this is not accurate I trust you will give publicity to the correction. It is only by the exercise of the greatest economy and a large amount of gratuitous labour on the part of:their members, together with the generous support of ourhonorary members, that we maintain the solvency of our institution ; and as we believe we have been of service to the town in helping to create and elevate the musical taste, we shall continue our work in the hope that our efforts may be estimated at their correct value, and that we may receive the better success which you say they deserve.—Yours truly, R. div.head: Prodsham, April 2, 1890.
div.p: Prodsham, April 2, 1890.

THE WATER QUESTION V. MANUFACTURERS. Sir,—ln reply to your young correspondent," W. H. Butler," I think it is too late in the day to discuss in a weekly paper the great question of our water supply— its causes and effects upon manufacturers, Sze., or upon dyeing. What I have aimed for,and what I would press now, is, that a public examination of the whole question should be gone into. My young friend had a full oppor- tunity of discussing the matter with me when on the platform at my meeting; why did he miss the chance then? Just let me remind my young friend that there is" no deception" about me, and that lam quite pre- pared to show, if need be, that the Winwick water is quite as injurious to pipes and boilers as any sample I have exhibited. Mr. Editor, let there be no mistake : I was always in favour of the town being in possession of the Water Works, but my object was to lesson the value as much as possible by showing its defects.—Yours truly, WM. DIGGLE.

div.head: MATTER FOR THE RUNCORN POLICE.,
div.p: A MATTER FOR THE RUNCORN POLICE.,

Sir,— rhe police arrangements of Runcorn have cer- tainly been on the amend since the advent of our present chiefs; but I would like to call attention, through the medium of your valuable paper, to a black spot on our local escutcheon, viz.—the disgraceful " rowdyism " in vogue, every Sunday evening, in and about Omen- way-road, during the time the congregations of the res- pective churches and chapels are dispersing. The writer on several occasions has been" jostled" from the foot- path to the middle of the road, and at another time his sister was struck in the face, by these—something be- tween lads and men—say" heathens," who parade these respectable haunts, to the especial terror of ladies and children. I feel sure that mention need only be made of these proceedings, to call for the prerogatives of our respected authorities, who will no doubt, speedily put ' an end to the scandalous behaviour practiced by these ruffians.—Yours truly, "WATCHING AND LIGHTING." Runcorn, April Ist, 1890.
ELECTION EXPENSES.

Sir,—l have often wondered when reading that the ex- penses of Mr. So-and-So, who contested the Parliamen- tary Division of this or that place, amounted to teens of hundreds of pounds, how so large a sum could occur. Being a farmer by profession (ought I to say trade?) I did not like to ask my literate friends if they could ex- plain, lest the idea of " Hodge " and " obtuseness " should crop up, so I have remained ignorant; but a few days ago, when looking over the "Manchester Guardian," I saw and read the heading—" Parliamentary Elections (Scotland) Bill ." Dr. Farquharson, M.P., said with respect to it—" It was too much to expect that hon. members, who gave their time and labour to the country, often at the sacrifice of their health, should submit to have their pockets picked for election expenses." Do you think, sir, he will be prosecuted for libel? or may we conclude that he spoke advisedly, and that what he asserted is true? If so I shall be somewhat enlightened as to what I have long 'had a desire to know. I have heard the remark that "In this age it is not the vulgar rascality of half- a-century ago that we need fear, but the respectable rascality' whose motto is 'lt is just the same whether you are hanged for a sheep or a lamb." Hence, now-a- days, all frauds (including exorbitant charges), with few exceptions, are on the "higher scale," and proceed from the class referred tn.—Yours truly, EX-FARMER.

WM. STINKS, Asssoc. M. Inst. C.E. 55, Horsemarket-st., Warrington, 3rd April, 1890. SUNDAY TRADING IN WARRINGTON.

Sir,—Permit me through the medium of your columns to call the attention of the police to a matter of which they seem to be utterly oblivious, viz., the ever increasing amount of Sunday trading that is now carried on within the borough. One cannot stir on what should be the Day of Rest without being struck with the shameless vaanner in which the 4th commandment is broken. Oysters, friedfish, sweets, tobacco, newspapers ; in fact, anything and everything that people have been too negligent or too drunken to purchase the night before, areas readily procurable on Sunday as on any day of the week in all parts of the town. Along St. James's-st., Latchford, for instance, nearly every door is oven for the transaction of trade on the Sabbath Day, and, as the same thing is observable throughout the town, it would seem as if the cotnmandment I have referred to were non existent. It is a pity that shopkeepers are so absorbed in business as to carry it on on the Sabbath, for they must, know that Sunday trading never did, and never will do, any good. But the whole town appears to be getting quite demoralised, when our clergymen go to their Sunday services ecn tricycles and in ha.ndsomes, and our towns- people generally ruin the Sabbath quiet of respectable people by patronising omnibuses which run to a Sunday flower show that attracts the majority of our Sunday school scholars. Matters are coming to such a dreadful pass, that I trust this little note will arouse the police from their supiness and stimulate the Chief Constable to sacrifice a little time from his devotions to suppress the disturbing elements of others' meditations.—Yours. A SABBATH OBSERVER.

"FACTS." Sir,—lf " Churchman " will Qngage a room at his expense, and meet me, I will prove my statement more efficiently than I can expect to do through the indulgence of your columns. It is absurd to say I delight to hear things said against Ritualists. Does " Churchman" de- light in quoting an extreme traitor (Ritualist) against Protestantism, and misquote tint catechism by omitting the question, what is the inward part or thing signified? and only giving a part of the answer—tho same as his party have tried to do with the answer to question, how many sacraments hath Christ ordained in His Church? They answer "two," and leave out the word "only," so that they may say two was not all, but there are five others.

I was not aware Bishop Stubbs was still a member of the English Church Union. I understood he ceased to be so when created a bishop. Will " Churchman" give proof for his statement ? This bishop was the first for 300 years who turned his back on the flock (eastward position) in Chester Cathedral,and the late Dean Howson rebuked him for it. He can write a book and give mis- quotations (all his Legal History; reviewed hy dlr. J. T. Tomlinson), and revile the Evangelicals as he did at Stockport by saying, "so far as lay in his power, no Evangelical clergyman should set foot in that town to any of the proposed extra churches." (See" Liverpool Courier," April 27, 1887.) • The Church of England is not apostolic only in so far as she teaches the doctrines of the apostles. There was no bishop of a diocese in Paul's day, nor a universal bishop (Pope), but several bishops in one church as at Philippi, Ephesus, Antioch, Crete. Apostolic succession cannot be proved when there were two or more Popes at one time, also through the doctrine of Intention which entirely destroys all certainty of any ordination. (See Homily for Whit Sunday, part of Article 35.) I am asked to prove that the E.C.U. seeks re-union with the see of Rome. Well, its own papers shall con- demn it. E.C.U. Gazette, vol. 6p. 202, "This Society is pledged for the restoration in the Protestant Church of England of the Eastward position, Popish vestments, i lights n the daytime, mixed chalice and unleavened bread," and in its report for 1878 it advocates restoration of visible communion between thfl Church of England and the Church of Rome. At its anniversary meeting in 1885, Lord Halifax, the president, urged re-union with what he called the Holy Roman Church, and which view he re-affirms in letters to Bishop King on February 27. 1888, and in the " Times " of April 29 last. Will "Churchman" tell me the date of any paper or journal of their party denouncing his views ? Bishop Jayne attended a meeting of the E.C.U. after his appointment to Chester, and he has the cheek to call himself a Protestant. _
. _ "_The Tablet," the leading Roman Catholic. paper,

published an article in January, 1885, condemnink -the Ritualists for stealing the prayers, chants, and hymns of the Church of Rome. They also steal from God's word. In hymns" A and M " 318, verse 4th, they leave out the little word" not." Hymn 394,tirst verse, last line, they say God dwells in temples made with hands,whereas the bible says, He dwelleth not in temples made with hands. This little word not is omitted so as to support Pr iest- craft, and give them some support for their absurd Pagan custom of turning when creeds, litany, are said, and at end of sermon, even though the church be built north and south. _ _ _ _ _

I am only bound to believe the prayer book in so far as it is in accord with the bible. The catechism teaches baptismal regeneration; a doctrine of Rome,and scouted by Cramner, Latimer, Ridley, Sandys, Pilkington, Nowell, Jerome, John Frith, Philpot Hooper, whilst Bishop Hooker says Faith is the first thing requisite for entering the fold of Christ; the custom of godfathers is no more instituted of God than the signing of children's foreheads with a cross, and that Baptism is valid when administered by a layman or a woman. I defy church- men to give me one verse out of the New Testament showing infants were baptized. There is no change of the elements (bread anu wine) during Lord's Supper, neither is he to be elevated or adored, as the Ritualists do. For not holding the present Romish view of Tran- substantiation the reformers Cramer, Latimer, Ridley, Hooper, John Bradford and others chose burning before turning from the Gospel. Perhaps " churchman " can inform me where in the New Testain ••,' rime apostles give instructions for early celebrations with candles burning ia open daylight, incense, crucifix, Romish Mass, vestments, wafer bread, &c. Such was the mockery at so-called churches of England in Cardiff and Clumber, near Nottingham, in October last. Verily their fruits are Romish. Did the Vicar of Runcorn a few Sundays since tell his flock that the Virgin Mary was only such till she brought forth her first-born, and afterwards became mother to at least six others ; that she is not named after Acts lc., nor is there one verse telling us to either worship her or to pray to her; that Christ never called her mother after He was thirty years old, nor does it appear He showed Himself to her after His resurrection? Yet they worship her in hymns A and M. Bishop King and others are not being prosecuted for what the prayer book directs but for what the Church of England in the prayer bit*, articles, and homilies plainly forbid, and the law declared illegal. He is Vice- President of the E.C.U., and advocates nearly every Romish doctrine. If "Churchman" will look at the prayer book, he will at once see the general thanks- giving is written in the plural, "we, us, our," so that it is meet and right for it to be said in a reverent manner by the congregation, not intoned and murdered as is done to the responses of the commandments, accom- panied by an organ. It is nothing less than mockery of worship. Just imagine a petition to the Queen being presented in a sing-song droning whine, along with musiclo match. Is this the coming boldly to the throne of grace? If "Churchman" will look at my letter he will find I said, they sympathise with the Jesuits, not saints. Poor fellow, he is so muddled, he fails to see the difference between a Jesuit and a saint. There was a branch of the Church Association in exist- ence in Runcorn over 16 years, not two. Bishops Stubbs' and Jaynes' withering disapproval may have had some- thing to do with its not showing much vitality!, combined with indifference on the part of officials. It is time they wakened up to their duties. It is something now to be told the clergy preach the laity are priests. Will "Churchman " quote me one Ritualistic parson who has written so, he being a mem- ber of any one of their societies, say ECU.. C. 8.5., S.H.C., or the A.P.U.C., or, as" Punch" calls them, the ' " Association for the Promotion of Universal Confusion." The Ritualists teach priestly arrogance—for example, ' "Tracts for the day," "Whenever there is a sacrifice there must be a priest to offer it. In the pulpit he de- clares the oracles of God ; and in the con fessional he sits in his judicial capacity." The catechism of Theology p. 58 says, "The priest at the altar is virtually Christ himself." I have briefly touched upon the various points named by "Churchman," and any ordinary mind should be convinced from the witnesses I have adduced that Ritualistic teaching is nothing less than the masterpiece of the devil. rhe prayer book needs reforming. Bishop Ryle says " Give me a really Protestant and Evangelical church, or no Church of England at all. Honest church- men who come forward to oppose Ritualism are de- nounced and disliked as agitators, firebrands, and troub- lers of Israel." Sad day for England if ever these men get the upper hand; only look at the disgraceful riot at a church meeting in Cardiff, on the sth instant, the Vicar of Blackpool the speaker. Thank God Protest antism is not dead so long a .we have our Bishop Ryle, Drs. Taylor, Hammond, Woodward, Lefroy, Blakeneys, Bardsleys, Bell, Crossthwaite, Wright, Canons Stratton, Burbridge, Rev. R. Hobson, with his 82 Sunday school teachers, 1,500 scholars, 700 communicants, 12 lay helpers, bible readers, three mission rooms, ragged school, all sprung from a congregation of four in a cellar ; be- sides our Dr. Barnard° with his 3,500 children, and Mr. Muller at Bristol. Who keep the church missionaries agoing ? The: Protestants, not Ritualists. The latter prefer spending it on bells, choir, and music. The Rev. E. A. Stuart. London. has a congregation of 2,000 and does without a choir ; all his flock are his singers ; he is doing a grand work. Prove all things ; hold fast that which is geol. Many false teachers had gone into the world in Paul's day. Ritualism was growine when he wrote to the Galatians. If Churchman will fairly take heed to John 20c. 31v. he will never speak disrespectfully of men who gave their lives for the cause of truth and the liberty we enjoy. "As men found that Tractarianism was a half-way house to Rome, so they will find that Ritualism is a stage or two further on." k" Tablet" January Ist, 18810 ROBERT FOULKES.
Frodsham, March 18, 1890.
LORD R. CHURCHILL DECLARES
AGAINST THE IRISH LAND BILL.

Lord Randolph Churchill, writing to the "Morning Post," says the policy of the Irish Land Purchase Bill may be right or wrong, but such direct relations of debtor and creditor of such magnitude between the State and the Irish tenant have hitherto been condemned by Parlia- ment and stigmatized by various authorities as relations which of all others ought tc be carefully avoided. The moment that the State lcan becomes very large and State debtors become very numerous, the power of the debtors to combine against repayment of what they owe becomes practically irresistible, and the power of the State to recover from the combined default of debtors becomes absolutely nil. He asks himself as an English member of Parliament whether he can as a sane man even for a moment contemplate he advance of £33,060,000 of the Imperial money to a class of the Irish community elated as they are by their past successes in repudiation. His lordship proposes in a further letter to examine the value of the proposed securities in the Bill.

The Berlin " Kreuz Zeitung," on Wednesday evening, published intelligence from St. Petersburg, stating that the Czar has been taken suddenly ill. He is said to be suffering from fainting fits. Under the provisions of the American Tariff Bill the impost on steel rails is to be reduced by about four dollars per ton, while an ad 'valorem duty of 15 per cent. is to be placed on bides.

div.head: TEIE EXAMINER; SATURDAY, APRIL 5, 1890.
div.p: TEIE EXAMINER; SATURDAY, APRIL 5, 1890.

motion—they would see that every one was a magis- trate and large preservers of game. Be did not wonder at them voting against that motion. He appealed to the Home Secretary, who was the biggest political humbug ' of this generation—(loud laughter) and he could get neither sense or satisfaction out of him ; and it was equally as bad as trying to get blood out of a stone. He knew a case at Runcorn where all the police were drafted out to Norton to watch poachers, whilst the inhabitants in their beds were left unprotected. He told the Home Secretary, as a pure question of right, that he ought to take into consideration the questions of the protection of lives and property. What was the good of having policemen if they did not do the duty for which they were paid. (Hear, hear.) He had also called the Home Secretary's attention to what was to his mind the biggest piece of rascality that had ever taken place in this century. Themagistrates had been in the habit for a long time of subscribing to a• fund out of which rewards of £1 to £2 had been offered to the police for every poacher captured and convicted. (" Scanda- lous.' ) The Home Secretary sent a certain communica- tion to Colonel Hamersley—he (Mr. Lewis) got to know that he did so. He knew how many letters passed between them—(laughter)—and also knew pretty well what was in them. (Renewed laughter.) He said in his reply that the Chief Constable had adequately dealt with the fund at Macclesfield for the reward of police officers securing the conviction of poachers; but he (Mr. Lewis) had never mentioned the fund at Macclesfield. and he discovered that it was a double-shuffle piece of business. (More laughter.) It now remained for them to probe the matter to the bottom, and have the magistrates who, acting in the manner charged, struck off the bench; especially those who subscribed to a fund for bringing perhaps innocent people up, by bribing policemen to get a conviction. He had sent a letter to the Clerk of the Joint Committee, insisting upon having the matter thoroughly thrashed out, and an inquiry being held, to give him an opportunity of bringing witnesses and proving the charges up to the hilt. (Applause.) He might fight the division again—(hear, hear)—he did not say that he should, as he never considered self. He would place himself in the hands of the electors as he did at the last election, and if the Liberal party thought that they could get a better man he would gladly give was; but if they could not find a better man he should stand. (Applause.) The Local Government Act was full of errors, and it was for the Liberals when they went into power to remedy them. As long as they had such vermln as landlords and lawyers in the House they could not expect to get anything out of them. Mr. Lewis then referred to various political reforms, and the meet- ing concluded with the usual votes of thanks.

div.head: IMPORTANT RATING CAUL
div.p: IMPORTANT RATING CAUL

At the Eddisbttry (Cheshire) Petty Sessions, on Mon- day afternoon, Mr. Fletcher, solicitor, appeared for the overseers of Frodsham lordship, who had taken out a summons against the Manchester Ship Canal Company to recover £3 63., monies due from them in respect of certain rates made on Nov. 3, 1888, April 20, 1889, and Oct. 19, 1889.—Mr. Fletcher said he should produce the rate book for the township, which showed the rate had been properly levied, and if he also showed that a legal demand had been made, then their worships' duties were merely ministerial. If the Canal Company were ag- grieved in any way by the making of any rate, there was a course open to them—they should give proper notice of appeal.—Mr. Challenor (assistant overseer for Frodsham lordship) proved the levying of the rate.— Mr. Riley (of the firm of Messrs. Grundy, Kershaw, and Co., solicitors, Manchester), on behalf of the Ship Canal Company, said it was a small matter but the magistrates would readily understand that if the case were allowed they would have many of a similar nature preferred against them. They had ap- pealed in the case of many townships in the Runcorn Union, and the Assessment Committee had seen the, force of the argument that they were not rateable. How Prod- sham lordship had not been dealt with, he did not un- derstand. The case for the Canal Company was that they were not rateable; there was no beneficial occupa- tion in the land they took for the purpose of construct- ing works, and if it were not for section 133 of the Lands Clauses Act they should be in no ratebook at all. It had been held so long ago as 1866, that a company such as the present were not liable to be rated at all to the re- lief of the poor or otherwise. If that were so, the autho- rities had no right to take advantage of any mistake that might have been made by placing their names in the ratebook. The application, he submitted, was illegal.— After a brief consultation, the magistrates made an order for the payment of the amount. ELECTION INTELLIGENCE

It is announced that Mr. O'Hea, M.P. for West Done- gal, is about to resign his seat. The Liberal Five Hundred of the borough of Leicester met on Tuesday evening and adopted Sir Janes. White- head as candidate for the seat which Mr. M'Arthur has announced his intention to vacate. Sir James Whitehead having resigned his candidature for North Westmoreland, a meeting of Liberals was held on Tuesday at Tebay to select an opponent of the present Conservative member, the Hon. W. Lowther. It was resolved to invite the Hon. Alfred Tufton tc contest the • seat. In the Carnarvon Boroughs the Conservative's are making most desperate efforts to retain the seat. Mr. Ellis Nanney, the Tory candidate, who was said at first to be in very delicate health, has been canvassing with as much vigour and vivacity as Mr. Lloyd George, the Liberal candidate. The Liberals in the constituency have need of speakers who can express themselves in Welsh with ease. The nomination of candidates took place on Wednesday' when Mr. Lloyd George, Glad- stonian Liberal, and Mr. J. Ellis Nanney, Conservative, were duly nominated. •

div.head: HAVERFORDWEST AND PEMBROKE BOROUGHS.
div.p: HAVERFORDWEST AND PEMBROKE BOROUGHS.

Mr. G. F. Egerton Allen. of Tenby. was on Monday adopted as the Liberal candidate for Haverfordwest and Pembroke Boroughs. Mr. Allen, who is a nephew of Mr. H. G. Allen, Q.C., formerly Liberal member for the boroughs, addressed the electors last evening, at Pem- broke Dock. THE WINDSOR ELECTION. The nomination of candidates for the vacancy in the Parliamentary representation of Windsor, caused by the retirement of Colonel R. Richardson Gardner, Conser- vative, took place on Monday. Mr. Francis Tress Barry (Conservative) and Mr. William Henry Gls-dell (Glad- stoniati Liberal) were duly nominated. Mr. Gladstone, writing on the subject of the Windsor election, says, in his opinion, the choice is now before the Royal borough of identifying itself with the late shamefullproceedings taken by the majority against the Irish members by rejecting Mr. Grenfell, or of conferring, by his whim to Parliament, honours on itself and great benefit to the country. The polling for Windsor took place on Wednes- day. Mr. Barry (Conservative) polled 1,522 and Mr. Grenfell (Liberal) 972. The late member was "a Con- servative.

div.head: MR. SLATER LEWIS, C.C., ADDRESSES . HIS CONSTITUENTS.
div.p: MR. SLATER LEWIS, C.C., ADDRESSES . HIS CONSTITUENTS.

On Saturday evening, Mr. J. Slater Lewis, C.C., paid a visit to Kingsley to give an account of his stewardship. The meeting was held in the National Schools, and there was a goad attendance. Mr. P. Hall was voted to the chair. Mr. Lewis, who was greeted with loud cheers, said it was a very great cry at the last election all over Cheshire that there were to be no politics in the County Council elec- tion—(A Voice: "There were none ")—but the Conservatives had introduced politics in a very peculiar kind of way. In future every division would_ be fought solely _on political lines. He did not know whether it ought to be so; it was not a question what ought to be, but what would be. When he first appeared before them he issued an address. He said in that address he should like to see an alteration in the poor laws (hear, hear), and he did contend that if the poor people had worked all their lives, and given their bone and sinew to the welfare of the country, they should have something different to look forward to than the cheerless walls of a whitewashed workhouse. (Hear, hear.) In the Liberal programme before the country poor law reform occupied a very prominent position, and he was pleased to state that this was due to the efforts he had himself put forward in his address, which had been put into the hands of Mr. Morley. (Loud cheers.) Of course, the County Council could do nothing in the matter,as they had no j urisdiction over Boardsof Guardians He had said in his address something about the Ship Canal assessment of the Runcorn Union. He had stated that he did not think it was :right to attack the Ship Canal Company at the outset of their work ; but that they should have been given time to finish their under- taking, and assisted in bringing an important industry into the neighbourhood. (Hear, hear.) The Ship Canal Company had been fought, and as a result the people bad lost, and he had previously 'told his electors that they would have a bill of £l,OOO to 'pay for fighting the Ship Canal Company. He was laughed at and ridiculed at the time, and it was stated that the bill would not be more than £4OO or £5OO, and even that amount he considered to be too much. The result was, however, 'hat a bill for £2,500 came in, and the members of the Runcorn Board of Guardians, when a precept was sent in from the County Council, were very busy in denouncing the Council; but they forgot to tell the people that that £2,500 had a great deal to do with the deficit. They had not been told how that mighty bill of £2,500 had been made up, and he should particularly like to see it. (Hear, hear.) He thought the River Weaver Trust ought to come under the County Council. From time immemorial it had been in the hands of the trustees, and by a peculiar clause in the Local Government Act, the County Council had no power to deal with the River Weaver Trust, They knew Mr. Ritchie and the people who had the framing of the Bill, and that they had something to do than to bother with the River Weaver, consequently they must have been put up to insert that clause. The charities was a very important subject for the poor to consider. There were thousands of pounds left for the good of the poor in that county years gone by, and it had all slipped through the Angers of someone, and where the money had gone no one knew. The County Council had no power to deal with that matter; the Charity Commissioners were the Alpha and Omega of the whole business. ("Shame.") They might as well deal with a mile post as try to deal with the Charity Commis- ssioners, as when they were written to, all they heard in reply was "We will consider the matter." (Laughter.) They knew perfectly well that he,had had a correspond- ence with the Home Secretary—(hear, hear)—concern- ing the Chief Constable and the police, and he felt strongly on the matter, and was determined not to let the matter drop through until he saw daylight in it. (Applause.) He had felt it his duty to raise a question in the Council respecting the retirement of Inspector O'Donnell, who was at the time an Inspector of the Run- corn police foroe. Mr. O'Donnell was present at that meeting. (A Voice: "And a good-looking chap, too.") He was not championing the cause of an indivi- dual; but he was championing the cause of ex- Inspector O'Donnell, and of other men who might possibly be placed in a similar position. (Hear, hear.) Inspector O'Donnell he had known ten years before he went to Runcorn; lie had known him to he a perfectly energetic, efficient, and good officer. He was sent to Runcorn to deal with a certain state of affairs in Runcorn which existed, and in dealing with that state of affairs he brought coals of fire on his head, and had suffered so much that they sympathized with him as Englishmen. (Hear, hear.) It was a fact that Mr. O'Donnell was not the only inspector who had been cent to Runcorn and been reduced, and nowhere else but in Runcorn had this occurred. Sergeant Blair was a good officer, and happened to do his duty, and take an active part in bringing about a better state of things ; but he was soon attacked, and had to go to America, where he lost his wife, and was in extreme poverty. (‘• Shame.")) lie had not the slighest opportunity of going before the Chief Constable and of stating his case, and of bringing those to book who ought to have been. There had been an amount of drunkenness in the force at Runcorn. Celonel Hamersley knew that there had been drunkenness in the force, and he (the speaker) wanted to know why he had not probed the matter to the bottom—(heal., hear)—and brought the guilty parties to justice. They would see that his motion to memorialise the Local Government Board was carried by 28 to 12, and would see who the 12 were who voted against this

div.head: SCRIPTURE READER AND THE DRESSMAKER. •
div.p: THE SCRIPTURE READER AND THE DRESS- MAKER. •

At the Newton Petty Sessions, on Saturday, be- fore Messrs. T. J. Gillespie, T. D. Grimke, and W. Mitchell, James Albert Smith, a respectably-dressed young man, and formerly a scripture-reader at Golborne, was charged with bigamy, by going through the form of marriage with Annie Clara Taylor, at Leeds, on the 23rd April, 1889, his wife, Mary Ann Seddon Mason, to whom he was married on the 19th May, 1880, being then and now alive. The first witness called was William Hayes, a booking•clerk; living at Chalmers-street, Liverpool, who said he had known the prisoner for over 20 years. He also knew his wife, Mary Ann Seddon Mason, and was present at their marriage on the 19th May, 1880, •at St. Catherine's Church, Wigan. He signed the register as ene of the witnesses present.—Annie Clara Taylor, living at 148, Clowes-streets Gorton, near Manchester, deposed: About Christmas, 1888. I was living with my aunt at Leeds, and was getting my living as a dress- maker. My aunt took in lodgers. The prisoner came to lodge with my aunt, whilst I was there. He lived there as a lodger for about three months. He said he went home at the week-ends to see his mother. He never said anything about having a wife. He always represented himself as a single man. He asked me to marry him, and I afterwards went through the form of marriage with him on the 23rd April, 1889, at the Superintendent Re-, gistrar's Office, at Leeds. He then gave the namei of James Herbert Mason. Since that time we have lived together as man and wife ufitil last Monday night, when he was arrested under a warrant. Until he was appre- hended that night I did not know that he had been married before. At the time I married him I had about £l4O. We have nothing left now ; it is all spent.—James Parkinson Blakley, deputy registrar of marriages at Leeds, deposed that he was present at the form of marriage between the last witness and the prisoner on the 23rd April, 1889.—Police Sergeant Daven- port, stationed at Golhorne, stated that he apprehended the prisoner living at West Gorton, Manchester, with the witness Taylor. He read the warrant to the prisoner, who replied 'yes."—The prisoner, on being charged and cautioned, stated that at the time his acquaintanceship with the witness Taylor commenced he was not aware that she had any money. After the marriage ceremony had been gone through she told him that she had £7O odd. Thai: was all the money she had, and whatever portion of that money had passed through his hands was at her giving, and she had given It for various purposes. —The prisoner was then committed for trial at the next Liverpool Assizes.

div.head: LYMM.
div.p: LYMM.

THE CHURCH INN.-At the Altrincham Petty Sessions, on Monday, the magistrates granted temporary authority to Mrs. McCread to sell at the Church Inn, Lymrn, under the licence of her late husband. AMBULANCE LECTUEE.-Dr. R. E. Williamson continued his lectures in connection with the St. John Ambulance Association in the Lyinm Institute, on Friday evening. There was a good attendance at this lecture, which was the fourth of the series.

SLEEPING OUT AT THELWALL.—At the Lymm Police Court, on Tuesday, before Dr. Brabazon, a tramp, named Frederick Smith, was committed to gaol for seven days' hard la'bour, for sleeping in a cabin on the Ship Canal, at Thelwall, on the previous night. SALVATIONIST CAMPAIGN.—The Salvation Army Com- menced a special campaign in Lymm, at their barracks, on Saturday, when Captain Northeast, of Altrincham, assisted by Lieutenant Hislip, conducted a service. Services were held on Sunday, and during the week. IN MEMORIAM.—A faculty has been abtained by Mr. William Battersby, of Lymm Hall, to place a stained glass window (the second from the porch) in Dumville's Chapel, on the north side of Lymm Church, in memory of the late Mr, and Mrs. Battersby, of Lymm Hall. The window will represent Christ healing the sick. THE Vor.ormeEns.—The Lymm Volunteers assembled in drill order at their headquarters on Sunday morning, and, under the command of Captain Jones, marched to the Parish Church for Divine service, which was con- ducted by the Rector, the Rev. G. W. Guest. There was a very good muster, this being the first Sunday parade this year. FOOTBALL.—A match came off on Saturday afternoon In a field,in Pepper-street, belonging to Lymm Hall, be- tween the boys from the Warrington Grammar School and a team from' Lymm Grammar School. 'rhe result showed that the strangers were unequally matched, as they only succeeded in kicking three goals as against eight for the home team. APPOINTMENT OF OVECISEERS.—At tll6 Altrincham Petty Sessions, on Monday, the following overseers were ap- pointed by the magistrates: Lymm, Joseph Stott and Joseph Ardern ; High Legh, Samuel Cowap and John Cooke; Partington I. M. Davenport and C. D. Occles- toti • Thelwall, Peter Warburton and William Hulton ; Warburton, Thomas Williamson and James M. Newton. Mr. John Moore was also appointed assistant overseer for the township of Warburton. ASSAULTING A STEP-DAUGHTER.—At the .Lymm Police Court, on Monday, before Mr. T. P. Norris and Dr. Bra- bazon, Paul Grant, a painter, Living at Newfield,Lymm, was cha‘•ged with having, on Saturday night, the 29th March, assaulted his step-daughter, Lillie Butterworth. Evidence in support of the charge was given by Thomas and Sarah Ann, brother and sister of the complainant, Mrs. Grant (mother), Dr. Williamson, ,and P.C. Griffiths, and the defendant was committed to take his trial at the linutsford Sessions. A Licescn WRONGLY DATED. At the Lymm Police Court, on Monday afternoon, before Mr. T. P. Nmris and Dr. Brabazon. William Harris, of Maccles- field, hawker, was charged with hawking without a licence on the same afternoon, at Church-green. Pri- soner, who seemed a very re.spectableman, said he lived at 254, Irkfield-road, Macclesfield. He was hawking at Walsall when his licence expired last year, and he got the licence produced at that place, for which he paid ss. He was not aware until his attention was called to it by the officer that it bore a wrong date. That was the mistake of the officials, as he was certain he took it out latit June: After inquiries had been subsequently made, it was ascertained that Harris's statement was correct, and he was of course discharged.

LYMM LOCAL BOARD. The monthly meeting of this Board was held at the Board offices, • Lymm,. on Thursday evening. Mr. Cameron presided, and there were also present Nlessrs. Roors, Duttcn, Brazendale, Forster, Gibbon, Appleton ; Ridgeway (law-clerk), Mullard (clerk), and Dr. Fox (medical officer!) Tan EitiseTtows I A MEMBER THINKS THERE WAS SOME- THING BEHIND A CORNER.—The Chairman announced, as returning officer, that the following three gentlemen had been elected without opposition 88 members• of the Board, namely, Messrs. R. Dutton, and H. Harrison (retiring members), and F. Swallciw. Their old friend, Mr. Apple- ton, did not send in a nomination paper.—Mr. Appleton , asked up to what time on the day of nomination nomina- -1 tion papers could be sent in.—The Chairman: Any time on that day.—Mr. Brazendale : Up till 12 o'clock.—Mr. Appleton : . What was the object, then, of Mr. Mullard telling me they were closed at half-past eight ?—Mr. Mullard : I neyer told you anything of the kind.—Mr. Appleton : Do you remember me asking you how a member was chosen.—Mr. Mullard : I remember telling you that if there was no nomination a casual vacancy would be 'mused audit would be filled by the Board.— Mr. .APPLETON It looked to me that there was some- thing behind the corner when I 'asked you up to what time nominations were received.—Mr. MULLARD again denied having said to Mr. Appleton what Mr. Appleton

alleged he had said.—The CHAIRMAN said he came to the office at a quarter past 9 o'clock on the day alluded to, and Mr. Mullard told him that Mr. Appleton had been there, and he (Mr. Mullard) seemed to be under the impression that Mr. Appleton would be sending a paper in later on. He thought Mr. Appleton must have misun- derstood the conversation between himself and Mi. Mullard.—Mr. APPLETON said he believed there was something behind a corner he did not understand.—Mr. MIILLARD lam sorry you should think so.—The CHAIR- MAN remarked that he had no doubt it was a clear mis- understanding.—Mr. APPLETON said he did not intend to send in a nomination paper, but frdm what Mr. Mullard said he had since thought there was something in it.— The subject then ,dropped. THE HEALTH OF THE DISTRICT.—Dr. Fox reported that during the previous three months there had been only 24 deaths in the district, not one of which was from the zymotic order of disease. The general health of the dis- trict was particularly good. A COMPLAINT.—A letter was read from Mr. Nash com- plaining of the condition of Reddish-lane and it was decided that a reply should be sent to the effect that the Board would attend to that part of the lane repairable by them. The rest of the business was formal.

div.head: MUNICIPAL VACANCY AT WARRINGTON.
div.p: MUNICIPAL VACANCY AT WARRINGTON.
By the death of the late Councillor John Greening a -vacancy in the representation of the North-west Ward has been caused, but no action in regard to filling it up will be taken until after Easter.
CHILD DROWNED AT WARRINGTON.

On Thursday evening,, a little girl named Mary Ellen Littlefair, four years of age, daughter of Thomas Littlefair, labourer, 39, Watkin-st., was drowned in a pit belonging to Messrs. Bolton's glass work, off Orford-lane. It appeare.l that the deceased• and a number of other children were playing at the edge of the pit, trying to catch "jack sharps," when she fell into the water awl sank. An alarm was raised by the other children, and a young man , named Charles Hughes went to the pit, and, with assistance, recovered the body soon afterwards. A doctor was sent for, 13,tt all efforts to save the child's life were of no avail. The body was removed to the house of the child's parents to await an inquest.

div.head: LITE RECTOR OF WARRINGTON.
div.p: THE LITE RECTOR OF WARRINGTON.

There has just been erected in the Parish Church, a tablet to the memory of the late Rev. W. Quekett, MA., It is placed between the stained glass in the chancel, which is to the memory of his son. The tablet is a splendidly engraved brass one, with black marble slab, 3 feet 5 inches by 2 feet 6 inches. The engraving is in old English, decorated in the Ecclesiastical style,and bears the following inscrip- tion ;—" In Loving memory of the Rev. William Quekett, MA., of St. John's College, Cambridge, nearly 34 years Rector of Warrington, who was born at Langport, Somerset, 3rd October, 1802, and died at the Rectory, Warrington, on Good Friday, 30th March, 1888: by whose exertions this Parish Church was rebuilt, and of whose work many traces are to be found both in Warrington and in the parish of St. George in the East of London. This tablet is erected by his widow,Louisa Quekett." The work of erecting the tablet was entrusted to Messrs. Essenhigh Brothers, sculptors, Manchester-road, Warrington, who have given entire satisfaction.

div.head: CAMELLIAS AT WALTON LEA.
div.p: THE CAMELLIAS AT WALTON LEA.

Alderman J. Eros&ld, of Walton Lea, hasfor some time observed a very generous custom of throwing open his grounds at Walton Lea to the public at a period of the year when they are unusually attrac- tive. The appreciation of the public has always been shown by the numbers in which they take advantage of the opportunity, and this was again the case on Saturday and Sunday, on which days Mr. Crosfield invited the public of Warrington and the district to visit Walton Lea, with the special ' object of seeing his show of camellias. The grounds were open from two to live on the afternoons of each day, and as the weather, especially on the second day, was simply splendid, crowds of people took the chance of having an enjoyable outing. On Saturday, it is estimated, about a thousand persons visited Walton Lea, but the visitors on Sunday afternoon were computed at three or four times that number. There was warm sunshine, and the afternoon was alto- gether so tempting for out-door exercise that it seemed as if almost everybody turned out. Most of them, it need hardly be added, walked in the direc- tion of Walton, and they were rewarded in full measure by the very beautiful show of camellias grown at the Lea. Many of the visitors made the journey in conveyances, and during the afternoon Wilderspool and Walton-roads had an unusually animated look. The flowers, which just now are at their best, were displayed in the camellia house. The plants range from 10ft. to Wt. in height, and some of them contain no fewer than 500 flowers each. There are about 40 different species. Some of the plants are 50 years old, and the collection is said to be one of the finest inEngland. The visitors were also allowed to pass through the plant and fruit houses, the ,condition of which reflects the highest credit upon the head gardener, Mr. Kipps.

div.head: WOMBWELL'S MENAGERIE AT WARRINGTON.
div.p: WOMBWELL'S MENAGERIE AT WARRINGTON.

On Saturday and Monday the people of War- rington had opportunities of seeing Wombwell's famous travelling exhibition, which, broadly speak- ing, is made up of a huge menagerie and a high- class circus. The almost unequalled collection of wild animals, birds, reptiles, &c.,—numbering in all over 500—was dis Played in a large marquee erected in a field at the bottom of ifinmarleigh-street, and once in here the spectator was considerably bewildered by the strange but interesting variety of exhibits that were to be seen. It is unnecessary to enumerate the , wild animals which have been brought together in this well-known show, but among the special sights may be mentioned a man, overgrown with hair, who had been i captured in a condition as wild arid unhuman as the original' state of any of the animals confined in the ad. joining cages. There were some further startling con- trasts of human development to be seen in the giant and the dwarf, and the giantess and her exceedingly small and tiny compeer. Some thrilling performances were given by °rent°, the lion tamer, who entered a veritable "lion's den," armed only with a small'whip, and there put the savage occupants through a variety of evolptions, including jumping. A similar display was given by "She," a female lion-tamer, in another cage. While some of the visitors were interested with the rare collection of wild animals, others were viewing two splendid circus performances which were going on simul- taneously. In the circus arenas there was a constant succession of wonderful equestrian and acrobatic feats, and the amusing "quips and cranks" of clowns. Trained animals were brought into the rings, including a tiger on horseback and numerous and very intelligent and highly-trained monkeys and dogs. Not the least interesting part of the circus programme was the graphic display of lassooing as it is practised on the prairies of the "Wild West" of America, and also some pony and chariot racing. It is scarcely necessary to say that this show is about the best of its kind, and the great number of persons who visited it in Warrington must have been pleased and interested with what they saw. ' It is stated that several snakes, two monkeys, 'and a bear died during the time that the menagerie was in Warrington. STARTLING INCIDENT AT EAR,LESTOWN.

_ On Tuesday WOmbwell's menagerie visited Earlestown, and at night a startling incident was witnessed during the exhibition. Madame Leo, one of the artistes, described as a snake-charmer, had a terribly narrow escape from losing her life. The show was packed with a very large audience, and the lady was going through her performances with several cobras. She put a very large one round her neck, when it suddenly tightened its embrace. The woman finding its toils becoming unpleasantly tight endeavoured to free herself, but not succeed- ing she screamed for help, and immediately fell to the ground. Assistance was quickly rendered, and. the cobra was with difficulty taken from her throat. She was picked up and assisted from the arena, the ringmaster (Mr. Taylaure), after allaying the ex- citement among the audience, explaining that she had a marvellous escape. Enquiries which have been made elicited that the cobra in question was only added to the collection on Monday last, and was of an Indian species.

div.p: SUICIDE OF AN AMERICAN CAPITALIST._

div.head: LATEST NEWS.
div.p: LATEST NEWS.

At the half-yearly meeting on Thursday of the Com- mercial Gas Company (London) the Chairman told the shareholders that they had nothing to fear from electricity. Their great enemy was cheap oil. The disabled Inman and International steamer City of raris entered the Alfred Dock On Thursday forenoon. and most of the crew shortly afterwards left for their homes. It is understood that an official survey to ascer- tain the amount of the damage will be made almost immediately.

div.head: CRIME MURDER.
div.p: THE CRIME MURDER.

On Thursday there was considerable excitement in Crewe owing to a statement that George Davies, the youneer of the two lads under sentence of death, had been respited. A telegram was received from the Home Secretary saying that he could not grant an interview for the production of additional evidence in favour of the brothers. Mr. Pedlev, the solicitor for the defence, yesterday received an intimation from the Home Secre- tary to the effect that he had advised Her Majesty: to commute the sentence on the younger prisoner, George Davies, to penal servitude for life, but in the case of Richard Davies, he saw no reason why the law should not take its course. THE MORFA DISASTER.

The inquiry as to this disaster was resumed on Thurs- day. Nettle, the night fireman, said he found gas in No. 9 working place,and also in Ewan Eley's stall. He some- times saw coal-dust about, but he gave instructions that it should be cleared away. The last time he was in the pit he sent up six corve-loads from three headings. Shots had been fired in the Cribbwr vein for about a month, but he never used dynamite. The doors were blown outward in No. si heading, and he thought the explo.ion originated there. Questioned about the non- working of the fan from Saturday to Monday, he said lc was very difficult to get men to go into the pit on Satur- day and Monday. The inquiry was adjourned until the , 23rd inst.

div.p: MARKETS.

• LIVERPOOL PROVISIONS, THURSDAY.—Beef is generally quiet, but for medium sorts there is a fair inquiry. Pork remains stesdy, the figures being unaltered. The market for Bacon has been quiet to-day, but a relatively fair business has been done at previous prices. In Hams, short cuts meet a steady consumptive demand at full prices, but long cuts rule quietly steady. Shoulders meet a fair demand at the quota- tions. Cheese has a firmer tone, the demand being brisker. Butter moves but slowly. The market remains quiet for Lard and prices rule in buyers' favour. CORE BUTTER, THURSDAY. TrIVENTY THOUSAND ACRES AMERICAN PRO- PERTY FREE. In allotments of Farm, Fruit. and Vineyard Tracts of 46, 20. 10, and 5 acres each, and selected Residence or Business Lots. ONE of the above divisions of Real Estate Pro- perty, located either in the Golden State of fruitful California, sr in the famous Oratigegrove State of Florida, will be unconditionally given free from anyeharge for the land to any respectable person who sends his or her full name and post address to the American Office of the Californian and Southern Land Company at Cincinnati, Ohio, U.S.A. As soon as your name and address ar., received by the Com- pany, a free Land Warrant for one of the allotments of free property will be returned to you by first ocean post. The only cost for the property will be an expense fee for executing a Warranty Transfer Vile Deed in your favour, and having the signatures thereto legally acknowledged before the "'loner officials. Such mcpense will in no case exceed 125., and is not to be paid until after you have received the Free Land War- rant. When one or more members of the same family, or friends, wish to-secure property together, the Company will Issue to any applicant as many Free Land Warrants as may be requested, not to exceed ten, to be given by the applicant to those whom he applies for. The object ill making this extraordinary offer is to secure a diversified interest and ownership throughout the different countries of Europe in the lands owned and controlled by the above-nomed Company. When this is accomplished, the Company will open branch offices in various European Cities, and offer its large remaining properties for sale at a uniform price of £5 per acre for Farm and Fruit Tracts, and £6 per Plot for Residence or Business Lots. It is believed by the Company that the diversified interest that will be thus secured by this preliminary method of advertising will amply compensate for the amount of pro- perty that is now offered FREE. If the number of names sent for free property is in excess of the amount of such property, those whose names are re- ' eeived first will secure it. Hence the advantage of sending name and address at once. All that need be sent is an envelope bearing your name and post address ; this envelope to be enclosed in another and the outer envelope to be addressed as follows.: THE CALIFORNIA AND SOUTHERN LAND CO., CINCINNATI, OHIO, U.S.A. NOTE.--If preferred, application may be made to the Com- pany's Branch Office in London. A penny stamped self- addressed envelope sent to the Company's London Agent, Mr. W. H. FULLER, 8, College Chambers, High Holborn. Lon- don, will secure a FREE LAND WARRANT, issued by the Home Company, the same as if sent direct to the Head Office.

CARDINAL MA NNING'S' EPISCOPAL • JUBILEE. • Sunday, June Bth, will be ,the ," silver jubilee" of Cardinal Manning's episcopaf'conseerittion, and it has been, decided on the first convenient day afterwards to present to. his t minence a personal testimonial. The Duke. of Norfolk, Monsignor Gilbert, and Mr. Alcleiman and Sheriff Knill have the management of the fund, towards which subscriptions have been received from all classes of the community and members of all, religious denominations. The zeal of the Cardinal-Archbishop for improving the dwellings of the poor, promoting educa- tion and temperance, as well as his generous sympathy with the working classes, have made him friends every- where, and contributions have been received from Ireland, France, Germany, India, America, Canada, and' Australia. In the broadest sense' of the word, the re- cognition will be thoroughly "Catholic."
